## #171 — Distribution and Config Direction: GitHub Releases as the APK Channel, Firebase Remote Config Retired (Owner direction 2026-10-17)

**Status:** Direction accepted; implementation deliberately deferred ("a task for another day" — owner). No code or dependency changed under this ADR. It records the direction so later design does not re-litigate it.

**Context.** ADR #10 designed an in-app updater around a signed manifest; the draft `app/plans/app-update-ota-implementation-plan.md` currently specifies a Firestore `releases/latest` manifest with the APK in a Firebase Storage bucket. ADR #56 introduced Firebase Remote Config for a single rollout boolean. The owner has now ruled the distribution direction: **GitHub Releases is the APK update channel for both development and production builds, and Firebase Remote Config is to be removed entirely.**

**Current Remote Config surface (verified 2026-10-17, so the removal is bounded).** Exactly one key is read: `partner_push_registration_enabled`, via `PartnerRolloutGate` (`accountability/sync/PartnerRolloutGate.kt`). Wiring: `AccountabilityModule.providePartnerRolloutGate` (default `true`, 15-min fetch interval); consumers `PartnerSyncWorker` and `PartnerLiveSync`; the gate is injected in `MainActivity`/`MyExodusApp` only to reach those. Dependency: `firebase-config` (`libs.versions.toml`, `app/build.gradle.kts:162`). No other file references `FirebaseRemoteConfig`. The SOS client flag was already removed (ADR #158), which is what left the single key.

**What removal costs.** The only capability lost is "halt push registration without shipping an APK" (plan v2 §13 line 564). With no production install base, the operational need is not real; if a remote kill-switch is ever needed again, the shipped pattern is the server-side Firestore switch read inside the transaction (the SOS `partnerSosEnabled` precedent), not a client config SDK. Removal shape when scheduled: delete `PartnerRolloutGate` + key + provider, replace `pushRegistrationEnabled()` call sites with unconditional behavior (today's default), drop `firebase-config` from the version catalog and build file, update ADR #56 with a supersede note and this document's dependency table.

**What GitHub Releases must preserve from ADR #10.** The trust anchor does not change: the updater verifies a **signed manifest** (signature checked against the pinned release key) and then the APK's **package name, versionCode, and signing-certificate SHA-256** against the installed app before handing it to `PackageInstaller`. GitHub's hosting is a transport, not a trust root — a compromised release asset must fail our own checks. Same-signature in-place update behavior (ADR #10 item 4) is unchanged.

**Feasibility facts to design against (recorded, not yet verified in-app).** GitHub Releases is static HTTPS hosting plus a public REST API; a public repository is required unless a token is embedded in the APK — rejected, an APK is not a secret store. The unauthenticated REST limit is 60 requests/hour per originating IP (cached daily checks fit comfortably; retry storms would not). The API response carries asset download URLs and a GitHub-computed digest, but the digest is only an integrity cross-check — the signed manifest remains authoritative. `browser_download_url` redirects to a CDN; the download client must follow redirects. Android 13+ "install unknown apps" friction and the `REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES` grant row are unchanged from the OTA plan.

**Open decisions for the implementation session (do not decide silently here).** (a) Repository name/visibility and whether dev and production releases are separate tags, a `pre-release` flag, or separate repositories. (b) Manifest format and signing tool (reuse the release-signing runbook, ADR #10; the manifest is a release asset alongside the APK). (c) `minimumSupportedVersionCode` policy — the OTA plan's "required update" rail. (d) Whether the daily check stays a WorkManager job or piggybacks on the existing foreground resume path (the OTA plan specifies both, throttled). (e) What replaces Remote Config's copy/rule-default role, if anything — today nothing else is remote-configured, so the honest default is build-time constants.

**Consequences.** The app's only remote-configuration SDK goes away; every behavior becomes build-time or server-side (Firestore callables), which is fewer moving parts and one fewer GMS-dependent fetch on the pairing rail. Distribution becomes a public artifact channel, which also makes beta/dev APKs shareable without Firebase App Distribution's tester-sign-in friction. The project gains a real dependency on GitHub availability for the update check only — the app must remain fully functional offline and when the API is unreachable (OTA plan UN5, unchanged).

**Revision 2026-11-06 — implemented.** The updater ships; implementation contract, states and release runbook: `app/docs/app-update-channel.md`. The five open decisions resolve as follows. (a) Repository: the existing public `github.com/Musila-ke/MyExodus`, stable asset URL `https://github.com/Musila-ke/MyExodus/releases/latest/download/<asset>` — no REST call, so the 60/h/IP `api.github.com` quota is never in play; "latest" excludes prereleases and drafts, so a prerelease is never offered. (b) Manifest: a detached-style JSON envelope `{"payload": base64(JSON), "signature": base64(DER ECDSA P-256 SHA-256)}` signed by an offline channel key pinned in `UpdateConfig.MANIFEST_PUBLIC_KEY_BASE64`; `scripts/update-manifest-sign.sh` produces it, `openssl dgst -sha256 -sign` interoperates with the app's `SHA256withECDSA` verifier (cross-checked 2026-11-06: an openssl-signed dummy manifest verified under the pinned key in a plain JVM). The channel key is separate from the release APK signing key. (c) `minSupportedVersionCode` is parsed, bounded and stored but the install rail does not yet force an update from it; the app only ever offers strictly newer versions. (d) WorkManager 24 h periodic with a CONNECTED constraint, enqueued post-unlock in `MyExodusApp` only when the channel key is configured, plus a manual check from Settings. No background download: the daily job only fetches and verifies the manifest; the APK downloads after the user taps Download and install. (e) Nothing replaces Remote Config's copy role — build-time constants, as recorded above.
Verification contract shipped as designed: manifest signature → versionCode monotonicity → APK SHA-256 → package name → archive versionCode → APK signing-certificate set equal to the installed app's, then `PackageInstaller` MODE_FULL_INSTALL. The status `PendingIntent` is mutable on API 31+ (targetSdk 35+ rejects immutable). Install feedback is reconciled on launch because the status broadcast is best-effort. 28 JVM/Robolectric tests cover manifest validation, checker responses (loopback HTTP), launch/upgrade bookkeeping and status mapping.
**Still owner-gated (blocking a real release, not the code):** no release APK keystore exists, so no installable release can be published yet; test APKs that are debug-signed cannot later be updated in place by a release-signed build (signer mismatch is enforced), and `allowBackup=false` makes uninstall destructive. The channel private key at `~/.myexodus-update-key/update-manifest-key.pem` must be backed up by the owner; losing it strands installed builds because the pinned public key cannot be rotated remotely. The live manifest URL currently returns 404, which the app surfaces as NO_RELEASE.

**Revision 2026-11-06 (later the same day), plan v1.1 supersedes the revision above.** The owner supplied `app/plans/direct-apk-self-updater-plan.md` v1.1 and the v1 channel was reconciled to it. What changed: the update channel is a **dedicated public releases-only repository**, not `github.com/Musila-ke/MyExodus`, supplied at build time through `-Pmyexodus.updateRepository=owner/repo` (`BuildConfig.UPDATE_RELEASE_REPOSITORY`, empty means fail closed); artifacts are immutable prereleases tagged `artifact-v<versionCode>` and policies are immutable `policy-<sequence>` releases explicitly designated latest, containing only `update-manifest.json`; the envelope is `{format, keyId, payloadBase64, signatureBase64}` with a signed **release policy** (monotonic `policySequence`, `OFFER`/`HALT`, `rolloutPercent`, `cohortSalt`, version-pinned `apkUrl`) rather than a bare APK pointer; cohort eligibility uses a local 128-bit ID plus the signed salt; floors reject `POLICY_ROLLBACK` and `POLICY_CONFLICT`; the client performs no signing-certificate equality check (Android PackageManager decides lineage); the install path re-fetches a fresh signed policy immediately before the first commit, stages with a dual hash and `session.fsync(out)`, and maps `EXTRA_DEVELOPER_VERIFICATION_FAILURE_REASON` where present. `minSupportedVersionCode` is gone. The v1 files `UpdateManifest.kt`, `ApkDownloader.kt`, `UpdateManifestTest.kt` and `UpdateCheckerTest.kt` were deleted. The implementation contract and PASSED/BLOCKED evidence are in `app/docs/app-update-channel.md`; `updater-research-2026-11-06.md` is retained only as research history. The releases-only repository does not exist yet (HTTP 404), and release APK signing remains owner-gated.

**Revision 2026-11-06 (owner-approved awareness and auto-download change).** Owner ask: the app should "just know" there is an update and inform the user without requiring a manual Settings check, and may download automatically once told to, while still asking before installing. Plan v1.1 was revised accordingly (§1 revision block, R01/R06, §7 steps 5–6, §8.7, §17). Shipped: a neutral `update_availability` channel with an "Update available" post (background checks only, once per offered `versionCode`), one in-app prompt per offered version on app open, an "Update ready to install" post after the expedited verify worker reaches `READY_TO_INSTALL`, and a Settings switch for standing auto-download (default off; connected, unmetered, non-roaming only). A notification tap routes through `EXTRA_OPEN_UPDATE` to the Settings tab and opens the existing update dialog; install remains a per-install user confirmation and keeps the fresh-policy pre-commit gate. Implementation contract and evidence: `app/docs/app-update-channel.md` §4–§9, §14. JVM-verified: compile, the updater suites plus `UpdateAutoDownloadTest` (consent/offer/network truth table) and store-persistence tests. Hardware legs for the notification/auto-download paths remain BLOCKED with the rest of the owner-gated release channel.

**Revision 2026-11-07 — debug-signed N to N+1 rehearsal on hardware, and the upgrade crash it caught.** The owner asked for a simple on-device update rehearsal (change a string, ship it, revert it) and for the revert semantics. On the physical X6532, canonical versionCode 2 was replaced in place with a debug-signed versionCode 5 build whose Settings title was deliberately changed: install `Success`, UI showed the new title and the one-time post-upgrade notice, and account, streak, rules and protection state all survived. The first launch attempt on the pre-fix build crashed on every start with `ClassCastException: Integer cannot be cast to Long` in `UpdateStateStore.recordLaunch`: builds before the updater rework stored `last_seen_version_code` with `putInt`, and the rewritten store read it with `getLong`. `recordLaunch` now accepts either encoding and still writes Long; `UpdateStateStoreTest.upgradeLaunchReadsTheLegacyIntEncodingWithoutCrashing` pins it, and the fixed build's upgrade notice (2 to 5) proved the legacy value was read. Downgrade semantics were proven too: `adb install` of versionCode 4 over 5 was refused with `INSTALL_FAILED_VERSION_DOWNGRADE` and left the install untouched; the canonical debug APK rolled back only with `adb install -r -d`, after which package state read versionCode 2 / `1.1` and every data store was intact. Consequence for releases: a bad release is recovered by fix-forward (higher versionCode, same signing key) plus a signed HALT; an ordinary user cannot downgrade without uninstalling, and uninstalling destroys the encrypted local state (`allowBackup=false`). Evidence: `app/docs/app-update-channel.md` §14; screenshots retained outside the repository because they show live account data.

## #172 — Website Daily-Limit Enforcement in the Browser URL Path + FR3 Threshold Warnings (device-caught 2026-10-17)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented and device-verified 2026-10-17.

**Context.** A 30-minute daily limit on instagram.com reached 30/30 in the app while the user was browsing it in Chrome; no warning appeared and the site kept loading. Two independent defects, both proven on the X6532:

- **The URL-bar path never evaluated the quota.** `BrowserUrlScanner` called `BlockDecisionEngine.decideUrl(canonical, System.currentTimeMillis())` with no `usageTodayMs`; the engine's quota branch is evaluated only when that input is provided. The URL path could enforce always-on, schedules and expiry — not the daily limit. Old build (PID 28881): `url scan gen=128 'instagram.com' -> Allow` at 20:10:13–20:10:26, *after* the 20:09:26 exhaustion (`dns_nxdomain_served` 0→313, `flow_resets_sweep` 0→12). The VPN path did enforce — the attributable flows were reset and DNS served NXDOMAIN — but Chrome's DoH/ECH traffic was unattributed (`sni_ech` 169→284, `flows_unattributed` 418→626 across the same window) and therefore unswept. That is the documented D-18/S-12/R-7/INV-8 limit, not a new leak; the URL path does not depend on attribution.
- **No website-limit warning existed.** FR3's thresholds lived only in the package-keyed `UsageAccountingEngine`; the domain ledger had no crossing concept at all.

**Decision.** (1) `BrowserUrlScanner` takes `usageTodayMs: (ruleId) -> Long?`; `BlockerAccessibilityService` injects `DomainUsageEngine.usageTodayMs`, and the scanner feeds the matched rule's total into `decideUrl`. Null (metering not attached) fails open — never a block on missing data. (2) `UsageLedger.takeLimitWarnings()` computes crossings with `UsageAccountingEngine.calculateWarningThresholdsMs` (one policy definition). Flags live on `RuleCounter`, are seeded from the persisted total on attach (a restart never replays a crossed threshold), re-seeded when the limit changes (raising re-arms above the current total; lowering never fires retroactively), reset at day rollover, and only the current revision can warn. The tick loop's new `onTick` hook posts through `DomainUsageHost.postWebsiteLimitWarning`, which `AndroidDomainUsageHost` renders as notification id 3 on the existing `domain_usage_status` channel with INV-7-safe copy (no site name; superseded in part 2026-10-18 by ADR #179 — the warning now names the rule's own site). No metering, attribution, DNS or relay code changed.

**Evidence (X6532, 2026-10-17).** Rules screen before the fix: `instagram.com — 30m daily limit — Used today: 30 / 30 min` (a quota rule, not always-on). New build (PID 17636): Chrome `url scan gen=3 'instagram.com' -> Block` at 21:01:24–21:02:00 with the `UrlBlocked` overlay on screen; Brave `gen=6 'instagram.com' -> Block` at 21:02:39–21:02:45 with the same overlay — usage is per domain, so every discovered browser consults the same exhausted counter. Warning leg: limit temporarily raised to 41m, usage 30→32 min, notification id=3 posted — title "Website limit almost used up", text "9 min left on a website limit today. Tap to review your rules." (no hostname), then the rule was restored to 30m. Internet sanity after the change: example.com rendered through the VPN (`url scan 'example.com' -> Allow`) and the VPN counters kept advancing.

**The 27→30 move is not an accounting defect.** `RulesScreen` displays `usedMs / 60_000` (whole minutes floored, `RulesScreen.kt:692`), and `RuleCounter.recompute` books one interval per tick from `max(lastAccountedElapsed, sessionStart)` to at most `now` (monotonic), so accrual is provably ≤ wall time; `RuleCounterTest` (doubled ticks), `UsageLedgerTest.eightOverlappingFlowsOnOneRuleCountOnce` and the idle-tail test pin the no-double-count and no-overcount properties. A +3 displayed-minute jump therefore required at least 2:01 of real accrual; domain metering spans every app's connections to the site (background/keep-alive flows included) plus the 15 s idle tail. (Revision 2026-10-19: the metering scope is now browser-owned flows only — ADR #189; this paragraph records the behavior at the time of the 2026-10-17 audit.) The exact per-flow source cannot be reconstructed after the fact — per-rule totals are not logged and INV-7 forbids hostnames in logs — so this is recorded as unproven detail, not as a second bug.

**Verified (JVM).** Full suite **1780 tests / 0 failures / 0 errors / 0 skipped** (was 1,772; +8 regressions): `BrowserUrlScannerTest` gains exhausted/under-limit/unavailable-usage and cross-browser (Chrome, Brave, Firefox) blocking cases; `UsageLedgerTest` gains once-per-threshold, seeded-total (no restart replay), limit-change (re-arm/never retroactive) and superseded-revision cases.

**Consequences / honest limits.** (a) The URL path is now the quota backstop when attribution fails, but it requires the accessibility service and a discovered toolbar ID; a browser using an unknown ID, or an in-app WebView, remains unenforced (the probe list is plan §16's ongoing maintenance surface). (b) Warnings are notifications only — no in-app overlay, matching the app-usage warning surface. (c) ECH/DoH flows remain unattributed by design; the URL decision closes the enforcement gap those flows opened, but usage they carry with no navigation change is still invisible to the ledger. (d) The Block overlay dismisses on the next Allow scan, so a user who edits the limit upward unblocks on the next address-bar change (device-confirmed during the warning leg).

## #173 — Widget v3: One Desert Dawn Surface, One Type Lockup, One Control Grammar (owner report 2026-10-17)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; device-captured 2026-10-17. Supersedes the visual layer of #161/#166 — the actions themselves (urge, relapse bound by `habitId`, reach-out, hold confirm) are unchanged.

**Context.** Owner report: "its incredibly ugly and inconsistent mostly the color". v2.1/v2.2 had the right privacy model (icon-only circles, no launcher text) but no shared visual system: the default Glance background read as a muddy near-black slab in dark mode and a glaring white sheet in light, the day count had no consistent type treatment across variants, and each control was styled where it was drawn. An inspiration folder supplied widget references; the component-reverse-engineering pass extracted the composition (surface, hairline, stat lockup, single control row), not any literal content.

**Decision.** (1) **Canvas** — `DesertDawnGlanceColors` overrides only `background` to `ContainerLowLight`/`ContainerLowDark`; the card must read as a raised warm surface over arbitrary wallpaper. All other roles stay Material 3 defaults so they resolve against the app's own schemes. (2) **Hairline** — Glance 1.1.1's theme contract predates M3 `outlineVariant`, so `HairlineColor` is a day/night `ColorProvider` over `OutlineVariantLight/Dark`; it draws the card hairline and the milestone track instead of overloading the much stronger `outline`. (3) **DayLockup** — one stat treatment everywhere: uppercase 9 sp gold micro-label over the ink numeral, with the numeral sized to the cell (Compact 28 sp, Narrow 30 sp, Expanded 38 sp, Tall 44 sp). (4) **Status** — `StatusChip` and the compact status word use semantic containers (`primaryContainer` / `errorContainer` / `secondaryContainer`). (5) **Controls** — one icon-only `ControlRow` across variants (36 dp circles, 28 dp in Narrow, 8/5 dp gaps); tonal fill is `secondaryContainer` (`surfaceVariant` vanished against the new canvas) and reach-out is `primary`. Narrow's text action is removed; no launcher action text remains. (6) **Layout** — `Scaffold(horizontalPadding = 0.dp)` plus per-variant insets, because Scaffold's default 12 dp per side cost roughly a quarter of the 2×1 cell's width; the tall footer is caption left / controls right over one weighted spacer.

**Evidence (X6532, 2026-10-17).** Captured dark and light, discreet and non-discreet, in Narrow and Compact cells; the widget preview PNG was replaced with the real render; device state restored afterwards. Existing `WidgetContentTest`, `WidgetSnapshotTest`, `DisplayedStatusTest` and `ProtectionSnapshotWriterTest` remain green — the redesign changed presentation only, no snapshot or action state.

**Verified (JVM).** Full suite **204 classes / 1783 tests / 0 failures / 0 errors / 0 skipped**, BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 12m38s.

**Alternatives considered.** Keep the default Glance/Material background (rejected — the dark/light reads above are the reported defect); style each variant independently (rejected — that inconsistency is exactly what the owner flagged); use `outline` for the hairline (rejected — too strong a line for a card edge and progress track).

**Consequences / honest limits.** (a) EXPANDED still matches no tested launcher cell (unchanged from #87) — its layout is code-reviewed, not device-captured. (b) Captures come from the X6532 launcher only; cell dimensions vary by launcher and OEM. (c) No motion/animation is introduced. (d) The Glance 10-children-per-container RemoteViews cap (#161) is untouched and still binds every band.

## #174 — Autocomplete Previews Are Not Navigations: Address-Bar Focus Defers the URL Scan (owner report 2026-10-17)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented and device-verified 2026-10-17.

**Context.** Owner report, verbatim: "it checks as you type and blocks sure but what if i want to go to instgram video downloader but my app sees instagram.com cause of auto complete then blocks me over and over and over". Root cause proven on the X6532: Chrome's omnibox writes the top suggestion into the **same `url_bar` node** `BrowserUrlScanner` reads, so while the user typed `insta` the bar's text was `instagram.com` and `decideUrl` blocked a site that had never loaded. Re-firing on each debounced content change produced the repeated blocks. The text alone cannot distinguish a preview from a commit.

**First attempt, falsified.** Gating on IME visibility via `AccessibilityWindowInfo.isVisible` failed on device with `NoSuchMethodException`: the method does not exist on the API 34 runtime, nor in the android-36/36.1/37.0 stubs. It was never a stub trim; the false claim in #36 is corrected there and in memory.

**Decision.** The platform seam is now `extractUrlField(root, viewId): UrlField?` where `UrlField(text, focused)`. The platform implementation reads `node.isFocused` on the matched address-bar node **at fire time** (not event time), so a commit that lands inside the 300 ms debounce still decides on that scan. While `focused == true`, the scanner returns before any decision — not even `Allow`, which would dismiss a still-blocked page's overlay. The decision log records `focused=` for future diagnosis. Focus is read through `runCatching { node.isFocused }.getOrDefault(false)`: a node/browser that never reports focus scans exactly as before, so this gate can only suppress a false block, never create a false allow. `BlockerAccessibilityService`'s IME seam (`isImeVisible`/`isVisibleCompat`/`isVisibleDetail`) is deleted.

**Evidence (X6532, 2026-10-17; debug PID 922).** Chrome `about:blank` → `focused=false 'about:blank' -> Allow`. Typing `insta` (bar autocompleted to `instagram.com`, uiautomator dump `focused="true"`) → `url scan deferred: address bar edit session active` ×3, screenshot shows suggestions plus keyboard and **no overlay**. Enter → `gen=1 focused=false 'instagram.com' -> Block` ×2 with the "instagram.com is blocked" overlay. "Go to a different site" → typed `instagram video downloader` → `google.com/search?q=… -> Allow` ×2 with results rendered. `example.com` → Allow and rendered. Brave: committed `instagram.com` → `focused=false … -> Block` ×4; typing `insta` → `url scan deferred` ×2. Only Chrome and Brave are installed on the device — Edge/Firefox/Opera are **not** claimed. Device restored (backgrounded, keyboard down, no overlay).

**Verified (JVM).** `BrowserUrlScannerTest` 24/24, including three new regressions: `editing_autocompletePreview_defersTheScan`, `editing_commitAfterEditing_blocksNormally`, and `editing_evaluatedAtFireTime_notEventTime` (a commit inside the debounce window still decides). Full suite **204 classes / 1783 tests / 0 failures / 0 errors / 0 skipped** (was 1,780 at #172; +3), BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 12m38s.

**Consequences / honest limits.** (a) The gate trusts the browser to report `AccessibilityNodeInfo.isFocused` on its address-bar node; every discovered browser that does not report focus falls back to the pre-gate behavior (fail-open — can only suppress a false block). (b) A navigation that somehow loads while the bar still owns focus is skipped until the next content change; the proven browser behavior is that a commit moves focus, reloads the page, and schedules a fresh scan. (c) In-app WebViews and browsers with undiscovered toolbar IDs were already outside the scan's coverage (#172 limit a) and remain so.

## #175 — The Relay Now Obeys the Device's Receive Window: Send-Side Flow Control, Retransmission, and Zero-Window Probing (owner report 2026-10-18)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented. JVM-verified; device leg recorded below.

**Context.** Owner report, verbatim: *"the vpn is making my downloads slow very slow in my browser and heck i tried downloading a whatsapp video it hang for a while then stayed at 53 for longer and its a small sized video then i turn off the vpn then it jumps to 83 and finishes in a short period of time"*. The userspace relay forwards device → upstream but synthesizes the upstream → device side of every TCP flow itself. It tracked no send window, buffered nothing, retransmitted nothing: whatever it read from the upstream `Socket` it wrapped into TUN packets immediately.

**Root cause, device-proven (X6532, debug build).** With the device's reader deliberately paused 8 s mid-download (`kill -STOP` on an `nc` fetching 10,485,760 bytes from cachefly through the tunnel), the relay forwarded 10,486,319 bytes in 1.887 s. The device's cumulative ACK then froze at **1575222470 with window 0** while the first data sequence was **1568727470** — the kernel had accepted exactly **6,495,000 bytes** and advertised zero. Over the pause the device sent **3,327 zero-window ACKs**; the relay ignored every one and wrote **3,991,319 more bytes past the window** (final `seq + len` 1579213789 − ack 1575222470). Linux discards out-of-window data and answers each with a duplicate ACK (`tcp_validate_incoming`/`tcp_send_dupack`); with no retransmission on the relay side, the transfer sat wedged forever — `nc` alive in `do_sys_poll`, file frozen at exactly the 6,495,000 bytes the kernel had accepted. Turning the tunnel off carried the flow over the normal network stack, which is why it completed. The same defect slows every ordinary download: any device-side pause (app not reading its socket, browser backpressure) permanently drains the relay's in-flight budget until the window closes, after which only timeouts and a new connection recover.

**Decision.**
1. **`vpn/TcpSendWindow.kt` (new, pure JVM-testable).** RFC 793 §3.3/§3.4 send-side accounting: SND.UNA / SND.WND, an in-flight segment queue, and the §3.4 SND.WL1/SND.WL2 rule so a stale out-of-order segment cannot shrink the window (a 16-bit field; RFC 7323 window scaling is not negotiated — the SYN-ACK carries no options, so the advertised field is the window). §3.7 retransmission of the oldest unacknowledged segment on an RTO that starts at 1 s and doubles to 8 s; RFC 1122 §4.2.2.17 zero-window probing with one tracked probe byte when nothing else is in flight. ACK progress resets the RTO and reopens the window. `onAck` runs on the TUN pump thread; reserve/probe/retransmit run on the flow's relay thread; the lock covers bookkeeping only — packet building and TUN writes happen outside it.
2. **The relay loop paces itself.** Upstream reads are bounded by `SO_TIMEOUT` (1 s), so a paused device can never park the relay thread on a full TUN queue. Every new send reserves room first; when the window is full the loop serves due retransmissions and probes rather than writing. Before FIN, the unacknowledged tail is drained (bounded 2 s) so the last bytes are delivered and acknowledged before the flow closes.
3. **Per-packet logging deleted.** The old hot path logged every forwarded packet (16,905 log lines during the single 10 MB test), which both costs relay CPU and buries real signal.
4. **Sequence space.** `TcpFlow.seqToDevice` is now `sendWindow.nextSeq`; the flow is constructed with `tcp.seq + 1` as the first data sequence and the device's advertised window from the triggering segment.

**Bug found in this fix's own first cut.** `reserveSend` called `lock.wait(waitMs)` unconditionally; a caller passing `waitMs = 0` ("do not block") parks the thread forever because `Object.wait(0)` waits indefinitely. Caught by the new unit tests hanging, not by inspection. Now the wait happens only for `waitMs > 0`; zero means a non-blocking check.

**Verified (JVM).** `TcpSendWindowTest` 6/6: window-limited sends and the per-segment cap; ACK advancing SND.UNA and reopening the window; impossible and duplicate ACKs leaving bookkeeping intact; RTO firing at 1 s then 2 s with ACK-progress reset; the zero-window probe as one tracked byte; a stale segment not shrinking the window. Full suite result is recorded with the final build below.

**Device verification (X6532, debug build installed 2026-10-18 12:24).** Endpoint `http://speedtest.tele2.net/10MB.zip`, advertised `Content-Length: 10,485,760` (a HEAD request measured the response header at exactly 240 bytes). The reader was paused 5 s into the transfer with `kill -STOP` on the `nc` process: the file held at exactly **1,243,200 bytes for the full 8 s pause** — the relay wrote nothing past the device's zero window, the precise behavior whose absence caused the pre-fix freeze. `kill -CONT` resumed the flow; `nc` exited on its own when the server closed, and the file measured **10,486,000 bytes = 240-byte header + 10,485,760-byte body**, an exact Content-Length match. A clean unpaused run of the same file completed in ~40 s (~262 KB/s on the test WiFi), and the first 5 s of the paused run moved at the same ~250 KB/s — the pacing change costs no first-pass throughput. Full JVM suite after the final edits: **1,792 tests, 0 failures** (`:app:testDebugUnitTest`, BUILD SUCCESSFUL).

**Consequences / honest limits.** (a) The relay implements go-back-N retransmission from the oldest unacknowledged segment, not SACK (no SACK was negotiated) and not congestion control — the tunnel is a local relay, not a general-purpose TCP endpoint, and the upstream leg is a real kernel `Socket` with its own congestion control. (b) RTO is a fixed 1 s → 8 s backoff, not an RTT-estimated timer (no Karn/RTT sampling); adequate for a local synthetic endpoint, revisited if the device leg shows premature retransmission. (c) The receive-side (device → upstream) path already used the kernel's `Socket`, so it needed no equivalent fix. (d) Window scaling is absent by construction; adding it would require SYN-ACK option generation, not needed while the 16-bit window is what the device offers on this tunnel MTU.

## #176 — One Day Scale Everywhere: Completed Days Floored at 1, With a Countdown That Adds Up (owner report 2026-10-18)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented and JVM-verified.

**Context.** Owner report, verbatim: *"we need a way to slow down but remain ie how we say we nevere show the user even if they relapse day 0 but logically and ux wise we cant confuse a user saying day 3 7 day mark in 5 days bro total is 8 we cant do that we need to solve this too."* After #128 (ordinal display, never 0) and #169 (rung copy as an amount), two scales coexisted: the rendered day was `completed + 1`, while the countdown was `milestone − completed`. Any truthful pairing therefore summed to the milestone **plus one** — at 2 completed days the hero read "3" and the caption read "5 days to the 7-day mark": 3 + 5 = 8. #169 fixed the rung's noun but could not fix an arithmetic contradiction produced by the display scale itself.

**Decision — the displayed day is the completed-day count, floored at 1.**
1. `daysFree(elapsed) = max(1, habitDays(elapsed))`: every user-facing count (Home hero, Streaks summary and relapse card, "Day N of 90", best run, widget) renders completed whole days, with 1 as the floor so a fresh or just-relapsed streak never reads 0 (#128's ruling preserved at its only value).
2. `daysUntil = milestone − daysFree`. From the first completed day onward both numbers are exact and **always sum to the rung**; at the crossing the "One week free" card fires with the hero reading 7, not 8. During the first 24 hours the floor makes the countdown one day less than the calendar clock (display 1, six days to the 7-day rung, milestone fires after seven). That is the one fiction the never-0 ruling forces, and it is the smallest possible: it disappears the moment day one completes, whereas the ordinal scale's mismatch existed on every day.
3. **One computation, every surface.** `HabitRepository.currentDay` (and therefore the widget snapshot), `PartnerActivityJournal.daysFree`, and `PartnerSyncCoordinator`'s aggregate all use the same floored completed count. The widget's two `(days − 1)` conversions (ADR #128's ordinal read-back) are deleted — `streakDays` now means exactly what the rung math needs.
4. **The relapse note uses true completed days**, not the floored display: "you showed up N days in a row" must not claim a day the user had not finished, so a same-day relapse gets the "Every run starts somewhere" line instead of a claimed day.
5. **Partner surfaces keep the same displayed count, not 0.** The floor is a product convention visible to the user; the partner's card showing 0 while the user's own card shows 1 would be the same cross-surface disagreement #128/#169 and the widget-snapshot reuse were built to prevent. A profile with no streak at all still reports 0.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Keep the ordinal day and shorten the countdown to display units* (`milestone − ordinal + 1`): 3 + 4 = 7 on screen, but then the rung fires a day after the countdown reaches 0 — trading a visible arithmetic contradiction for a wrong claim about when the milestone happens. (b) *Keep the ordinal and show the truthful countdown*: this is the reported bug. (c) *Drop the floor and show 0 on the relapse day*: explicitly rejected by the owner in #128. (d) *Days-since-start calendar dates*: contradicts Decision 17 (24-hour units, no calendar math).

**Verified (JVM).** `StreaksPresentationTest`: `daysFree_isCompletedDays_flooredAtOne` (0, <24 h → 1; 1 day → 1; 2 days → 2; 3.5 days → 3) and `dayCountPlusCountdown_alwaysEqualsTheMilestone` (the owner's exact case pinned: seven elapsed samples all satisfy `daysFree + daysUntil == 7`; 0 at the crossed rung). `daysUntil` now reads 6 at a fresh streak and still 27/0 in the existing cases. `HabitRepositoryTest` (5 completed → 5; one completed → 1 and its STREAK_UPDATED row → 1; fresh relapse → 1), `PartnerActivityJournalTest` (7 completed → 7; 3 completed → 3). Full-suite result recorded with the final build.

**Consequences / honest limits.** (a) A widget snapshot or partner projection persisted by a pre-#176 build carries an ordinal `streakDays`; for at most one update window after the upgrade the widget can read one day high until the writer republishes. No migration: the snapshot is a cache, the writer re-reads on the next publish (30-minute backstop at worst). (b) The day-0 floor means the first-24-hours countdown understates the calendar wait by one day — stated above as the deliberate cost of never showing 0. (c) The rung distance still renders as "%d days away" (no singular form) and #169's copy fix is unchanged; pluralization at exactly 1 day is a pre-existing copy nit, not part of this ruling.

## #177 — The App-Block Cover Is Bounded by the Display Until Its App Is Actually Foreground (owner report 2026-10-18)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented, JVM-verified, device-proven.

**Context.** Owner report, verbatim: *"sometimes lets say i open instagram block screen appears but the wrong size or it apers the right size but when i click close its changes to the wrong size or is it 2 block screens but on rare occasions but it still happens"*. Reproduced on the X6532 on 2026-10-18 with the Instagram rule enabled: the accessibility cover window measured `(0,80)(480x1440)` while the display's bar-free bounds were `(0,80)(720x1440)` — the card occupied one third of the width, first over the blocked app and then over the launcher.

**Root cause, device-proven.** The accessibility service's restricted-window pass re-bounds the freshly shown cover to the blocked app's window rect. XOS animates window *bounds* (not just the surface) during a task switch, so after the app was evicted its window was still listed at its exit-animation rect (480x1440). The cover was re-bounded to that stale rect. The `settleCover` re-sampler should have corrected it, but its liveness guard was the state generation: the launcher's Allow decision advanced the generation ~400 ms after the eviction (log: decide Block gen=1 at 05.089, cover shown 05.725, evictions 06.044/06.173, launcher Allow gen=2 at 06.504), the guard ended the loop, and the 480-wide rect froze permanently. The same mechanism explains the "2 block screens" observation: the a11y cover plus the durable BlockerActivity, each with its own bounds history.

**Decision.**
1. **Foreground-gated target.** Pure `coverTarget(foreground, windowBounds, displayBounds)`: the app's window rect is the cover target only while that app is the active foreground package (`rootInActiveWindow.packageName`); otherwise the display's bar-free bounds. A non-foreground window rect is never a target — an evicted app's exit-animation rect cannot capture the card, and an empty window list falls back to the display.
2. **Scene-based liveness.** `settleCover` continues while the overlay's current scene is still `AppBlocked(packageName)` — not while a generation matches. The generation guard was the bug when an unrelated decision (the launcher's Allow) advanced it mid-settle. Re-shows use `stateMachine.currentGeneration`; a block→block `show()` only re-bounds, so the scene check is the authority.
3. **Bounded sampling unchanged.** Six attempts at 700 ms; two consecutive equal foreground samples stop early.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Sample longer*: the stale rect is not a sampling-duration problem — after eviction it is the wrong candidate forever, so longer sampling still freezes it. (b) *Always use display bounds*: loses the pane-accurate cover in split-screen, where an app's window legitimately occupies one pane. (c) *Keep the generation guard and also re-show on generation change*: a generation change says nothing about which window is real; the foreground package does.

**Verified (JVM).** `BlockerAccessibilityServiceConstructionTest` 4/4, including three new cases: the pane rect is kept while foreground; the exit-animation rect is ignored once evicted (display bounds returned); a momentarily empty window list falls back to the display in both foreground states.

**Device verification (X6532, 2026-10-18).** Re-ran the exact pre-fix sequence (decide Block gen=1 → evictions → launcher Allow gen=2). Overlay window attrs ended at `(0,80)(720x1440)` instead of `(0,80)(480x1440)`; the screenshot shows the full-width card, and Close still dismisses it.

**Consequences / honest limits.** (a) If the platform briefly reports the wrong active-window package, the cover stays at display bounds — the safe failure is a full-screen card, never a partial one. (b) A window resized after the six-attempt window (4.2 s) keeps the last sampled bounds; no device evidence of that case. (c) This fixes the a11y cover only; BlockerActivity is full-screen by construction.

## #178 — Same-Millisecond Attempt Rows Get a Stable Order (test-caught 2026-10-18)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; full suite green.

**Context.** `AttemptLogTest.pendingEventCreation_returnsUnlinkedOldestFirst` failed on 2026-10-18: expected `com.b`, got `com.a`. Both `recordBlocked` calls landed in the same millisecond, and `recent()` ordered only by `occurred_at_epoch_millis DESC`; with a tie, which row sat at index 1 was undefined, so the test linked the wrong row. `pendingEventCreation` had the same exposure for its "oldest first" delivery order.

**Decision.** Add the autoincrement primary key as the tie-breaker: `recent` → `ORDER BY occurred_at_epoch_millis DESC, id DESC`; `pendingEventCreation` → `ORDER BY occurred_at_epoch_millis ASC, id ASC`. Insertion order is the only meaningful secondary key, and `id` is its exact record.

**Verified.** Focused `AttemptLogTest` green; full suite **1,792 tests, 0 failures** (BUILD SUCCESSFUL). No schema change; rows in different milliseconds are unaffected.

## #179 — Website-Limit Warnings Name the Rule's Site (owner report 2026-10-18)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; JVM suite green; device leg PASS on the X6532 (2026-10-18 14:56 EAT) — see below.

**Context.** With one rule (`instagram.com`, 30 min/day), warning notification id 3 read "9 min left on a website limit today. Tap to review your rules." — no site name. ADR #172 chose that copy to satisfy domain-usage INV-7 ("Hostnames, IPs, DNS names never appear in logs, exceptions, notifications, or storage"). The owner rejected that tradeoff explicitly: "It's supposed to specify for what website."

**Decision.** Amend INV-7's **notification** clause only, on explicit owner direction (2026-10-18); logs, exceptions and storage keep the invariant unchanged — the usage ledger still persists `(rule_id, revision, day_key, active_ms)` and never a hostname. `RuleCounter` now carries the rule's normalized `pattern` (a pattern can only change with a new revision, D-32, so the value is always the current one); `LimitWarning` carries it through `takeLimitWarnings()` → `DomainUsageHost.postWebsiteLimitWarning(level, remainingMs, pattern)` → the notification: "%1$s: %2$d min left today. Tap to review your rules." The notification is `VISIBILITY_PRIVATE`, so a secure lock screen conceals the text (a user who has enabled "show all notification content" on the lock screen can still see it). `RuleEditor`'s scope notice now also states that metering spans every app on the device, including the site's own app — the fact behind the owner's "I haven't touched Instagram" reading while the Instagram app had been foreground for ~20 minutes that day (usage stats, 2026-10-18). (Revision 2026-10-19: the scope-notice sentence is superseded by ADR #189 — website metering is browser-only and the notice was rewritten accordingly.)

**Verified (JVM, 2026-10-18).** `domainusage` package: **257 tests, 0 failures/errors/skips** (test-result XMLs at 14:21); full suite **205 classes / 1,792 tests / 0 failures / 0 errors / 0 skipped** (XML results at 14:26). `UsageLedgerTest` assertions now pin the pattern on each crossing (level 1, level 2, seeded-restart, re-armed limit). APK build `assembleDebug` succeeds.

**Verified (device, X6532, 2026-10-18).** Debug APK installed with `install -r` over the existing app; the on-device binary matched the built APK byte-for-byte (SHA-256 `8b18fb1a…64aa5`). First attempt was blocked mid-session: the phone left the network (`adb connect` → "Host is down", ping 100 % loss). On reconnect the rule (`instagram.com`, 30 min) was first moved to 25 min while today's metered total was ~21 min — that edit fired nothing, correctly: thresholds for limits ≥ 10 min are `limit − 10` and `limit − 5`, both already below the total, and `seedWarnings` marks crossed thresholds as already fired so a lowered limit cannot warn retroactively. The rule was then restored to 30 min (threshold 2 = 25 min stays armed), which also restored the original device state. Instagram was driven to `Used today: 25 / 30 min`; notification **id 3** posted at `when=1792324576827` (14:56:16.827 EAT) on channel `domain_usage_status` with `vis=PRIVATE`: title "Website limit almost used up", text **"instagram.com: 4 min left today. Tap to review your rules."** The remaining-minute display floors (crossing 25.0 min leaves 4.99 min → "4 min"), consistent with ADR #172. Final state: rule at its original 30 m, usage genuine at 25/30, VPN `VALIDATED` over Wi-Fi, enforcement FGS up.

**Consequences.** The name shown is the owner's own configured rule on the owner's own device — the previous copy hid information the user already saw on the Rules screen. Devices that redact private notifications keep the generic title. No metering, attribution, relay or storage change.

## #180 — R-03 Tracks the Sweep's Success Series, So Recovery Closes the Incident (owner report 2026-10-18)

**Status:** Accepted; applied to the live policy and read back.

**Context.** The owner received a "no retryDispatchSweep execution for 30 minutes" warning on 2026-10-18 (~14:10 EAT), a day after the 2026-10-17 billing outage was fixed, and asked what the issue was now. Evidence: it was the **close** of incident `0.odxda781y58n` (opened 2026-10-17T10:20:59Z, closed 2026-10-18T10:47:25Z), not a new incident. The sweep was healthy: scheduler target logs show `POST 200` every 2 minutes through 11:14 UTC, and the `status=ok` execution series is continuous (288 points over 24 h, no gap > 10 min). R-03's conditionAbsent filter carried no `status` label, so the incident was anchored to the `status=error` series created by the billing rejections. When executions resumed as `status=ok` — a different series — the error series never returned; under Google's absent-data semantics an incident with no new data closes only after `autoClose + 24 h` (1 h + 24 h), matching the observed close (last error point ~09:47Z + 25 h = 10:47Z). The close notification is indistinguishable from a new warning in the email/UI, which is what the owner saw.

**Decision.** Add `AND metric.labels.status = "ok"` to the R-03 conditionAbsent filter. The policy now measures "the sweep is succeeding": no executions → no `ok` points → fires after 30 min; executions all failing → no `ok` points → fires; recovery → `ok` points resume → closes promptly instead of lingering for 25 h. Platform metrics for gen2 functions dual-emit under `resource.type="cloud_function"`, so the ADR #131 log-metric resource trap (`cloud_run_revision`) does not apply here.

**Verified.** PATCH `updateMask=conditions` on `alertPolicies/4769902381008384079`; read-back returns `… AND metric.labels.status = "ok"`. `autoClose` stays 3600 s. The old incident was already closed; no state migration was needed.

**Live re-verification (2026-10-18, read-only).** `GET monitoring.googleapis.com/v3/projects/myexodus-53804/alerts` (the `projects.incidents` path 404s): policy enabled, filter still pins `metric.labels.status = "ok"`, `autoClose` 3600 s, duration 1800 s, ALIGN_SUM 600 s. 22 alerts total, all recent ones CLOSED (latest = the billing incident above); `state=open` returns zero. The pinned `ok` series holds 358 points from 07:27Z to 13:24Z with no gap — the sweep is executing continuously.

## #181 — Meter Arithmetic Made Invariant-Exact: Closed Streaks Survive a Stalled Tick, and a Day Split Never Reopens Pre-Activity Time (owner mandate 2026-10-18)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; JVM- and device-verified.

**Context.** The owner's standing mandate is proof, not assurance, for the VPN's duration accounting ("no chance of it giving me the wrong duration"). To test the §4.7 formula independently, I wrote a differential oracle: 500 randomized timelines (80 events each: sub-tick motion, idle tails, > `T_IDLE_MS` gaps, `touch`/`recompute` interleaving, half the seeds splitting the day mid-run) checked against a separately written union-of-activity-tails oracle. It found two defects that the hand-written U-14 cases missed.

1. **Tick-stall undercount.** `touch` starts a new streak whenever `now − lastActivityElapsed > T_IDLE_MS` by resetting `sessionStart`. If no `recompute` ran during the old streak — a stalled tick thread, process scheduling, GC — the old streak's unbooked tail (or the whole streak, if no tick ran at all) was gone: the next `recompute` clamps `intervalStart` to the *new* `sessionStart`. This violates INV-16 ("a delayed or skipped invocation still produces the exact correct total on its next run").
2. **Day-split overcount.** In `splitDayAt`'s no-live-interval branch, `sessionStart` was set to the midnight boundary unconditionally. When the new streak began *after* the boundary (a touch at 182,894 ms with the boundary at 179,713 ms — oracle seed 14), the next tick credited the idle `[boundary, firstTouch)` span as activity: +3,181 ms observed. The boundary floor is already enforced by `book(boundary)`; pulling `sessionStart` backward was the defect.

**Decision.**
1. **`pendingStreaks` (`ConcurrentLinkedQueue<LongArray>`).** When `touch` closes a streak (gap > `T_IDLE_MS`), it enqueues `[oldSessionStart, oldLastActivity + T_IDLE_MS]` before starting the new one. Relay threads append; the tick thread drains in `recompute` and `splitDayAt`. Records are clamped to `lastAccountedElapsed`, so a duplicate produced by two relay threads racing a session boundary books nothing extra and a record already covered by a tick is a no-op. The per-chunk path still allocates nothing (INV-12): a record exists only when a gap closes a streak.
2. **Split without rewinding.** Both `splitDayAt` branches now set `sessionStart = maxOf(boundary, sessionStart.get())`; `book(boundary)` keeps accounting monotonic. `resetForNewDay` clears the queue and the last-activity sentinel; `discardPendingStreaks()` drops records for a rule that is not enforced today (their time must never count).
3. **Exact-total readout.** `UsageLedger.debugTotals()` / `DomainUsageEngine.debugTotals()` expose `pattern → totalMs` for the current revision, rendered only on the debug build's Protection page. This is the ground-truth seam every device claim below reads; it is not a production API and does not change INV-7 (patterns are already visible on the Rules screen; no hostname enters logs or storage).

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Per-rule list of all intervals* — unbounded memory and work for exactly one consumer (day bucketing). (b) *Run `recompute` on every `touch`* — puts tick-thread state on the relay path and violates the single-writer rule. (c) *Record only a count of missed streaks* — cannot reconstruct the tail's start. (d) *Clamp `sessionStart` to the boundary on split* — the reported defect.

**Verified (JVM, 2026-10-18).** Three deterministic regressions: `aTickStalledAcrossAnIdleGapStillBooksTheEarlierStreak` (touch 0 → touch 20,000 → recompute 21,000 = 16,000 ms), `severalIdleGapsBeforeOneTickBookEveryStreak` (31,000 ms), `aStalledStreakClosedAcrossMidnightSplitsIntoTheRightDay` (old 10,000 / new 6,000). The 500-seed oracle (`randomizedTimelinesMatchTheIndependentUnionOfActivityTails`) uses an independently written `unionMs` merge — no shared code with the sequential booking. `domainusage`: **29 suites / 261 tests / 0 failures / 0 errors / 0 skipped**; full suite **205 suites / 1,796 tests / 0/0/0** (`:app:testDebugUnitTest` BUILD SUCCESSFUL).

**Verified (device, X6532, 2026-10-18, debug APK `install -r`, on-device SHA-256 matched the build).**
- **Duration.** Temporary rule `speedtest.tele2.net`. Two `nc` transfers: run 1 wall 1,751 ms, run 2 wall 25,284 ms. Activity-window + 15 s tail prediction 1,751 + 25,284 + 30,000 = **57,035 ms**; exact readout **55,708 ms**. The 1,327 ms difference is DNS + upstream connect + first-qualifying-chunk latency before each window opened.
- **Idle gap.** The runs were separated by 34 s of genuine idleness. A wall-clock meter would have booked first-byte→last-byte + one tail ≈ **75 s**; the exact total correctly excluded the gap.
- **Overlap.** Two parallel 10 MB downloads, wall 30,277 ms. Union + tail prediction ≈ **44.8 s**; observed delta **44,644 ms** (a summed meter would be ≈ 90 s). Both flows touched one counter concurrently.
- **Display floor.** Exact 100,352 ms rendered `Used today: 1 / 720 min`; Instagram 1,805,473 ms rendered `30 / 30 min` — integer division by 60,000 (RulesScreen.kt:692) matches the ledger's exact value.
- **Persistence.** `am force-stop` + relaunch (new PID, VPN re-established): totals returned byte-identical (100,352 / 1,805,473) — the flush/reload path neither loses nor duplicates.
- **Attribution isolation (both installed browsers).** With Instagram, Chrome and Brave force-stopped, baseline rule totals pinned at 1,805,473 / 0. Chrome and Brave then browsed Google and example.com (53 new TCP/443 flows through the tunnel, `flows_tcp_total` 87 → 140, `tls443_flows` 84 → 137). Both rule totals were unchanged afterward. `sni_ok` stayed flat because Chromium sends GREASE ECH on every TLS connection: `sni_ech` rose 11 → 37 in the same window, exactly the documented `Result.Ech` path (RFC 9849 §6.2; 20/20 captured Chrome hellos carry `0xFE0D`; the plaintext name is a cover name and the tap falls back to DNS attribution). No parser failure counter moved (`inspect_pool_exhausted`, `inspect_timeout`, `sni_malformed`, `sni_toolarge` all 0); `rst_injected` rose on Happy-Eyeballs connect failures, and `flow_resets_new` stayed 0, so no rule-driven reset occurred.

**Consequences / honest limits.** (a) The device ground truth bounds each activity window to the `nc` wall window minus DNS/connect/first-byte latency; it is not an ms-exact observation of the relay's first qualifying chunk (the 1.3 s reconciliation is the bound, not a measured per-event timestamp). (b) Midnight rollover is oracle- and JVM-proven, not device-run across a real midnight. (c) A hard process kill can still lose up to `PERSIST_INTERVAL_MS` (10 s) of unflushed accrual by design (§4.9/NFR-8); a graceful force-stop flushes. (d) GREASE ECH means Chromium TLS flows are attributed by DNS, not SNI; a flow whose DNS observation expired before open is unmetered — the conservative choice (never block on missing attribution). (e) The 15 s tail is credited even when the user stops using the site; this is the designed idle model (FR-5), and it is why one short visit books ~16 s.

**Addendum — UDP/QUIC device leg (X6532, 2026-10-18).** The TCP legs above could not exercise `UdpActivityTap` or the ENFORCE exhaustion path. A temporary `example.org` rule (1 m/day) was created, resolved to 104.20.26.136 through the tunnel, and driven with toybox `nc -u -q 1`: two single 600-byte datagrams in separate >15 s sessions booked exactly **30,000 ms** (15 s each, the model's tail). A sustained loop (17 accepted datagrams over 30.3 s) plus one tail read **75,014 ms** against a 75,000 ms prediction (+14 ms tick alignment). The 18th datagram was dropped at flow open after exhaustion: `udp_dropped=1` on the official §14 counter line, `hook_exceptions=0`, `fatal_vm_error=0`, `flow_resets_new=0` (`flow_resets_sweep=19`), and the site-named warning fired ("example.org: less than a minute left today"). The temp rule was deleted and the original four rules restored the same session. The one wedged invocation was a toybox-netcat harness quirk (a dropped UDP flow leaves `nc` blocked on read even with `-q 1`), not an engine defect — the drop counter had already incremented.

## #182 — Website Expiry Is Decided at the Moment, Not at Snapshot Publish (audit A-02, owner mandate 2026-10-18)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; JVM- and device-verified.

**Context.** A website rule with an end date was honest in the accessibility path — `BlockDecisionEngine` consults `blockExpiresAt` — but not on the DNS/VPN path. `RulesSnapshot` dropped expired rules only when the snapshot was *built*, `DomainRule` carried no expiry, and `DomainBlocklist` read no clock. Between a rule's end instant and the next publish, Chrome still received NXDOMAIN and the meter kept accruing, for an unbounded window that ended only when the app happened to be opened or a rule was edited. The audit recorded this as A-02 (verified defect, Medium): two enforcement authorities disagreeing on the same predicate.

**Decision.**
1. **Carry the expiry on the snapshot model.** `DomainRule` gains `expiresAt` (epoch ms, 0 = never) and `isExpiredAt(nowMillis)`, with the one comparison `expiresAt > 0 && nowMillis > expiresAt` — the expiry instant itself is still live. This is the same boundary as `RestrictionRule.isExpiredAt`, `BlockDecisionEngine`, and the existing snapshot filter. `DomainRuleProvider.adaptOne` copies `blockExpiresAt`.
2. **Re-decide at every use.** `AttributionResolver.liveMatch` ignores expired candidates, so a lapsed rule can neither bind an SNI flow nor treat a DNS candidate as limited; `DnsShaper.decide(..., nowMillis)` forwards every qtype on an expired match; `DomainBlocklist` entries carry the expiry and answer live only while `nowMillis <= expiresAt`; `DnsSinkholeVpnService.handleDns` passes `System.currentTimeMillis()` into the decision. A stale entry in a published snapshot is now harmless: correctness no longer depends on publish timing.
3. **Stop accrual at the exact instant.** `RuleCounter.markExpiry` books the active window up to the expiry and nothing after, including a streak closed while the tick was stalled; `retargetExpiry` re-arms accrual if an edit extends the date; `UsageLedger.tick` marks and then skips expired counters. The wall-clock instant selects *where* the clamp lands; the arithmetic stays on the monotonic clock (S1.4 unchanged — the raw wall read lives only in `SystemWallClock.nowMillis()`; INV-2 durations unchanged).
4. **The publish-time filter remains.** `RulesSnapshot` still drops expired rules at build time — one filter point, unchanged. The rebuild is now an optimisation, never a correctness requirement.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Schedule a rebuild at the earliest expiry* — needs a wakeup primitive inside the service, still races the boundary, and leaves correctness dependent on a scheduler; the decision-time filter is smaller and unconditional. (b) *Filter only in the shaper/meter* — blocking would still be stale in the blocklist. (c) *Drop end dates from website rules* — a product regression; app rules already honour expiry.

**Verified (JVM, audit-fix batch).** `DomainRuleProviderTest.expiryIsCarriedOntoTheDomainRule_auditA02`; `DomainBlocklistTest.expiredRule_stopsBlockingWithoutARebuild_auditA02`; `DnsShaperTest.aLapsedRuleForwardsEveryQtypeEvenIfTheIndexStillCarriesIt_auditA02`; `AttributionResolverTest.expiredCandidatesAreIgnored`, `aLapsedSniRuleDoesNotBindEvenThoughTheIndexStillCarriesIt`, `aLapsedDnsCandidateIsTreatedAsUnlimitedNotAsALimitedSite`; `UsageLedgerTest.expiryFreezesTheTotalAtTheExpiryInstant`; `RuleCounterTest.markExpiryBooksUpToTheExpiryInstantAndNothingAfter`, `markExpiryClampsAStreakClosedWhileTheTickWasStalled`, `retargetExpiryReArmsAccrualForAnExtendedRule`. The tests drive expiry with injected clocks — no test file under `domainusage` reads wall time (S1.4 check stays green).

**Verified (device, X6532, 2026-10-18, debug APK `install -r`, on-device SHA-256 matched).** A temporary website rule was added through the `du-*` harness with a short `expiresInSec`, and the published snapshot still carried it (no app interaction after the harness command). AAAA queries through the tunnel returned NODATA while live (`an=0`, shaper path) and, after the expiry instant passed, the same stale snapshot forwarded the query upstream and returned the real Cloudflare AAAA record (`an=2`) — with the app never opened and no rebuild. That is decision-time expiry on the network path, not a filter observed at publish. The temporary rule was removed and the device's original rule set restored in the same session.

**Consequences / honest limits.** (a) Expiry is a wall-clock predicate by definition; a user manually changing the device clock can expire a rule early or keep it alive late — the same exposure the accessibility path has always had, now consistent across authorities. (b) A locked-boot DE snapshot can still carry a stale expiry until the authoritative load (A-11), bounded to the locked window. (c) Window-only DNS over-blocking (A-05) is unchanged: `DomainBlocklist` deliberately excludes limit-only rules, and windows remain a decision-engine concept.

## #183 — The Editor No Longer Rejects a Limit Longer Than Its Window (audit A-01, owner mandate 2026-10-18)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; JVM-verified.

**Context.** ADR #138 introduced a `LimitExceedsWindow` rejection on the premise that a daily quota longer than the rule's time window "could never fire". The implemented engines do not work that way. `BlockDecisionEngine` Rule 1 blocks inside the window; Rule 2 independently blocks when `usageTodayMs >= dailyLimitMs` on an active day, with no reference to the window. `UsageAccountingEngine` accrues all day, and the DNS meter accrues whenever a limited rule matches — outside the window too. The rejection therefore barred a coherent, meaningful rule — "block 22:00–07:00 nightly and cap me at 2 h/day" — and told the user something false about how the app works. Audit A-01 recorded the copy/validation premise as a verified defect; the engines were authoritative.

**Decision.** Remove `ModeError.LimitExceedsWindow` and the `editor_limit_exceeds_window` copy entirely. `validateBlockMode` keeps only the real bounds: at least one mechanism selected; a live window must have distinct endpoints; a live limit must be between 1 minute and one day (`MINUTES_PER_DAY` is still the only upper bound); all checks skip mechanisms that "all the time" overrides. The doc comment records the day-scoped quota semantics and cites this ADR so the rejected premise cannot quietly return. No engine behavior changed — this is copy and validation only.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Scope the quota to the window* — would change shipped meter semantics and the product model (quota is a per-day budget; the window is an additional block period), and would make the existing meter's day-scoped totals wrong relative to enforcement. (b) *Keep the rejection with corrected copy* — still forbids a valid configuration. (c) *Warn but allow* — unnecessary once the premise is known false.

**Verified (JVM).** `RuleModeTest.validate_limitLongerThanItsWindow_isAccepted_dayScopedQuota` accepts a 1 h window + 2 h quota, an overnight 9 h window + 10 h quota, a limit with no window, and all three mechanisms under always-on; it still rejects exactly 24 h (`LimitTooLarge`). The full-boundary cases remain pinned by `validate_limitAtOrOverAFullDay_isRejected` and `validate_zeroLimit_isRejected_butNotWhenAlwaysOnOverridesIt`.

**Consequences.** ADR #138's validation request is superseded in this one respect; its other decisions stand. The user-visible model is now consistent with both engines: window = when the site is blocked, quota = how much of the day can be used.

## #184 — No qname, IP, or URL Reaches logcat in a Release Build (audit A-04, owner mandate 2026-10-18)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; JVM- and build-verified.

**Context.** INV-7 forbids hostnames, IPs, and DNS names in logs, and the CI check enforced it only over the `domainusage` package. Audit A-04 found baseline diagnostics from before the invariant — `DnsSinkholeVpnService` logged qnames, destination IPs/keys, and packet hex — which the test report had documented as a carve-out rather than fixed. While closing it, a second violation the audit missed surfaced: `BrowserUrlScanner` logged raw address-bar text in its "unparseable/not page-like" no-op paths (the main `url scan` line was already gated). Release builds evaluate these interpolations today.

**Decision.**
1. **Gate every sensitive diagnostic on `BuildConfig.DEBUG`.** In `DnsSinkholeVpnService`: TUN interface addresses; parse-drop hex; DNS query source byte, qname, and the `nxdomain` line; TCP parse hex; SYN retransmit keys, flow keys and hex; RST keys; upstream connect destination/success/failure; SYN-ACK key/hex; first-segment hex; swept UDP flow key. In `BrowserUrlScanner`: address-bar discovery, both no-op address-bar texts, and the existing scan line (already gated). Markers, counts, generic I/O errors, and the `dns shaped` line remain ungated — they carry no host/IP/URL, and `dns shaped` performs the TUN write inline, so gating it would have skipped a side effect in release.
2. **Side-effect safety over copy-paste gating.** Two lines interpolated `writeTun(...)` inside the log expression. Both were restructured to `val written = writeTun(...)` with only the log guarded — a blind `if (DEBUG) Log…` would have stopped writing packets in release, a far worse bug than the log leak. This is the one place where the fix was not mechanical, and it is called out in the source.
3. **CI check 7 in `scripts/domainusage-ci-checks.sh`.** Scans every main `.kt` for `Log.` lines containing sensitive tokens (`qname`, `hostAddress`, `inetAddresses`, `hex=`, `key=`, `dst=`, `$text`, `%02x`, …) without a `BuildConfig.DEBUG` guard on the same or previous line, and fails with `FAIL [INV-7]`. The shipped script is the tested artifact.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Strip via ProGuard/R8 in release only* — build-configuration dependent, leaves debug builds noisy with user data, and cannot be tested by the JVM fixture. (b) *Remove the diagnostics entirely* — loses first-line debugging value the owner's evidence mandate relies on. (c) *A logging façade* — new abstraction for a one-line policy; the existing guard is the pattern the feature logs already used.

**Verified (JVM).** `DomainUsageCiChecksTest` extended with `ungatedSensitiveLogInTheVpnService_fails` (a fixture service that logs `"nxdomain " + q.qname` fails) and `aDebugGuardedSensitiveLogInTheVpnService_passes` (the same line behind `if (BuildConfig.DEBUG)` passes); both run the real shipped script through `ProcessBuilder`, not a copy. The suite is 12/12. `assembleDebug` and `compileReleaseKotlin` both succeed, proving the guarded interpolations compile in the release variant (where `BuildConfig.DEBUG` is the constant `false`).

**Consequences / honest limits.** The CI check is a pattern list, not a type check: a future log introducing a sensitive token outside the listed patterns would pass. The list covers every token the current baseline and feature logs use; extending it is a one-line change when a new diagnostic introduces a new shape. INV-7's letter now holds for release builds; debug builds intentionally keep the full diagnostic surface (logcat exposure remains adb/system-only).

## #185 — The Rule UI States the Truth About Website Limits in Non-Enforcing Builds (audit A-03, owner mandate 2026-10-18)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; device-verified.

**Context.** Release builds configure `EngineMode.OFF` (`build.gradle.kts`), so website daily limits are stored but never meter, shape, or block; only the accessibility path applies. The editor nevertheless offered the limit switch everywhere, and the Rules banner rendered nothing for a `Dormant` engine — so a release user could create a limit rule that silently did nothing, with no notice. App limits are unaffected: they ride the accessibility usage accounting and are live in every mode. OPD #27 (whether release should ever enable the website engine) remains an owner product decision; this ADR makes the UI honest in either direction rather than deciding that question.

**Decision.**
1. **One predicate.** `websiteLimitMechanismAvailable(isApp, mode) = isApp || mode == EngineMode.ENFORCE` — the single place the UI asks whether a website limit can take effect.
2. **Rules list banner.** When the domain engine is not enforcing, the list shows `domain_usage_banner_unavailable`: "Website limits aren't available in this build. Blocking and time windows still work." Static rules and windows remain fully functional, and the copy says so. The mode is read from the engine (`@Volatile`, refreshed by the existing 5 s tick) rather than inferred from `Dormant`, which conflated empty-rule dormancy with mode.
3. **Editor row.** The daily-limit switch is disabled for websites when unavailable, with `editor_website_limits_unavailable` below it: "Website daily limits aren't available in this build — website metering is turned off. Blocking and time windows still work." An existing limit value is preserved and remains checked — the rule is not silently rewritten — but a new inert limit cannot be created without the explanation on screen. App rules and always-on/window mechanisms are untouched.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Hide the limit row* — destroys an existing value's visibility and makes the form differ between builds in a harder-to-explain way. (b) *Show a toast on save* — the notice must be present at the point of the control, not only at commit. (c) *Force-enable the engine in release* — that is OPD #27, an owner product decision, not a UI fix.

**Verified (device, X6532, 2026-10-18, debug APK with the debug mode override set to `OFF`).** The Rules list rendered the unavailable banner. Opening the existing instagram rule showed the caption, "30 Minutes" preserved, and the accessibility node dump confirmed the design: "Block all day" and "On a schedule" switches `enabled=true`, "Limit daily use" `checked=true, enabled=false`. The override was then cleared and the app process restarted; `du-status` returned `status=Active mode=ENFORCE vpn=ACTIVE`, the original rule remained, private DNS stayed `off`.

**Consequences.** The UI now derives its claim from the same mode the engine enforces, so flipping OPD #27 later needs no UI change. Honest limit: a rule stored by an older APK or an import can still carry a website limit; the banner keeps the state visible rather than pretending the rule will fire.

## #186 — UDP Replies Are Never Truncated: 64 KiB Receive Buffers and a 1500-Byte TUN MTU (owner defect report 2026-10-18)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; device- and wire-verified.

**Context.** With the VPN on, video on websites did not load at all while the same Wi-Fi streamed instantly with the VPN off; WhatsApp video downloads had shown the same shape before ADR #175. The relay's UDP path sized its `DatagramSocket` receive buffer to the TUN MTU (1400 bytes), and the DNS path used 2048. `recvfrom(2)` discards the excess of a datagram larger than the buffer ("If a message is too long to fit in the supplied buffer, excess bytes may be discarded"), and QUIC servers size datagrams to the real 1500-byte path, not to our TUN: payloads of 1401–1472 bytes were silently cut, then rebuilt with valid lengths and checksums and delivered, so the client saw corrupt QUIC packets and stalled. TCP pages kept loading, which is why the failure looked site-specific rather than tunnel-wide. The old 1400 MTU was also incoherent with the physical link: the relay crafts raw IP with no encapsulation, so a 1472-byte upstream datagram had nowhere to fit.

**Decision.**
1. **Receive buffers bound the datagram, not the link.** `VpnPacket.MAX_UDP_DATAGRAM = 65535`; both `udpReceiveLoop` and `dnsReceiveLoop` allocate it. The UDP length field is 16 bits, so no legal datagram can exceed this; DNS gets the same buffer because EDNS0/DNSSEC answers routinely exceed any MTU-sized read.
2. **TUN MTU 1400 → 1500.** The TUN is a plain 1500-byte path with no encapsulation; 1500 − 20 IP − 8 UDP = 1472 must fit. `MAX_TCP_SEGMENT` stays 1200 (the SYN-ACK advertises no options, so the device keeps its 536 MSS).
3. **What does not change.** `buildUdpPacket` still recomputes the IP header checksum (a zero field broke all v4 replies once — the kernel verifies it on TUN ingress) and applies RFC 768's zero-checksum substitution; ICMP port-unreachable construction is untouched.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Clamp upstream payloads to the MTU* — silently corrupts QUIC exactly as before, and QUIC has no way to ask us for smaller datagrams. (b) *Keep MTU 1400 and rely on IP fragmentation* — the TUN does not fragment writes, QUIC sets DF, and reassembly is not implemented. (c) *A 2048-byte buffer as a "large enough" middle ground* — still truncates 2049+ and DNS responses can reach that; the 16-bit length field is the exact bound and costs one allocation per loop, not per packet.

**Verified (X6532, 2026-10-18, old vs fixed APK, host UDP echo replying 1472 bytes).**
- *Old build:* request sent, server replied 1472 bytes, device received **1400** — exactly the buffer size.
- *Fixed build:* same request → device received **1472**; a client-sent 1472-byte datagram reached the host server intact (`recv len=1472`).
- *Real media through `vpn-state=ACTIVE`:* YouTube app 4K test video advanced 0:01 → 0:14 with ~8 MB of video data; the same video played in Chrome; an Instagram feed video advanced frame-to-frame. All three were checked by paired screenshots and `dumpsys netstats` byte growth.

**Consequences / honest limits.** Every UDP datagram the platform will deliver now crosses the relay intact, including QUIC/HTTP-3 media. The relay still drops IPv6 packets carrying extension headers (pre-existing spike ceiling, documented in `VpnPacket.parseIpv6`), and Chrome on this handset negotiates h2 even with the VPN off, so the h3 upgrade path itself was not observable on-device — the datagram-level proof plus real media playback is the evidence chain. WhatsApp's live video-download leg could not be reproduced without sending a message to a contact; the same relay path is covered by the wire test and ADR #175's regression.

## #187 — Usage Sessions Survive Screen-Off and Unlock; the Meter Self-Heals Against the Platform Record (owner defect report 2026-10-18)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; device- and emulator-verified.

**Context.** An Instagram app rule (06:00–18:00 window + 2 h daily limit) walled at the metered 2 h while Digital Wellbeing showed 2 h 42 m. The owner's own estimate (~42 m) and the wall disagreed; the investigation found the wall was right about the metered total but the meter had **lost a 42-minute foreground span**: `ACTION_SCREEN_OFF` closed the usage session at 19:44:05 and nothing reopened it at unlock. The app that was already foreground emits no window-state change when the keyguard goes away — the pipeline sees the keyguard transition instead — and XOS window-list lag can drop the deferred WSC. The process stayed alive, so the FGS's start-only credit-edge audit never ran and the span never reached the counter. The owner reasonably expected the meter to heal itself toward Digital Wellbeing; it did not.

**Decision.**
1. **Screen-state re-acquisition.** The screen-off receiver now handles `ACTION_SCREEN_ON` and `ACTION_USER_PRESENT` by re-acquiring the session; screen-off still hides overlays and closes the session. `ACTION_SCREEN_ON` covers devices without a keyguard; `ACTION_USER_PRESENT` covers the keyguard path.
2. **30-second watchdog.** `verifyUsageSession()` runs every `SESSION_WATCHDOG_MS = 30_000`: if enhanced mode is on, the FGS oracle names a tracked app with fresh confirmation (≤5 s), and no session is open, it restarts a dead ticker (`syncUsageTicker` is a no-op when alive) and re-opens the session. This is cause-agnostic: dropped deferred WSC, event storm, lost unlock broadcast.
3. **Periodic credit-edge audit.** The FGS runs `reconcileUncreditedSpan(now, minStaleMs = 45_000)` every `PERIODIC_AUDIT_INTERVAL_MS = 60_000`, guarded against overlap with a still-running pass. The staleness gate exists because a healthy ticker rewrites its edge every 10 s; probing fresher than 45 s would race the in-flight tail and double-count. §8.9's overlap check already refuses to re-credit written ACCOUNTING/RECONCILIATION rows in the same boot, so repeated passes are idempotent.
4. **Never re-acquire while the screen is dark.** `PowerManager.isInteractive` gates `reacquireUsageSession`. Device-caught on the emulator: without it, the 30 s watchdog re-opened sessions during a 45 s screen-off window because the XOS-style oracle lagged the power state. Accrual stayed correct in that run (the platform record had no foreground marks for the span), but the contract "a session means visible foreground" must hold on ROMs where the oracle lags.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Trust Digital Wellbeing directly instead of metering* — violates D-05/INV-4 (the in-memory ledger is the enforcement source of truth) and DW itself has reporting lag. (b) *Re-open a session on every watchdog tick regardless of the oracle* — would credit keyguard and screensaver time and fight the screen-off close. (c) *A shorter staleness gate* — double-credits the in-flight tail; a longer one delays healing. 45 s = 4.5 ticker periods, chosen so a healthy ticker always rewrites the edge first.

**Verified.**
- *X6532, live credit (2026-10-18 23:15–23:19):* temporary quota-only rule on `com.android.settings` (59:59 limit — could not wall), baseline journal 0 ms vs platform 1,169,882 ms; after 3 m 40 s of foreground, journal **220,088 ms** vs a DW delta of **223,981 ms** (≈4 s apart).
- *Emulator `MyExodus_API37`, unlock leg:* the handset has a pattern lock I could not reproduce without the owner's credential, so the screen-off → keyguard → unlock cycle ran on the sanctioned second target. Baseline journal 0 / platform 0; after 2 m of foreground and the user-stop re-enable, journal 197,948 ms vs DW 209,510 ms (the FGS start audit had healed the gated span). Then: keyguard verified `showing=true` at wake → swipe unlock → `showing=false`, Settings top-resumed; final journal **348,236 ms** vs DW **355,987 ms** — **7.8 s apart (2%)** across the full cycle, with the two 47 s screen-off windows correctly not credited.
- *Watchdog seam evidence (logcat):* `session watchdog: tracked foreground without session pkg=com.android.settings` followed by `session re-acquire ...` on the emulator; the same labels ship in the instrumented build.

**Consequences / honest limits.** The wall now reflects metered foreground time continuously across screen-off, lock and unlock; the audit heals spans the session machine missed after the fact, using the platform record as the repair source. The 42 minutes already lost on 2026-10-18 are not retroactively recovered on that device (the journal rows were never written and the rule was disabled by the owner). The phone's unlock seam itself remains emulator-proven rather than handset-proven because the handset lock credential is the owner's; the broadcast and platform APIs are identical on both targets.

**Addendum (2026-10-18 late, emulator-caught).** The re-acquire initially ran inline in the SCREEN_ON receiver; the accessibility binder calls (`rootInActiveWindow`, window list) blocked past the ~10 s broadcast budget under load and the emulator recorded a `SCREEN_ON` broadcast ANR (`anr_2026-10-18-23-51-17-158`, timeout 11240 ms). The receiver now posts the work — `mainHandler.post { reacquireUsageSession() }` — still on the main thread, but after the broadcast returns. The watchdog and unlock legs re-ran green on the posted build.

## #188 — A Disabled Website Rule Keeps Its Day's Counter: No One-Toggle Quota Reset (owner mandate 2026-10-19)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; JVM-verified.

**Context.** The owner asked what happens when a rule is toggled off and back on mid-schedule or near its limit.
