The engine snapshot drops disabled rules (`RulesSnapshot.build` skips `!isEnabled`), and the ledger treated absence as removal: once the counter's pending write landed and its flows closed, `dropStaleCounters` deleted it. Re-enabling the same rule adapts the same `(id, revision)` pair — revisions bump only on pattern edits — and `applyRules` then created a fresh counter at 0, because only `start()` ever passed seeded totals. Toggle off, toggle on, and the site was browsable for another full limit: a one-control bypass of the daily quota, contradicting `UsageLedger` S5.2's own contract ("new `(id, revision)` pairs start from their persisted total or 0"). A second path exists across a restart: a rule disabled when the engine loads is absent from the startup snapshot, so enabling it later never consults the persisted total that `loadStartupState` did read.

**Decision.**
1. **Absence ≠ supersession.** `dropStaleCounters` drops only a counter whose rule id is still in the snapshot under a *different* revision — the pattern-edit case the drop exists for. A counter whose rule id is absent (disabled or removed) is retained for the rest of the day.
2. **The startup totals seed late arrivals.** The ledger keeps the startup load's `(id, revision) → total` map for the day and consults it when a counter first appears mid-session, covering the disabled-at-load → enabled-later path. Cleared at the rollover so yesterday's totals can never seed today.
3. **Prune at the rollover.** `rolloverTo` retains only keys in the new day's active snapshot; a rule that stays disabled across midnight starts the new day at zero like every other counter.
4. **App rules unchanged.** App daily limits are keyed by package/day in the tracker and already survive a pause; re-enable additionally reconciles against platform usage (`RulesScreen`, OPD #28(a) seam), so a toggle cannot lower the app total either.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Re-seed from the database on re-enable* — `applyRules` runs on the tick thread and persistence is suspend; an asynchronous seed would briefly show 0 and allow seconds of browsing, and adds a cross-thread seam for no benefit. (b) *Make the provider emit disabled rules* — "which rules are live" is deliberately single-sourced in `RulesSnapshot`; the ledger already owns enough identity to solve this locally. (c) *Never drop counters* — unbounded across a long-running process under heavy pattern edits; pruning at midnight bounds it to one day of edits. (d) *Refuse re-enable near the limit* — changes product behavior the owner did not ask for; the honest model is that the total persists.

**Verified.** JVM: `aDisabledRuleKeepsTodaysTotal_soReEnablingCannotResetTheQuota` (accrues past a 10 s limit, disables, acknowledges the write, ticks past the idle tail, re-enables → total intact and `exhausted` re-derived), `aRuleFirstSeenMidSession_seedsFromTheStartupLoad`, and `absentRulesCountersArePrunedAtTheDayRollover_andYesterdayTotalsNeverSeedToday`; the existing pattern-edit and volume pins stay green. Device: the toggle wiring is the already-device-verified `setEnabled` → publisher → `updateRules` path; the fixed semantics are pure ledger logic.

**Consequences / honest limits.** A disabled rule's counter occupies memory until midnight — one small object per rule disabled that day. Usage accrued *while disabled* is still not counted (the rule is absent from the matcher, so no flow attributes to it); re-enabling resumes from the pre-disable total, which matches "off means off, on resumes". For app rules, the platform reconcile can raise — never lower — the resumed total.

## #189 — Website Limits Meter Browser Traffic Only (owner decision 2026-10-19)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; JVM-verified; device-verified (X6532 + API-37 AVD, 2026-10-19).

**Context.** On 2026-10-19 the owner reported `instagram.com` at 11/30 by 08:38 while having made no browser visit to the site that day. The evidence dossier (`~/Documents/MyExodusEvidence/2026-10-19-instagram-counter/README.md`) proved the counter metered attributed flow time from **every** app: the Instagram app was foreground 08:27:22–08:32:02, its API hosts (`i.instagram.com`, `graph.instagram.com`) dot-suffix-match the rule, launching the app moved the counter exactly +15,000 ms (one ≥512 B chunk + the full 15 s idle tail) with no browser foreground, and a temporary `googlevideo.com` rule accrued 91,275 ms from ~90 s of YouTube-app playback. Source-verified: no UID or package filter existed anywhere under `domainusage/`. The owner then chose the product semantic: a website limit is about time spent browsing the site; the site's own app belongs to app rules. Option selected 2026-10-19: **"Browser time only."**

**Decision.**
1. **Resolve the flow owner once, at flow open.** `FlowOwnerClassifier` calls the official `ConnectivityManager.getConnectionOwnerUid(protocol, local, remote)` — API 29+, active VpnService only, `IPPROTO_TCP`/`IPPROTO_UDP`, `Process.INVALID_UID` when the tuple is not found or not observable — with the TUN packet's source as `local` and the destination as `remote`.
2. **Classify browsers by package.** A UID counts as a browser when any package sharing it holds `RoleManager.ROLE_BROWSER` (the default browser) or appears in the curated known-browser set (Chrome/Chromium forks, Brave, Firefox/Focus, Edge, Opera, Samsung Internet, Vivaldi, DuckDuckGo, AOSP/OEM browsers). `RoleManager.getRoleHolders` is invoked reflectively because the compileSdk 37 stubs omit it (ADR #17); `PackageManager.getPackagesForUid` handles shared UIDs.
3. **Gate metering, not just counting.** `DomainUsageEngine.tcpFlowOpened`/`udpFlowOpened` take a `FlowOwner`. `BROWSER` flows run the existing attribution/metering/reset path unchanged. `NON_BROWSER` and `UNKNOWN` flows return `PassThroughTap`/allow before attribution: they are never metered, never registered in `FlowRegistry`, never swept or RST-reset by a website quota, and never counted in `flows_attributed_total`. New §14 counters `flows_owner_browser`, `flows_owner_non_browser`, `flows_owner_unknown` make the split observable.
4. **Fail-open, never false-block.** API < 29, an unresolved 5-tuple, a `SecurityException` during teardown, or a null package list all produce `UNKNOWN` → not counted. The cost is under-reporting; on API 26–28 website daily limits therefore do not enforce (schedule/expiry blocks still do). This matches the owner-selected "unresolvable flows are not counted".
5. **UI copy.** `editor_limit_scope_notice` now says limits count the site in browsers and that other apps, including the site's own app, are not counted.
6. **Unchanged.** App rules (platform-usage-keyed), always-on DNS blocking, the URL-scanner quota block, DNS shaping, warning thresholds, persistence, and the ledger's `(id, revision)` identity.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Per-app website counters (schema/UI breakdown)* — the owner chose the simpler semantic; a breakdown would need a new key dimension, UI, and migration. (b) *`queryIntentActivities(http)` as the browser set* — includes social apps' in-app browsers and link handlers, which would count exactly the traffic the owner asked to exclude. (c) *DNS-layer per-app attribution* — DNS packets carry no UID, so the same owner lookup would still be needed, and DoH/ECH flows would stay unattributable. (d) *Keep app-agnostic metering on API < 29* — counts the site's own app on old devices, contradicting the chosen semantic.

**Performance.** One binder lookup per flow open — never per packet or per chunk; the per-UID browser decision is cached for the session. In `OFF` mode no lookup runs. No new permissions, exports, or persisted data; debug logs carry only protocol/UID/boolean, never a hostname (INV-7).

**Consequences / honest limits.** A WebView embedded in a non-browser app is not counted (its sockets belong to the host app). A browser that is not the role holder and not in the known list is not counted until it is added to the set. Installing a browser or switching the default mid-session is picked up on the next VPN start (the UID cache is session-scoped). DNS NXDOMAIN shaping for an exhausted rule remains app-global, as before; this ADR changes metering and flow-reset scope, not DNS blocking.

**Verified (2026-10-19).** JVM: full suite 206 suites / 1,821 tests / 0 failures / 0 errors / 0 skipped; `assembleDebug` OK (debug APK 49,714,378 B, built 13:53). X6532 (Android 14, XOS), debug APK installed `install -r` (data preserved):
1. **Golden regression.** `instagram.com` counter `1,660,933 ms` before and after a 25 s Instagram-app foreground launch (the exact path that previously added +15,000 ms); `flows_owner_non_browser` 7→13. Counter flat to the millisecond.
2. **Non-browser app.** `media_session` reported YouTube `state=PLAYING`; after 45+ s a temporary `googlevideo.com` rule stayed **0 ms**; uid 10133 flows logged `browser=false` (TCP and UDP); `flows_owner_non_browser` 150→211.
3. **Chrome.** Temporary `example.com` rule accrued **32,711 ms** after a 20 s page load (34,543 ms at the next probe); uid 10114 logged `browser=true` on TCP and UDP; `flows_owner_browser` 0→100; page rendered.
4. **Brave (cross-browser).** Temporary `example.org` rule accrued **16,155 ms**; uid 10318 logged `browser=true`; Brave foreground.
5. **API-37 AVD.** Current APK installed `install -r`; temporary `example.org` rule accrued **14,808 ms**; Chrome uid 10172 logged `browser=true`; `flows_owner_browser=44`, `flows_owner_non_browser=4`, `flows_owner_unknown=2`.
6. **Cleanup.** Every temporary rule deleted on both devices; the phone's rule list shows only the owner's `instagram.com` rule and its counter still reads exactly `1,660,933 ms`.

Honest notes: mid-test the owner toggled the phone's Wi-Fi; the first Chrome run stalled with `ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED` until the network recovered, after which a raw DNS query through the tunnel answered normally and every accrual assertion passed — environmental, not code-related. The owner's rule was never exhausted, so this pass did not re-drive the quota-reset path on device (covered by `anExhaustedRuleStillCutsABrowserFlow` on JVM). API 26–28 have no device in the test pool; the `UNKNOWN` fail-open path is covered by `anUnknownOwnerIsNeverMeteredAndNeverReset` on JVM.

## #190 — Every Re-Enable Carries Its Own Platform Delta: Carryover Identity Includes the Credit Instant and Target Total (owner defect report 2026-10-20)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; JVM-verified; defect device-evidenced.

**Context.** The owner's Instagram rule (`com.instagram.android`, 2 h daily limit, 06:00–18:00 schedule) had been toggled off/on through the day and had used a recovery session. Digital Wellbeing read **3 h 11 min** while the tracker blocked at about **1 h 29 m** short of it — the quota fired roughly an hour late, after the owner had already been warned at ~3 h 11 m. Device forensics (X6532, 2026-10-20): the tracker row read `used=7203882ms anchor=2026-10-20/Africa/Nairobi`, the journal audit read `sum=7203882ms`, and the platform comparison read `DELTA journal=7203882ms platform=12577498ms diff=5373616ms` (1 h 29 m 33.6 s). A re-enable reconcile logged `reconcile com.instagram.android platform=10265878ms carried=0ms`, and the next top-up logged `ledger id collision event=a5876e1042d159e5881de123888e28fb`.

**Root cause.** A pause drops the rule from the snapshot, so usage spent while paused is invisible to both live accounting paths. The re-enable seam (`RulesScreen` toggle-on, `RuleEditor` save) therefore calls `UsageAccountingEngine.reconcileWithPlatform(package, platformMs)`, which credits the uncovered platform delta as a `MIGRATION_CARRYOVER` row. Those reconciles are zero-length intervals by construction (the platform number is an absolute total, not a span), and `UsageLedgerMapper.eventIdFor` derived identity from `(source, packageName, elapsedStartMs, elapsedEndMs, bootCount)` — all identical for the next top-up in the same boot. The sequel credit deduplicated against the first row as an accidental "retry", wrote nothing, and returned carried=0. Once is harmless (the first top-up lands); **every re-enable after the first silently lost the whole paused window**, permanently within a boot. The owner's repeated toggling is exactly this shape.

**Decision.**
1. **Carryover identity names the state it records.** `UsageLedgerMapper.carryoverEventIdFor(packageName, wallClockTsMs, targetTotalMs)` returns `carryover:<package>:<wallClock>:<targetTotal>`, passed as the draft's `eventIdOverride` by `reconcileWithPlatform`.
2. **The pair is unique per real credit and stable per retry.** A new top-up always changes the target total (the credit is positive by construction); a retry of the same platform reading produces the same id, so crash-after-write/retry still deduplicates. The `carryover:` prefix keeps the namespace disjoint from SHA-derived accounting ids.
3. **No change to the interval or day-split rules.** Zero-length carryovers remain the §8.2 exemption and keep attributing to the day they closed on; a stale previous-day tracker still rolls first (existing behaviour).
4. **Both app seams share the fixed path.** `RulesScreen.kt` (toggle-on) and `RuleEditor.kt` (save) already route through `reconcileWithPlatform`; the harness `usage-seed` path is a different seam and was used only for evidence.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Random UUID per carryover* — rejects retry dedup: a crash after insert but before acknowledgement would double-credit on the retry. (b) *Wall clock only in the id* — two top-ups inside one millisecond collide again; the target total is the value that actually differs. (c) *Recompute cumulative carryover from the platform total instead of delta rows* — a redesign of the ledger's append-only contract for one seam; the identity fix is smaller and keeps the journal replayable. (d) *Credit a nominal one-millisecond span* — fabricates duration the platform did not report; the ledger's values must stay real.

**Verified.** JVM: `reconcile_repeatedTopUps_sameBoot_eachDeltaLands` — three top-ups (45/62/71 min) leave `msUsedToday=71 min`, journal carryovers `[9, 17, 45] min`, and `rebuildProjection()==0`; pre-fix the second and third credited 0. `UsageLedgerMapperTest.toRow_usesTheOverrideWhenGiven_andRecordsSourceVersion` pins the override path. Device: the failure itself is evidenced above; the post-fix real-toggle confirmation (owner-permitted) is recorded in the 2026-10-20 session evidence.

**Consequences / honest limits.** Reconcile remains a UI-triggered seam: if the process dies between the enable commit and the reconcile, the paused window is still carried by the *next* reconcile because the platform number is absolute and the merge is monotone — it is delayed, not lost. The tracker can only ever rise from reconcile; a stale-lower platform read never unblocks (existing monotone test). Nothing here changes the pause semantics: usage accrued while paused is counted at re-enable, exactly as OPD #28(a) decided.

## #191 — A Carryover Anchors the Credit-Edge Audit: the Repair May Not Re-Credit Carried Paused Time (device defect 2026-10-20)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; JVM-verified (13 classes / 204 tests / 0 failures in `blocking.usage`); device-verified on the X6532 (2026-10-20, real toggle seam; evidence below).

**Context.** While proving ADR #190 through the real Rules toggle seam on the X6532, the tracker ended **ahead** of Digital Wellbeing instead of behind it. Evidence (`MyExodusVerification` TAG, 2026-10-20):
- Pause window 1: Instagram foreground 21:13:42–21:15:19 (96,129 ms); re-enable at 21:15:42 credited `carried=5004027ms` (row `id=18108 MIGRATION_CARRYOVER`, wall 21:15:42).
- Pause window 2: 21:16:02–21:17:11 (68,869 ms); re-enable at 21:17:28 credited `carried=68869ms` (row `id=18112`, wall 21:17:28).
- Seconds later the FGS audit wrote `id=18115 RECONCILIATION src=MAINTENANCE credited=164998ms` (wall 21:18:12, elapsed span 1,314,665 ms, boot 128) — exactly pause window 1 + pause window 2.
- The day audit then read `journal=12911364ms platform=12746366ms diff=-164998ms`: the tracker was 164,998 ms ahead of the platform record.

**Root cause.** `lastCreditWallPerPackage` anchored the audit on `OVERLAP_KINDS` (ACCOUNTING, RECONCILIATION) only — ADR #160's original exclusion, justified by "a carryover row owns a zero-length interval." That justification misidentified what the anchor means: the anchor is the wall through which some path has *answered for* the package's usage. A carryover's credited value is an absolute platform total, so it answers for everything up to its wall even though it owns no interval. With the anchor stuck at the last live ACCOUNTING row (~20:56:17), the paused windows looked uncredited; §8.9's overlap check (also ACCOUNTING/RECONCILIATION-only) found no covering interval either, and `UsageGapRepair` credited the paused foreground a second time. The stop clip could not help: the paused usage precedes the user's exit, so the clip bounds the span's tail but not this middle.

**Decision.**
1. **`CREDIT_EDGE_KINDS = OVERLAP_KINDS + MIGRATION_CARRYOVER`** is the anchor set for `lastCreditWallPerPackage` / `creditEdges`. `OVERLAP_KINDS` stays ACCOUNTING/RECONCILIATION for §8.9's interval-overlap check, where interval ownership is the actual question. The two questions are now answered by two sets instead of being conflated into one.
2. **Nothing else changes.** Carryovers stay zero-length aggregates (ADR #190), §8.6 identity is untouched, and the wall-cutoff/midnight/boot/stop clips remain as built.
3. **ADR #160 is annotated**, not rewritten; its liveness-vs-credit reasoning stands for HEARTBEAT/GAP_DETECTED/RULE_EVALUATION.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Credit the carryover as a spanning interval* — the platform total is absolute and may span prior days or another boot; fabricating elapsed endpoints would corrupt §8.5's boot framing and the day split. (b) *Subtract carried totals from the repair's credit* — duplicates state the edge already encodes and needs a second per-package aggregate. (c) *Rely on the stop clip* — falsified by this evidence: the usage happened before the stop. (d) *Trust the top-up alone and drop the repair* — the repair exists for process-death gaps the seams never see; removing it would reintroduce the undercount class.

**Verified.** JVM: `lastCreditWallPerPackage_carryoverAnchorsTheEdgeToo` (a later carryover now wins the edge) and `carryoverAdvancesTheCreditEdge_soTheRepairCannotRecreditThePausedWindow` (ACCOUNTING at the pause, paused foreground marks, reconcile at wallNow → edge == carryover wall; the repair window's foreground sum is 0). Package run: 13 classes / 204 tests / 0 failures / 0 errors / 0 skipped (2026-10-20).

**Device verification (X6532, fixed APK installed `install -r`, data preserved).** The pre-fix surplus was first reversed through the designed §8.12 seam: `ledger-correct target=e4a89023 deltaMs=-164998 outcome=Written projectionRewritten=1`, after which `usage row used=12746366` matched the platform exactly. Then the failing cycle was repeated through the real UI:
1. **Pause** via the Rules toggle ("Pause Instagram"); authoritative snapshot dropped to `1 app, 3 url rules`.
2. **Use while paused:** Instagram foreground 21:30:55–21:32:05.
3. **Re-enable** via "Resume Instagram" at 21:32:29: `reconcile com.instagram.android platform=12820472ms carried=74106ms total=12820472/7200000ms blocked=true`; journal row `id=18143 MIGRATION_CARRYOVER credited=74106ms wall=21:32:29 elapsed=0..0 ev=carryover:com.instagram.android:1792521149297:12820472`. The paused 74,106 ms is counted exactly once.
4. **Audit:** 89 s after the edge (periodic passes probe once the edge is 45 s stale), the day audit read `journal=12820472ms platform=12820472ms diff=0ms`, and no `gap repair: credited` line exists for the window. Pre-fix, the same shape re-credited the paused windows (`RECONCILIATION credited=164998ms`, audit `diff=-164998ms`).

**Consequences / honest limits.** The carryover wall is stamped just after the platform read inside the reconcile transaction, bounded by the 2 s binder timeout. The repair therefore may not claim live foreground in that sub-second-to-2 s seam; that is an under-credit strictly smaller than the systematic double credit it replaces, and the live path normally journals those seconds anyway. The anchor remains wall-clock bounded by the caller's midnight floor, so a carryover cannot pull the audit behind today. The measured pre-fix surplus on the device (164,998 ms) was reversed through the §8.12 `CORRECTION` seam (`deltaMs=-164998`, projection rebuilt from the journal), leaving the journal append-only and every row inspectable; the failing and passing cycles are both recorded above.

## #192 — The Day Scope Is Re-Evaluated at the Midnight Boundary, Not at the Last Snapshot Publish (audit finding F-DC-3, 2026-10-20)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; JVM-verified with a mutation check.

**Context.** Metering plan §6.5 step 5 requires the engine to re-read the rule snapshot when the effective day key changes so `enforcedToday` is re-evaluated. `DomainRuleProvider` computes `enforcedToday = dayScopeCoversToday(activeDaysOfWeek, timezone)` once per snapshot emission (DomainRuleProvider.kt:63), and the engine's only rule-refresh point was `rules.collect { updateRules(it) }` (DomainUsageEngine.kt:367). A website rule whose day mask changes at local midnight therefore kept the previous day's mask until the next publish — any rule edit. On an excluded day the quota could keep enforcing after midnight; on a newly included day it could stay inert until someone saved a rule. App rules were never affected: `RulesSnapshot.isLimitTracked` (RulesSnapshot.kt:31) and `UsageAccountingEngine.processUsageObservation` evaluate `dayScopeCoversToday` per call.

**Decision.** The `UsageTickLoop.onRollover` hook re-reads the rules flow (`updateRules(rules.first())`) after the rollover is booked. It runs on the tick thread (the ledger's single-writer rule, §4.3); `first()` starts a fresh collection, so the provider's map re-runs and `enforcedToday` follows the new day. The tick loop already catches ordinary exceptions around the hook and keeps metering (UsageTickLoop.kt:30-44).

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Cache the day mask inside `DomainRule` and recompute in `updateRules`* — recomputation needs the rule's active-days and zone, which `DomainRule` does not carry (deliberately: the adapter is the only day-scope authority). (b) *A midnight timer inside `DomainRuleProvider`* — a second clock and a second writer for state that the rollover already marks. (c) *Leave app rules in scope* — they never had the defect; touching them would add work with no behaviour change.

**Verified.** JVM: `DomainUsageLifecycleTest.aDayRolloverReReadsTheRulesFlow_soEnforcedTodayFollowsTheNewDay` — a cold flow emits a rule whose mask flips at midnight; the ledger crosses midnight on the real tick thread, the live counter's `enforcedToday` becomes false, and an emission counter proves a fresh collection rather than a replayed cached value. Mutation check: commenting out `updateRules(rules.first())` fails exactly at "the rollover applies the new day's scope to the live counter"; restored, the class runs 15 tests / 0 failures.

**Consequences / honest limits.** The re-read is a suspension point added to the rollover path; a provider that never emits makes `first()` throw, which the tick loop counts and survives. The re-read happens after the rollover booking and before the next tick's evaluation, so the first tick on the new day already sees the new mask.

## #193 — Partner Plans: A Revisioned Checklist Rides the Pair Transport (owner ask 2026-10-21)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; JVM-verified (22 tests); v16↔v17 migration legs instrumented; UI paths device-verified on the X6532 (2026-10-21: list, chooser, editor, local-plan detail/check); two-device delivery exercised on the local two-AVD rig via the virtual-partner harness (2026-10-23 01:15:56Z: the recipient checked "Breathe for two minutes", the encrypted `plan_progress` frame `4830aa89-…` reached the author's mailbox, and the author's copy rendered "1 of 2 done"). A production-attestation two-phone run remains blocked on a second physical device.

**Context.** The owner asked for partner-authored coaching plans that actually reach the other phone: a sponsor creates a checklist for a specific user, saves, and shares it; the user is notified on creation and edit, views and checks the lines, and the author sees progress; multiple plans and multiple partners; the recipient may also author their own plans. The shipped 2026-09-19 coaching plan is none of this — it is a local, single-user editor on the Recovery tab, and the partner only ever received an aggregate count (ADR #61/#115). The owner's verdict on the shipped surface was "incredibly wrong"; when asked where the original card's data came from, the only true answer was "a list this phone wrote for itself."

**Decision.**

1. **Local rows are the outbox.** Schema v17 adds `partner_plan` (head: `plan_id`, nullable `pair_id`, `authored`, `title`, `revision`, `updated_at_ms`, `pending_publish`, `pending_progress`) and `partner_plan_task` (composite key `(plan_id, task_id)`, `task_order`, `text`, `done`, `done_at_ms`, FK → head `ON DELETE CASCADE`). No service table, no relay-side state: a pending flag means "this pair owes a frame," and `PartnerSyncCoordinator` drains it through the existing signed, end-to-end-encrypted per-pair transport after the activity loops (plans ride the same housekeeping pass, never inline with a save).
2. **Authorship is per device.** `authored = 1` means this phone wrote the plan. On the author's device a *shared* plan is display-only — checking is the recipient's act and the progress signal; the author never fabricates progress locally. A *self* plan (`pair_id = null`, `authored = 1`) never leaves the phone and is checkable by its owner, since there is no recipient device. (The first implementation refused every authored plan, which made a local plan permanently un-checkable; the test `selfPlan_isLocalAndCheckable` now pins the distinction.)
3. **Revision is the idempotence key.** A published revision applies only when it is strictly newer than the recipient's copy; an equal or older one is ignored. The merge is by `task_id`, so a checked line survives the author rewording it; lines the author dropped are deleted. A newer revision re-raises `pending_progress` when any line is checked, so the author converges without a separate acknowledgement message type.
4. **Progress applies at exactly one revision.** A `plan_progress` event is honored only on the author's copy of the same pair at `plan.revision == body.revision`; a stale event never touches a newer revision. The recipient replaces the checked set with the author's reported set (`clearDone` + re-mark).
5. **Wire.** `PlanWire.TYPE_PLAN_PUBLISHED` / `TYPE_PLAN_PROGRESS`, `PLAN_PROTOCOL_VERSION = 1`, `PLAN_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1`; the body travels under the CBOR key `pl`, which is **absent when null**, so every pre-existing payload keeps its byte-identical encoding. Decode enforces identity bounds (non-blank ids, revision ≥ 1, non-zero timestamp, ≤ 40 lines, unique task ids) and clamps text (80 title / 200 per line); a body that violates a bound decodes to null **without discarding the envelope that carried it**, and a payload with an unknown protocol version is declined before any row is touched.
6. **Notifications.** Only `plan_published` alerts (`partner_alerts` channel, per-pair ids, FR-13 generic public copy); `onlyAlertOnce = false`, so an edit alerts again. `plan_progress` is filtered out of the tray by design — progress is a silent convergence signal, not an event to interrupt the recipient.
7. **Consent and disclosure.** The plan text is a shared artifact by construction: it is written on one phone to be read on the other, so the recipient seeing it is the point of the feature, not a leak. What the author receives back is the checked/unchecked state at a revision, never the recipient's local edits (there are none) and never their other plans. This deliberately supersedes, for *plans only*, the earlier "the partner never sees the text" posture that the recovery-resource coaching plan still keeps (ADR #61/#115). The plan UI sits on the Partner tab, not Settings.
8. **UI.** Partner hub adds a single-destination `LinkRow` below the 2×2 grid → `PartnerPlansScreen`: three groups ("From your partner", "You shared", "Just for me"), a "Who is this plan for?" chooser (each partner by name, or "Just me — stays on this phone"), an editor that enforces the same caps at input and keeps the draft on a failed save, and nested back handlers (editor → detail → list → hub). The hub row's subtitle carries the unhidden count of unchecked incoming lines; it reads "no plans yet" only after a successful empty read, never when the store refused.
9. **Orphan pruning.** `sweepActivity` deletes plans whose pair no longer exists, alongside the activity rows for the same orphans. Unpairing therefore does not leave a plan pointing at a counterpart that can never receive it.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Extend the existing `CoachingStep` editor* — local and single-user by shape; it cannot carry a counterpart, a revision, or a per-line completion state. (b) *Relay-side plan tables* — the backend never sees plaintext message content (accountability pairing plan §24); holding plan text server-side would break that. (c) *Explicit acknowledgements for progress* — a new message type and a second idempotence scheme for a signal the revision re-raise already converges. (d) *Edit-in-place without revisions* — a replayed or reordered publish would silently overwrite a newer state.

**Migration.** `MIGRATION_16_17` creates the two tables and their indexes (DDL is the exported `17.json` verbatim); `MIGRATION_17_16` drops exactly those two tables so a v16 build reinstalled over a briefly-v17 database still opens, matching the rollback convention every prior version follows. `AppRulesStoreMigrationInstrumentedTest` gains the forward leg (validated against `17.json`, tables start empty, a plan + line round-trip, the line table declares its CASCADE FK, pre-existing rows survive), the rollback leg (only the plan tables drop, data survives), and the re-upgrade (tables rebuilt empty).

**Verified.** JVM (22 tests, 0 failures): `PlanWireCodecTest` (6 — field round-trip; `pl` absent when null; envelope round-trip; an invalid body is declined without losing the envelope; identity violations declined; long text clamped), `PartnerPlanRepositoryTest` (7 — trims/drops/caps at input; 40-line cap; blank title refused; shared plan publishes and the author's copy is display-only; self plan local and checkable with no progress flag; update bumps revision, keeps task ids, drops removed lines; update refuses a copy this device did not author), `PartnerPlanReceiverTest` (9 — recipient copy created; older/equal ignored; newer keeps checks and re-raises progress; the author's copy is never overwritten; dropped lines removed; progress only at the held revision; progress on the recipient copy ignored; wrong pair ignored; wire version mismatch ignored). Instrumented: the three v16↔v17 legs above, added 2026-10-21.

**Honest limits.** Delivery is best-effort on the existing pair transport — both peers' keys must be live and the peer must sync for a plan to land; there is no read receipt and no server copy, so a plan delivered while the recipient is uninstalled is retried from the author's pending flag, which is the pre-existing behavior of every activity event too. A plan whose pair is unpaired is pruned on the next sweep, not at the moment of unpairing. The two-device evidence above comes from the local rig (Firebase emulators with `ATTESTATION_STUB=1`), which exercises the real wire, mailbox, encryption and UI but not the hardware-attestation pairing wall; that leg needs a second physical phone.

## #194 — Mailbox Create Requires the Recipient to Be the Pair's Other Member (Step 2 gate, 2026-10-21)

**Status:** Accepted; fixed and rules-emulator verified. **Deployment completed 2026-10-22** — recorded in ADR #199 ("ADR #194 rules deployed") and exercised live by the Step 12 kill switch at the mailbox-create boundary (ADR #207); the earlier "deployment pending" note is historical.

**Context.** The partner accountability event-delivery plan's Step 2 security gate asked for proof of cross-partner isolation at the storage boundary. A rules-emulator test run against the shipped `firestore.rules` showed the mailbox **create** rule checked only that the caller was a member of an `active` pairing named by `pairId` — never that the mailbox owner (`recipientUid` in the path) was the pairing's other member. Any user with one active pair could therefore write ciphertext documents into any user's mailbox by naming their own `pairId`. The Cloud Function relay rejects such a document as `PAIRING_INVALID`, but the pairing check runs *before* the rate limiter, so the rows were stored and never throttled — unbounded mailbox-fill abuse (bounded per document by the 8192-character rule, not in volume). No plaintext or decryption exposure existed: a foreign recipient has no CEK for the sender's pair, and `MailboxMessageHandler` skips documents whose pairing is not its own.

**Decision.** Add `recipientUid in get(pairings/{pairId}).data.members` to the mailbox create condition. It rides the `get()` the rule already performs (no extra document read), and it makes storage authorization match the relay's own `pairingUsableForRelay` check, restoring the plan's §10.7 requirement that consent be rechecked server-side **before storing**.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Rely on the relay rejection alone* — leaves an unthrottled storage path and contradicts §10.7's "before storing"; rejected. (b) *Move the rate limit before the pairing check* — would count and throttle doomed messages but still store them and still leave the authorization gap; rejected. (c) *Client-side recipient check* — no security value; the sender controls the client; rejected.

**Verified.** `functions/emulator-test/firestore-rules.emulator.js` against the real rules in the Firestore emulator: 17/17 after the fix, including "another relationship's pairId cannot be used to post into a mailbox" (failed before the change, passes after), revoked-pair create denial, sender spoof denial, create-only replay denial, field-allowlist and oversize rejection, cross-partner read/list denial, unauthenticated denial, and ack ownership. Run with `npm run test:rules` in `functions/`. Step 2's broader evidence (166 JVM accountability tests, 104 Node tests) is recorded in the plan's Appendix S2.

**Consequences / honest limits.** The rule is in the working tree but not deployed; production keeps the weaker condition until the next rules deployment, which is the owner's action. The relay's members-bound acceptance of `terminated` pairings (ADR #107) is unchanged — it closes the unpair deletion-request race and cannot be reached by a non-member. Existing stored junk from before the fix is removed by the normal cleanup (ack or 30-day cap).

## #195 — Website Category Presets Live Where a Website Rule Is Created (owner ask + correction 2026-10-21)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; JVM-verified; device-verified on the X6532 (2026-10-21).

**Context.** The owner asked for a way to block a category of sites without opening a triggering site to copy its address: "the empty Rules page has to let a user block a whole category." The first implementation put the category chips only in the empty website section. The owner corrected the placement the same day: "categories should appear when creating a website … somewhere logical." An empty-state-only affordance disappears the moment the user has one website rule, which is exactly when they are most likely to add more.

**Decision.**

1. **One curated catalog, shared by both entry points.** `ui/rules/WebsitePresets.kt` holds six categories (social, adult, betting, video, news, shopping) as bare lowercase hostnames (no `www.`, no scheme) that pass the same `isValidWebsiteTarget`/`targetKey` validation as a typed rule. A preset rule is an always-on, all-days, no-limit `WEBSITE` rule — the list is the recommendation, not a quota surface.
2. **Review before writing.** Both entry points open `WebsitePresetSheet`: per-category chips, every not-already-blocked host pre-selected, per-host checkboxes, select-all/clear, a count, and a Block button. Nothing is inserted until Block is tapped. Hosts that already have a rule (in any state, including paused) are filtered out by `unblockedSites`, so a partially failed insert and a later visit do not create duplicates.
3. **Placement (the correction).** `CategoryPresetChips` — a shared FlowRow of icon+label chips — renders in the empty website section **and** in the new-website-rule editor below the address field, with the hint "Don't know the address? Start from a category." The editor shows it only for a *new* rule; when editing an existing rule the address is already known and the chips would be noise. Tapping a chip opens the sheet directly on that category.
4. **The sheet is keyed on the category.** Switching lists starts a fresh review of that list rather than carrying a partial selection across categories; a failed save leaves the current selection intact and shows the error inline.

**Verified.** JVM `WebsitePresetsTest` (5 tests): category ids unique and addressable; every host bare, lowercase, globally unique, valid under the real validation and matching the stored key; `unblockedSites` skips every stored website rule regardless of state; nothing stored returns the whole list; the preset rule shape is always-on block-only. Device X6532 2026-10-21: Rules → Add website shows the hint and all six chips; tapping Betting opens "Block by category" on Betting with "10 of 10 selected" and the betting hosts; the empty website section still shows the same chips.

**Consequences / honest limits.** The catalogs are static, hand-curated lists — no remote updates and no redirect-chain discovery; a site not in a list is still typed by hand. Presets are ordinary rules once saved, so editing, pausing, and deleting them behave like any other rule. The category list is not evidence that a host serves only that category.

## #196 — The Partner Event Body Is a Closed Versioned Allowlist with No Free-Text Field (plan Step 3, 2026-10-21)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; 13 JVM tests green.

**Context.** The partner accountability event-delivery plan's Step 3 asks for a versioned allowlisted event body that cannot carry raw URLs, hostnames, package names, app labels, notification text, keystrokes, screenshots, location, or arbitrary JSON. The plan's §2 FR2 names five normalized categories (blocked app attempt, blocked domain attempt, monitoring permission changed, monitoring component unavailable, device status changed); §8.1's field examples name coarse content categories (adult content, social media, gambling, shopping, other). Carrying both taxonomies would add a field §8.1 forbids or drop a category FR2 explicitly requires.

**Decision.** `accountability/serialization/AccountabilityEventWire.kt` defines a fixed CBOR body: schema version 1, canonical UUID `event_id`, positive `relationship_seq`, `event_kind` (`ACCOUNTABILITY_EVENT` / `MONITORING_STATUS` / `GAP_MARKER`), `event_category` (the five FR2 categories plus `GAP_MARKER`, with kind agreement enforced), `occurred_at_minute` (floored), monitoring-only fields (`monitoring_state`, `outbox_age_bucket`, `latest_relationship_seq`), and gap-only fields (`missing_seq_start`/`end`). The decoder is closed: unknown keys, wrong types, unknown enum values, missing or forbidden fields, invalid ranges, malformed CBOR, and bodies above 512 bytes all return null without throwing. FR2 is treated as the explicit minimum and §8.1's content categories as illustrative; content-level categories are deferred to a later schema version if a content consent scope ever ships. Recipient relationship and delivery state stay in outbox metadata, not the body (§8.1); the seven §8.4 delivery states are declared for Step 4's mapping.

**Why the minimizer is structural.** The data class has exactly one `String` property — the UUID-checked event id — and no map/list/bytes field. A caller cannot put a URL, package name, label, location, or free-form JSON anywhere; there is no field and unknown keys are declined. A reflection test pins the single-String property so a future field addition fails loudly.

**Verified.** `AccountabilityEventContractTest` (13 tests): all six categories round-trip; minute flooring; deterministic bounded encoding; rejection of 12 prohibited-field names; non-UUID ids rejected in builder and decoder; unknown version/kind/category/enum and wrong types declined; kind/category mismatch and per-kind field presence enforced; invalid sequences/ranges declined; malformed bytes never throw; delivery states match §8.4 exactly.

**Consequences / honest limits.** The category is a client-authored claim, not cryptographic proof of what happened — a compromised sender could misreport its own category (plan §5 accepts this). No content category means a partner learns "a blocked app attempt" without knowing which kind of content; that is more private and satisfies FR2, and can be widened only by a schema version that both ends understand. The 512-byte bound is far below the relay's 4096-byte ciphertext ceiling, leaving room for the envelope.

## #197 — Step 4 Extends the Existing Chain Tables Instead of Adding a Parallel Outbox (2026-10-21)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; full JVM suite green; device migration v12→v13 proven on the X6532.

**Context.** The partner accountability event-delivery plan's Step 4 (§8.9) asks for a durable sender outbox with event id, install identity, relationship, per-relationship sequence, schema version, prepared envelope, delivery state, idempotency key, attempts, next attempt, expiry, and last error code, plus two uniqueness constraints and a pending-work index. Its logical schema names a standalone `partner_event_outbox` table and a `relationship_sequence` table. The repository already had two databases: `AppRulesStore` (SQLCipher — rules, journals, plaintext until an envelope exists) and `AccountabilityDatabase` (plain FBE — chain rows, `outbox`, `processed_events`, enrollment public keys). Appendix S1.7 established that new sender-side event rows belong with the existing chain/outbox state and the detector journal stays in SQLCipher, and that `events.event_id` is the link between them. Creating a second outbox would duplicate the drain, split delivery state across two rows for one event, and add a synchronization problem between them.

**Decision.**

1. **Split schema, one row per concept.** The chain row gains `events.event_id` (TEXT, the Step 3 wire UUID) with a unique index `(pair_id, sender_key_id, event_id)`; NULL is exempt because SQLite treats NULLs as distinct, which is exactly what pre-contract and gap-marker rows need. `outbox` already pointed at `events.id`; it stays the delivery row. The journal (`partner_event_journal`, AppRulesStore v18) holds the plaintext minimized body until reconcile builds the envelope.
2. **Identity mapping.** `sender_install_id` = `sender_key_id` = SHA-256 of the install's signing public key (`EnrollmentTranscript.senderKeyId`), regenerated on re-enrollment/clear-data; `relationship_id` = `pair_id`; `relationship_seq` = `events.sequence`. The two §8.9 uniqueness constraints are therefore the pre-existing sequence index plus the new event-id index — no new columns needed for identity.
3. **Transactional allocation.** Sequence read, head advance, chain-row insert, and outbox-row insert remain inside one `withWriteTransaction`; `expires_at = createdAt + 30 days` is stamped in that same transaction. A failed outbox insert now rolls back the chain append (previously the append could report success with no durable delivery row).
4. **Backoff and due filtering.** `OutboxBackoff` computes the retry time deterministically from `(messageId, attemptCount)`: first retry 30–60 s, doubling, capped at 6 h, per-message jitter so a fleet never retries in lockstep. The drain selects `PENDING`, `next_attempt_at <= now`, unexpired, in chain order, and records a closed error code (`FirebaseFirestoreException.Code` name or `TRANSPORT`), never exception text.
5. **Retention (§8.7).** Every drain first runs `expireDue`: a `PENDING` row past its window becomes `EXPIRED` (state recorded, row kept) and ciphertext is cleared from both `PENDING` and `SENT` rows past the window — the relay's copy dies on the same 30-day cap. Migration 12→13 backfills `expires_at` for pre-existing rows so no queued work is silently immortal.
6. **Migration and rollback.** `MIGRATION_12_13` adds the column/index/outbox fields; `MIGRATION_13_12` rebuilds both tables from the exact v12 DDL and copies every row, because `DROP COLUMN` needs SQLite 3.35 (API 34) and minSdk is 26 — a downgrade is a schema step, never a data loss (the D-33 convention). `AppRulesStore` gains v17→v18 with the journal table and the matching `MIGRATION_18_17`.
7. **Backup exclusion.** `allowBackup="false"` and both extraction-rule files exclude databases, shared prefs, the rules snapshot, and datastore — no counter, chain, outbox, or crypto state can enter a cloud backup, which satisfies the plan's exclusion requirement without inventing a restore path.

**Interpretation notes (from the plan's literal field list).** `schema_version` lives inside the prepared, signed envelope (Step 3 body `v=1`) rather than as a duplicate column: nothing in Steps 4/6 routes by version before decryption, and a second copy of the value could disagree. The "scoped idempotency key" is `outbox.message_id` — minted once, reused byte-for-byte by every retry, and equal to the create-only mailbox document id — while the `(pair, sender, event_id)` scope is enforced by the unique index. `outbox.status` is unconstrained TEXT that admits all seven §8.4 states; Step 4 reaches `PENDING`, `SENT`, and `EXPIRED`; `IN_FLIGHT`, `ACKNOWLEDGED_BY_RECIPIENT`, `CANCELLED_BY_REVOCATION`, and `FAILED_NEEDS_REPAIR` acquire writers in Steps 5/6/10.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *New `partner_event_outbox` + `relationship_sequence` tables per §8.9 literally* — two outboxes, two drains, and a cross-table consistency problem for state that describes one event; rejected. (b) *Ride only the chain tables with no outbox columns* — no durable backoff/retention metadata, and expiry would have to be derived per row at drain time; rejected. (c) *Store `schema_version` as a column* — duplicate source of truth for a value already inside the signed bytes; rejected. (d) *DELETE expired rows* — destroys the delivery state the partner-summary and monitoring surfaces must report; rejected in favor of `EXPIRED` + ciphertext clearing.

**Verified.** Full JVM suite 1,884 tests, 0 failures (2026-10-21), including `ChainStateStoreTest` 38 (4 new: wire-id idempotency on local and remote paths, retention stamping, outbox-failure rollback), `AccountabilityDatabaseMigrationTest` 13 (forward 12→13 preserving seeded queued work; rollback 13→12 preserving every row), `PartnerEventJournalDaoTest` 4 (both row shapes, pairing cut-off + expiry + order + limit, boundary-strict sweep, entity contract), `EnrollmentDaoTest` (its v1 fixture now uses a true v1 entity because the live entity's generated DDL already carries `event_id`), plus the re-run concurrency, reopen-durability, and drainer byte-identical tests. Device X6532 2026-10-21 (`install -r`, never uninstall; force-stop; relaunch): accountability DB `user_version` 12→13, every pre-migration row count identical (events 0, outbox 0, chain_heads 0, enrollments 1, processed_events 17, approval_requests 0, unpair_state 1, identity_epoch 1), the three new outbox columns and both events indexes present, no `.corrupt` files; rules DB v17→v18 opened intact with Home stats and all five rules unchanged. Full detail in the plan's Appendix S4.

**Consequences / honest limits.** The device outbox was empty, so the live-row `expires_at` backfill is JVM-proven (seeded rows) but not device-proven. "Process death" validation is transaction atomicity plus a reopen stand-in, not real SIGKILL fault injection; the true kill test belongs to the Step 11 device matrix and is not claimed here. `schema_version` and the install/relationship ids are not queryable on the outbox row itself — they are reachable through the `events` join, which every drain path already performs. Backoff state is persisted per row, so the 15-minute worker cadence is an upper bound on retry latency, not the retry interval itself.

## #198 — Step 5 Is a Verification Gate: the Existing Relay Already Implements the Mailbox Contract (2026-10-21)

**Status:** Accepted; gate PASS with no code change; both server suites re-run green.

**Context.** The partner accountability event-delivery plan's Step 5 asks for the relay API: authenticated upload of an opaque envelope, recipient-only fetch, ack, stable acceptance receipt for retries, per-sender/per-pair limits, and no plaintext or payload logging. The mailbox pipeline predates this plan (built for the pairing transport), so the step could be either new code or a proof that the existing pipeline meets the contract. The plan's step is written to allow both; the honest work is to map every requirement to code and run the suites, not to rewrite a working pipeline.

**Decision.** Step 5 closes as a gate, not a construction step. The requirement-to-code mapping (recorded in the plan's Appendix S5) is: upload = create-only mailbox document under a client-minted id, authorized by rules (`request.auth.uid == senderUid`, sender is an active-pair member, recipient is the pair's other member — ADR #194); fetch = recipient-only read/list on `mailboxes/{recipientUid}`; ack = recipient-side `ackedAt` transition with ownership enforced both in rules and in the relay; stable receipt = the document id is the client's `message_id`, so a retry is a create-collision the relay treats as already accepted; opaque payload = the 4096 decoded-byte cap and no plaintext field in rules or relay code; limits = 10 per pair per minute and 200 per sender per day, charged after authorization; no payload logging = relay logs ids and closed error codes only.

**Interpretation notes.** (a) "Authenticated installation identity" on the wire is Firebase uid auth plus pairing-membership authorization; the *installation* is proven cryptographically on the receiving side by the signed envelope from Step 3/4, which is stricter than authenticating a device token at the relay. (b) The stable acceptance receipt is the create-only document plus the explicit `relayStatus` markers the client already reads; there is no separate receipt table to keep consistent. (c) The plan permits deleting local ciphertext after relay acceptance; the implementation keeps it until the 30-day cap because the same bytes are the repair path (Step 10) for a recipient that never received or acknowledged — permitted, not required, and recorded here so it is a decision rather than an accident.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Build a second relay endpoint specific to accountability events* — duplicates auth, limits, retention, and cleanup for the same mailbox; rejected. (b) *Add an installation-token header to the relay* — the relay never sees plaintext, and the crypto proof lives on the recipient side; a relay-side device identity would add a credential to guard without closing a reachable gap; rejected. (c) *Delete local ciphertext on acceptance* — saves disk but removes the repair source; rejected for now.

**Verified.** `npm test` in `functions/`: 104/104. `npm run test:rules` against the Firestore emulator: 17/17, including cross-partner isolation (ADR #194's fix), create-only replay, oversize, and rate-limit cases. No application or server code changed in this step; the tree change is documentation only (the plan's Appendix S5 and this ADR).

**Consequences / honest limits.** A message rejected by the relay after storage (rate limit, pairing revoked) remains as a stored document until cleanup — it is never delivered and never readable by a foreign user. A crash between relay acceptance and the first dispatch record leaves the message fetched on next client sync (Step 6), not pushed; that ordering is intentional and Step 6 owns the backstop. The rules fix from ADR #194 is still undeployed in production (owner action), so the deployed rules are weaker than this gate's verified state. **Revision 2026-10-21:** deployed and verified in production — see ADR #199 / Appendix S6.

## #199 — Step 6 Hardens the Ack Window and Makes Notification Health Actionable Instead of Assumed (2026-10-21)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; full JVM suite green; device-proven on the X6532 and the API-37 AVD; ADR #194 rules deployed.

**Context.** The partner accountability event-delivery plan's Step 6 requires the receive path to fetch after push, on start/resume, and on the scheduled pass; decrypt, validate, sequence-check, deduplicate, persist, then acknowledge; check notification permission, channel enablement, and provider registration at onboarding with a user-triggered test notification; banner when notifications are off or the provider is unsupported; and (for the DMS availability notice only) at most one six-hour reminder per install/relationship/outage generation. The receive pipeline predates this plan and already implemented the ordering, so the honest work was to find and close the gaps rather than rebuild it. Two real gaps existed: the chain commit and the ack are not atomic, and the only health signal was a raw `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` check that could not see a muted channel or a missing push provider.

**Decision.**

1. **Ack completion on re-delivery.** `MailboxMessageHandler` already short-circuits `ALREADY_PROCESSED` before any fetch (AD-10b). It now retries the idempotent, create-only ack before returning: a process death between chain commit and ack leaves the message unacked, and the next delivery completes the ack without re-applying the event. A failed retry is swallowed — the message stays unacked and retryable, which is the safe direction.
2. **One health model, three actionable states.** `PartnerAlertHealth` reports `NOTIFICATIONS_OFF` (permission or app-level), `CHANNEL_OFF` (`partner_alerts` importance NONE), `PROVIDER_UNSUPPORTED` (Google Play services unavailable) in precedence order — a local switch the user can flip outranks a device capability. A channel that does not exist yet counts as enabled: the absence of a switch is not a mute.
3. **Surfaces, not a gate.** The Partner tab renders a banner per state with the matching fix path (permission dialog on API 33+ while still requestable, app notification settings afterwards, channel settings via `ACTION_CHANNEL_NOTIFICATION_SETTINGS` with package and channel id, or no action for the provider). The pairing ceremony's terminal panel shows the same states. Pairing itself is never blocked by notification health: blocking enforcement works independently of notifications, and coupling an unrelated capability to a notification permission would make the wrong thing fail. (**Test alert removed 2026-11-05** — see Consequences.)
4. **User-triggered test alert (removed 2026-11-05 — see Consequences).** `PartnerNotifications.notifyTestAlert` posts on the real `partner_alerts` channel with a dedicated id (2006) and tag, so it proves the same display path a real alert uses without replacing one. This is the only honest proof of display the platform offers.
5. **Startup channel agreement.** `ensurePartnerAlertsChannel` runs at application start and is create-only. Re-creating an existing channel can silently rewrite its importance (device-observed 2026-10-04), which would turn a healthy channel into `CHANNEL_OFF` behind the user's back.
6. **Fetch triggers unchanged and verified.** Push wakes (`onMessageReceived`, `onNewToken`, `onDeletedMessages`), foreground/permission/settings resume, and the 15-minute periodic worker all route into the same `PartnerSyncCoordinator.syncOnce`; the mailbox, not the push channel, is the source of truth.

**Interpretation notes.** (a) "Provider registration" as an onboarding check is satisfied by the sync pass's `PushInstallationRegistrar`, which registers provider+token and records a truthful `pushEligible` snapshot on every pass. It is deliberately not a banner state: registration failures are transient (offline, token rotation, first-run timing) and the mailbox pull still delivers, while a banner implies a user fix that does not exist. Only provider *unsupported* is persistent and user-visible. (b) The DMS six-hour availability reminder is **deferred to Step 8**, not dropped: it needs `outage_generation` and the DMS availability notice, both created by Steps 7/8; implementing it now would invent the generation identity. No reminder of any kind ships in Step 6, which also satisfies "no per-event reminders." (c) The health model reads only `partner_alerts`; approval and nudge channels keep their own paths and are not repainted by this step.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Leave the ack gap to dedup-only semantics* — a permanently unacked message is re-fetched forever and pollutes the relay's retention accounting; rejected. (b) *Gate pairing on notification permission* — couples blocking (which does not use notifications) to an alert channel and blocks a legitimate pairing over a fixable setting; rejected in favor of a persistent banner. (c) *Banner on token/FID registration failure* — transient and not user-fixable, and the event still arrives via pull; rejected as noise. (d) *Re-create the channel to force HIGH importance* — Android cannot raise an existing channel's importance and recreation can lower it; rejected in favor of create-only. (e) *Implement the DMS reminder now* — wrong layer, invents Step 7/8 state; rejected and recorded.

**Verified.** Full JVM suite `./gradlew testDebugUnitTest`: 1,890 tests, 0 failures, including `PartnerAlertHealthTest` (4 precedence cases), `PartnerNotificationsTest.testAlert_ridesThePartnerAlertsChannel_withoutReplacingARealAlert`, and the two ack-completion pins in `MailboxMessageHandlerTest` (22 total). Device X6532 (2026-10-21): OK state posts test alert id 2006 / tag `partner_alerts_test` / channel `partner_alerts` / importance 4 in the tray and `dumpsys notification`; revoking `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` shows `NOTIFICATIONS_OFF` and granting clears it; muting the channel shows `CHANNEL_OFF`, the deep link lands on the channel, re-enabling restores importance 4 without the app rewriting it. API-37 AVD: unpaired Partner tab shows the test row; with Google Play services disabled the `PROVIDER_UNSUPPORTED` banner renders, the push registrar refuses registration, and the rest of the app remains functional. Production/replay: `PartnerSyncScenariosInstrumentedTest` (new, production ceremony + live relay) passed duplicate, out-of-order/gap, valid-signature-invalid-ciphertext, and crash-window ack-completion stages; `PartnerRoundTripInstrumentedTest` passed gap repair; a live unauthenticated Firestore probe returned 403. The ADR #194 rules fix was deployed and the production ruleset (`42262fca-6962-4cf0-ac54-24fbf4a43a9e`) was fetched and confirmed to contain the recipient-membership gate. Full detail in the plan's Appendix S6.

**Consequences / honest limits.** `PROVIDER_UNSUPPORTED` is proven by disabling Google Play services on the emulator, not on a true non-GMS device. The ceremony's terminal health branches mirror the device-proven Partner-tab branches but were not themselves device-exercised, because that requires unpairing the live X6532 pair. The process-death validation seeds the post-commit/pre-ack state; a true SIGKILL mid-pass belongs to the Step 11 device matrix. A notification dropped by an OEM after a successful local post cannot be detected in-app — Android exposes no per-notification read receipt — which is exactly why the plan forbids reading provider acceptance as display. **Superseded in part by ADR #203 (Step 9):** the `partner_alerts` channel id is retired in favor of `partner_accountability_events_v1`; the health reading and test alert now use the new id, and the legacy id is deleted at startup. The precedence model and fix paths above are unchanged. **Revision 2026-11-05 (project closeout):** the user-triggered test alert was removed from the Partner tab, the pairing ceremony, `PartnerNotifications`, the strings and its test; there is no in-app test notification. `PartnerAlertHealth` remains the health surface, and display proof now rests on an actually delivered alert plus the device's own notification state. The 2026-10-21 device evidence above is the historical record of the removed path, not a claim that it still ships.

## #200 — Step 7 Rides the Existing Enforcement FGS, and the Heartbeat Carries Only Liveness (2026-10-21)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; `submitHeartbeat` deployed; device-proven on the X6532; two validation items blocked by hardware and recorded as limits.

**Context.** The partner accountability event-delivery plan's Step 7 asks for authenticated best-effort availability and a truthful monitoring-health snapshot. The conditional it sets is strict: piggyback an existing, legitimately active Monitoring FGS if one exists; never add or keep a service alive solely for heartbeat traffic; otherwise use WorkManager. The repository already runs `EnforcementForegroundService` (`specialUse`, subtype `app_blocking_and_daily_usage_limit_enforcement`) while enforcement is active, so the honest implementation is an additive beat on a service that already exists for a different, user-visible purpose — not a new liveness service.

**Decision.**

1. **The heartbeat rides the enforcement service.** `EnforcementForegroundService` calls `heartbeat.checkIn()` on its existing 10-minute `HEARTBEAT_TICKS` cadence; the client window is 15 minutes plus 0–2 minutes jitter (jitter only stretches), forced at service start when the authority stamp moved and at every observed `ProtectionAuthority` change. Nothing starts, restarts, or keeps the FGS alive for heartbeat traffic. The fallback is the production 15-minute periodic `PartnerSyncWorker` with `NetworkType.CONNECTED` (policy KEEP→UPDATE so already-installed devices adopt the constrained shape); `syncOnce` beats only after the unpaired early return.
2. **Only an accepted beat is liveness.** The server transaction on `dms_install_state/{uid}_{installId}` refuses `counter <= last_counter` as `STALE` (returning the server counter) and any beat inside the 30 s abuse floor as `RATE_LIMITED` (prior receipt stands); only an accepted beat increments `liveness_generation` and writes `last_received_at`, `last_counter`, and `next_deadline_at = last_received_at + 6 h`. The relay is identity-blind (ADR #198) and §8.10 forbids monitoring fields in plaintext metadata, so attributing mailbox traffic to an install would leak a stable device identifier to the relay; heartbeat beats are the liveness signal by design, not by omission.
3. **Counters burn, never reuse.** The client persists the next counter before the call. A failed or refused send burns its number — the server never saw it, and the next honest beat is a higher one. A client that lost its counter while keeping its namespace resyncs to `max(serverCounter, local)`; a new anonymous uid or reinstall is a fresh document starting at 1, so a lost counter can never lock a device out forever.
4. **App Standby is read, explained once, and never gated.** `checkStandby` reads `UsageStatsManager.getAppStandbyBucket()` at most once per 6 hours and once per process at the first check-in, persisting only the bucket name. `RARE`/`RESTRICTED` emits one non-intrusive snackbar per transition and re-arms after recovery. No new permission is requested, and no copy claims Unrestricted is required or guarantees delivery.
5. **The snapshot is journaled, consent-gated, and minimal.** `MonitoringSnapshotRecorder` journals a `MONITORING_STATUS` row on change or hourly (forced at service start/material change — a first stamp counts as material because a fresh process has proven nothing). `PartnerSyncCoordinator.reconcileEvents` then builds one sealed envelope per consenting pair and only for rows created at or after `availabilityEnabledSinceMs`, with `senderKeyId` as the install generation, an `OutboxAgeBucket` from the oldest pending outbox row, and the sequence allocated by `EventCreator.createBody` inside the create mutex (the event's own allocation, not a stale read).
6. **ACTIVE is a claim.** It requires a live FGS in this process AND an authority computed within 90 seconds. Alive-but-stale reports `UNKNOWN`; no service reports `UNAVAILABLE`; a snapshot not received for 2 hours degrades to `UNKNOWN` on the dashboard rather than showing a stale `ACTIVE`.
7. **The heartbeat carries nothing else.** Payload `{installId, counter}` only; the server row holds liveness counters, generations, receipt times, and the next deadline — never monitoring state, permissions, categories, or sequence numbers.

**Interpretation notes.** (a) "Count all fresh authenticated requests as liveness" is satisfied by accepted beats only, for the identity-leak reason above; replayed, stale, and floor-refused requests never count. (b) "Eligible check-ins" means hourly steady state plus forced snapshots at service start and material change; the change-debounce row advances even when no pair consents, so enabling sharing later cannot replay a stale transition. (c) Consent uses a watermark: a consenting pair receives only rows created at or after enabling, so enabling never backfills pre-consent monitoring history. (d) The six-hour partner alert is Step 8's; Step 7 writes `next_deadline_at` and leaves `last_notified_generation` at 0.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Add a heartbeat-only FGS* — explicitly forbidden by the plan and a battery cost for no user-visible function; rejected. (b) *Let the client choose the heartbeat window and treat its own timer as liveness* — the server would have no abuse floor and a stopped process would look alive; rejected. (c) *Carry monitoring state in the heartbeat* — §8.10 forbids plaintext monitoring fields, and the E2EE snapshot already exists for exactly this; rejected. (d) *Client-side deadline reminders* — a local timer cannot distinguish a dead device from a sleeping one, which is the fact the partner needs; server-owned deadlines; rejected. (e) *Tight-loop standby polling* — the plan forbids it and it burns battery for a diagnostic; rejected.

**Verified.** Full JVM suite: 218 classes / 1,935 tests / 0 failures / 0 errors / 0 skipped, including `PartnerHeartbeatClientTest` 13, `decideHeartbeat` unit 11, `MonitoringSnapshotRecorderTest` 9, `LivenessSnapshotTest` 4, `MonitoringSnapshotReceiverTest` 3, plus the monitoring queue and dashboard staleness tests. Server: `npm test` 115/115 (11 heartbeat-logic cases), `npm run test:rules` 18/18, `npm run test:heartbeat` (Firestore emulator) 12/12. Device X6532 (2026-10-21): main leg — production registration under App Check, first beat accepted, a forced beat inside the 30 s floor returned `RESYNCED` with `burned=17` and the prior acceptance intact, counter 18 accepted, `RESULT standby=EXEMPTED`, nothing posted; WM leg — no FGS before/during/after, real 15-minute floor waited, startup standby read, `RESULT wm=PASS counter=13`; no-network leg — `offline=FAILED burned=14 accepted=13`, then `offline=PASS counter=15` after recovery; snapshot sender half — `RESULT monitor=JOURNALED event=… state=UNAVAILABLE outbox=UNDER_1H`, delivered through the production relay, `RESULT monitor=LINKED pair=… linked=1`. The live FGS then advanced the production row to counter 23 / generation 16 with `next_deadline_at = last_received_at + 6 h`. Full detail in the plan's Appendix S7.

**Consequences / honest limits.** Reboot-before-unlock was not run: the X6532 is reachable only over wireless adb, which does not survive a reboot; Step 7 adds no boot path of its own, and the FGS re-arm behavior is device-proven under ADR #152. Rare/Restricted buckets are not device-observable on this hardware (deviceidle-whitelisted, bucket pinned `EXEMPTED`, instrumentation foregrounds the app); the mapping and once-per-transition notice are JVM-proven. Reinstall/clear-data was not run on the X6532 by owner rule (`install -r` only); the new-namespace and lost-counter paths are JVM- and emulator-proven. The snapshot receive half is JVM-proven, not peer-device-proven — rendering ACTIVE/Limited on a second device needs a second consenting device this environment does not have. WorkManager cadence is platform-owned: the leg proves one due pass end-to-end, not repeated periods over hours. A harness defect (asserting the persisted-before-send bump while cancelling the worker mid-call) was found and fixed; the product behavior was correct.

## #201 — Step 8 Uses the Database as the Deadline Queue and Pages the Operator Through Monitoring (2026-10-21)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented; four functions, the scheduler job, the composite index, the rules denials, and the alert policy deployed; 100k soak, emulator suite, and device leg green; one rollout finding recorded.

**Context.** The partner accountability event-delivery plan's Step 8 allows a durable delayed-job facility only if the existing infrastructure already supports scheduled execution, retry, idempotency, and stale-job validation; otherwise the deadline row itself is the job, read by a bounded indexed worker. It forbids a new queue service without separate cost/operations approval, forbids using a Redis Pub/Sub or key-expiry event as the sole trigger, requires compare-and-set state changes, requires the notification outbox to commit in the same transaction as the state transition, and requires a dispatch-time rejoin and consent recheck. It also requires a fleet circuit breaker that holds dispatch, pages the operator, and releases at a controlled rate. The repository's persistence is Firestore and its scheduler is Cloud Scheduler; no durable job queue existed.

**Decision.**

1. **The deadline row is the job; Cloud Scheduler is only the clock.** `dms_install_state.next_deadline_at` (written by Step 7's acceptance transaction) is the delayed job. `dmsDeadlineWorker` (gen 2, `*/5 * * * *` UTC, `maxInstances 1`, 300 s) runs a bounded due query — `.where('next_deadline_at','<=',now).orderBy('next_deadline_at').limit(dueBatch)` with `dueBatch` default 100 and clamped 1–500. No full-table scan, no new queue service.
2. **Every transition is compare-and-set, and the outbox commits with it.** `processDueRow` re-reads the row and validates the expected generation, receipt time, and not-yet-notified state; the state transition (`notice_state = NOTIFIED`, `outage_generation += 1`, `last_notified_generation`, deadline cleared) and a deterministic outbox document commit in one `runTransaction`. A stale or losing transaction writes neither — the plan's "stale jobs become no-ops" is the CAS result, not a separate cleanup path.
3. **Dispatch rejoins the authority.** `dispatchOutbox` reads `pairings/{relationshipId}` and requires `status == active`, both members present, and the monitored member's `availabilityConsent.{uid}.enabled === true`. Refusal marks the row `SUPPRESSED` rather than retrying (a revoked consent will not come back by retrying); expired `DISPATCHING` claims are requeued by lease, and provider failures back off deterministically to the attempt bound.
4. **Display is read-time derivation; only the six-hour notice is persisted.** `deriveAvailability` computes `CHECKING_IN` (<45 min), `LATE` (45–90), `NOT_CHECKING_IN` (≥90) and the coarse buckets at read time; `readPartnerStatus` returns no precise timestamp. Storing display states would create a second source of truth that can drift from receipt times. The only external transition the worker persists is the initial six-hour notice.
5. **Scheduler outages never rebase; ingestion outages do, separately.** Nothing in the worker writes `last_received_at`; catch-up processes the same receipt times. A heartbeat-ingestion outage is recorded by the operator-gated `recordIngestionOutage` callable (one open record at a time). While one is open the worker holds transitions AND dispatch; after close, rows whose interval overlapped it rebase to `max(last_received_at, relevant_outage_end) + 6 h`, and the read path applies the same compensation so the display never claims a false late state for a gap the operator acknowledged.
6. **The breaker holds dispatch and pages through monitoring, not through credentials in code.** When notified transitions exceed `late_burst_threshold` (default 50, clamped 1–100,000) in a pass, the worker writes `config/dms.dispatch_hold = true` plus incident fields and logs at ERROR. A Cloud Monitoring log-based alert policy on that line routes to the existing owner email channel and auto-closes after 24 h without a re-fire. The hold itself remains until an operator sets `dispatch_hold = false`; `dispatch_batch` bounds each release pass, so catch-up is controlled rather than a second burst.
7. **Client: intent is local, authority is server, acknowledgement is memory-only.** `PartnerSyncCoordinator.syncPair` converges `PairProfileSharing.shareAvailability` through `setAvailabilityConsent` on every pass — but only when a local sharing row exists, because no row means this install never expressed a choice and a second install must not overwrite a value it did not set. The write is a dotted-path update (`availabilityConsent.{uid}`) so one member's entry never erases the other's. `PartnerDmsClient` caches acks in memory and the status read for 60 s, never invents a reading on failure, and retries an unacked value on the next pass. `PartnerScreen.PartnerConnectionCard` renders consent, the three display states, and the no-data state as a third card distinct from monitoring and sync health (§8.13). `availability_alerts_v1` is created at startup, create-only, `IMPORTANCE_HIGH` — the channel Step 6's deferred six-hour reminder needed.
8. **The dispatched notice is generic, and the server owns its copy.** `buildDmsMessage` sends fixed OS copy (silent/recovered), a data-only generic sync key (`{v:'1', type:'SYNC_AVAILABLE'}`), high priority because it produces a visible notification, a TTL, and `channelId=availability_alerts_v1` — no relationship id, uid, install id, category, or precise time, so a notification holder learns nothing beyond "check the partner tab". The app fills in state by an authenticated read when it syncs. This also closes the plan's Step 6 deferral: at most one notice per `(install_id, relationship_id, outage_generation)` (the outage generation is the idempotency key), and at most one recovery.

**Interpretation notes.** (a) The delayed-job facility is the deadline row; the row carries retry (next tick), idempotency (CAS + deterministic outbox id), and stale-job validation (generation/receipt re-read) — the plan's conditional required no more. (b) "Page the operator" is a monitoring alert on a log line, not an in-code side effect: the worker holds and logs; the policy notifies. (c) The client ack cache is memory-only because offline revocation is "pending until acknowledged" by contract, and a process death should re-send the idempotent callable rather than persist a completion flag that could lie. (d) A local sharing row gates convergence for multi-install safety. (e) Consent entries are per member on one document. (f) The connection card is distinct from monitoring/sync because it reports a different fact ("the app talked to the server"); mixing them would imply one causes another.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Introduce Cloud Tasks or Pub/Sub* — the plan forbids a new queue service without separate cost/operations approval, and the existing database already supports scheduled execution through the scheduler clock plus bounded reads; rejected. (b) *Persist display states on the install row* — drift and a second source of truth; rejected. (c) *Page from worker code via the Admin SDK* — needs credentials and a delivery mechanism that Cloud Monitoring already provides; rejected. (d) *Converge consent on every install unconditionally* — a second install of the same identity would overwrite a choice it never made; rejected. (e) *Nested-merge the consent object* — erases the sibling member's entry (the Firestore nested-merge trap already recorded for the pairing record); dotted paths chosen. (f) *Treat a late worker as an ingestion outage* — only an operator can assert heartbeats were not arriving; a late worker changes when a transition is observed, never the device's receipt time; rejected.

**Verified.** Server: functions unit `npm test` 131/131; DMS emulator `npm run test:dms` 28/28 covering stale jobs, concurrent workers, CAS races, transaction-crash structure, lease requeue, scheduler outage, ingestion outage, correlated-client burst, and bounded catch-up; 100k soak PASS (100,000 installs, 1,000 due, due query 100 rows/3,297 ms, 10 passes, median 9.9 s, p95 11.2 s under the 60 s bound, exactly 1,000 notifications and 1,000 outbox rows, future rows untouched). JVM: 1,952 tests, 0 failures, including `PartnerDmsClientTest` 12 and five new coordinator consent tests. Device X6532 (`PartnerDmsInstrumentedTest`, OK): `RESULT channel=HIGH id=availability_alerts_v1`; no local row → nothing written, partner read `consent=false` (`noLocalRow=PASS`); explicit toggle through the production pass → partner read `consent=true` (`consentOn=PASS`); client status about an unconsented partner `NO_DATA` (`statusAboutUnconsentedPartner=PASS`); after the partner set its own scope through the deployed callable, `consent=true` (`statusAboutConsentedPartner=PASS`); revocation through the pass → `consent=false` (`consentOff=PASS`); foreign pair refused without throwing (`refusedWrites=PASS`); nothing posted; `RESULT dms=PASS`. The production pairing document contains both members' entries (`B: enabled=true`, `A: enabled=false`), proving the dotted-path update preserved the sibling. Deployment: `setAvailabilityConsent`, `readPartnerStatus`, `recordIngestionOutage`, and `dmsDeadlineWorker` ACTIVE in `us-central1` (2026-10-21T18:30Z; App Check enforced on all callables), scheduler job ENABLED at `*/5`, outbox composite index READY, ruleset `75b62e73-5feb-463c-8514-4c0407f0c7ca` with all three deny-all matches, alert policy `projects/myexodus-53804/alertPolicies/12571310519408075705` enabled to channel `18347258884556077313`. The first production tick after the index became READY returned HTTP 200 in 0.64 s with `due=0 … dispatchHeld=false sent=0`. Full detail in the plan's Appendix S8.

**Consequences / honest limits.** The 100k soak runs on the Firestore emulator: it proves bounded query shape, batching, and pass cost, not production multitenancy; staged production load is Step 12's. A crash between transition and outbox is not representable — atomicity is the proof — and a crash immediately after commit is exercised structurally by the dispatch tests that start from a committed PENDING row, not by SIGKILL. The device leg reads `NO_DATA` because the virtual partner never heartbeats; the 45/90-minute and six-hour derivations are emulator-proven, and a two-device live display is Step 11's matrix.
