(c) *Auto-restore the cloud snapshot when it is missing* — a restore replaces the whole database, needs the backup key, and is the user's decision; the card links to that flow instead; rejected. (d) *Fail the import permanently on a transient network error* — the guard returns `Unavailable` with a retry action and the quarantine stays for its full seven days; rejected. (e) *Inline the conflict choice into the restore flow* — the import coordinator already owns the quarantine and the dry run; routing the choice back through it keeps one writer and one journal; rejected as more moving parts.

**Verified (2026-10-30).** JVM: `BackupImportGuardTest` 7/7 (no pointer → proceed; materialized → proceed without rewriting anchors; unmaterialized → `RestoreRequired` with the observed high-water persisted; rollback → hard stop, nothing persisted; equivocation → hard stop; unreadable pointer → `Unavailable`; unreadable anchors → `Unavailable`). `GuestImportCoordinatorTest` 15/15, including `localDataWithANewerCloudSnapshot_offersTheConflictChoice` (BaseConflict shown, local rows and quarantine untouched), `mergeIntoThisDeviceOnly_importsTheGuestRows_andLeavesTheCloudSnapshotAlone` (option b imports, journal written, pointer untouched), `preserveLocalForRestore_thenBothSnapshotsImportAfterTheCloudIsMaterialized` (marker staged with the target's rows, both import additively after the restore, final state includes both habits), plus the earlier `aCloudSnapshotThatIsNotMaterialized_blocksTheImportUntilItIsRestored`, `aConfirmReChecksTheCloudAndStopsOnAHardConflict` and `anUnverifiableCloudBase_isNeverImportedInto`. `LocalSessionManagerTest` 19/19 unchanged. Device legs (real backup-key account + bucket round trip) run under #45/#47 on the API-37 AVD and the X6532.

## #247 — Backup Expansion Bound Recalibrated to 100:1 From Measured Real History

**Status:** Accepted; implemented and JVM-verified 2026-10-31 (account plan §6.6 item 6; §16 item 10; supersedes the 5:1 bound and ADR #246 consequence 2).

**Context.** ADR #246 shipped the payload enforcing the plan's maximum 5:1 uncompressed:compressed ratio on both creation and restore — its alternative (f) rejected enforcing it only on restore, because an uploaded object the restorer must refuse is worse than a refused creation. Its consequence (2) recorded the risk honestly: a legitimate snapshot that compresses better than 5:1 is refused, and v2 must revisit the bound "if real data ever hits it." Plan §16 item 10 asked for exactly that measurement before Release 2: "Measure representative and high-history fixtures… if legitimate text-only snapshots exceed the cap, change the envelope/storage limits in a separately versioned spec."

**Measurement (2026-10-31, JVM, exact payload records through `LogicalSnapshotCodec`, standard deflate).** Attempt rows as the app records them (rule id from a 50-rule set, target from a 200-app set, two thirds BLOCKED) plus recovery sessions carrying a ~75-byte journal entry:

| attempts | sessions | uncompressed | compressed | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 50 | 161,223 | 6,439 | 25.04:1 |
| 5,000 | 200 | 789,273 | 26,776 | 29.48:1 |
| 10,000 | 400 | 1,578,723 | 51,680 | 30.55:1 |
| 20,000 | 800 | 3,157,623 | 100,085 | 31.55:1 |
| 50,000 | 1,500 | 7,724,823 | 238,611 | 32.37:1 |
| 100,000 | 2,000 | 15,108,823 | 463,052 | 32.63:1 |
| 150,000 | 2,000 | 22,321,323 | 682,030 | 32.73:1 |

Driving the real writer (`BackupPayload.write`) with 10, 25, 50, 100, 200 and 1,000 attempts returned `TooLarge: snapshot exceeds the 5:1 expansion limit` every time. The feature could not back up any user with block history — not an edge case, the default state of an active user. Plan §16 item 10's answer is "yes, legitimate text-only snapshots exceed the bound." Neither absolute cap is close: even 150,000 attempts is 22.3 MB uncompressed / 682 KB compressed against 100 MiB / 20 MiB.

**Decision.** `BackupPayload.MAX_EXPANSION` is **100** (was 5); both the creation check and the restore cap `min(100 MiB, 100 × compressedLength)` use it. Everything else is unchanged: 100 MiB uncompressed, 20 MiB compressed, 21 MiB object, 16 MiB per record, streaming on both sides, GCM before decompression.

**Why 100.** The measured worst case is 32.73:1 — 3.05× headroom. Real data diversifies (unique timestamps, free-text journals) and compresses less as it grows. The absolute 100 MiB cap still binds decompression work: a 20 MiB compressed object can never expand past 100 MiB whatever this constant is, and records are streamed, never materialized whole. Deterministic-repeat bombs still fail the ratio: the existing 60 KB compressed bomb and the 200 KB single-record fixture both exceed 100:1 and remain refused.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Keep 5:1 and accept that no active user can back up* — the feature would be dead on arrival; rejected. (b) *Remove the ratio check entirely* — the absolute cap alone bounds output, but the ratio is a cheap second layer and the plan requires a bounded expansion; rejected. (c) *Exclude attempt history from the payload* — §6.4 item 6/§17 require the logical history in the backup; rejected. (d) *Split large snapshots across objects* — new partitioning, manifest and restore machinery for no benefit under the absolute caps; rejected. (e) *Raise the absolute caps* — unnecessary; the largest measured fixture uses 22% of the uncompressed cap and 3% of the compressed cap; rejected.

**Verified (2026-10-31).** `:app:testDebugUnitTest --tests "com.example.myexodus.backup.*" --tests "com.example.myexodus.account.GuestQuarantineCodecTest"` **152 tests across 15 classes, 0 failures, 0 errors, 0 skipped**, including the new `BackupPayloadTest.aHighHistoryTextOnlySnapshotStaysFarBelowTheCompressedCap` (150,000 attempts + 2,000 sessions + 60 milestones round-trip; asserts both absolute caps with the measured sizes in the assertion message), the still-refused `aSnapshotThatWouldBlowUpOnRestoreIsNeverProduced` (200,000-byte single entry) and `expansionBomb_isStoppedBeforeItCanFillTheHeap` (60,000-byte compressed bomb). The full-suite and device gates re-run under #45/#47.

**Consequences / honest limits.** (1) The plan's §6.6 item 6 ratio text is superseded here; a dated amendment note is added where the clause appears. (2) A payload that still compresses above 100:1 is refused at creation by design — that needs roughly three times the repetition of the measured worst fixture. (3) The check runs after `stream.finish()`; a snapshot that trips it surfaces through R2.14's upload surface as a size refusal, never as a partially written object. (4) The measurement is JVM-only; it uses the same `LogicalSnapshotCodec` records and standard deflate the runtime uses, and no physical-device renderer exists for this constant.

## #248 — App Check Enforcement Stays On; the Plan's "Off in v1" Clauses Are Superseded, and Non-GMS Limits Are Stated

**Status:** Accepted; reconciliation of live production controls with the plan, recorded 2026-10-31 under the Release 3 audit (account plan §2.1 item 28, §6.7, §10 item 17, §11, §13 risk table, §17 item 30, §18 item 14; discharges the deferral ADR #226 alternative (d) recorded).

**Context.** The plan states in five places that App Check enforcement stays **off** in v1: §2.1 item 28 ("Keep enforcement disabled… use Auth, rules, callable authorization and rate limits as the actual controls"), §6.7 ("App Check telemetry only in v1"), §10 item 17 ("enforcement remains disabled in v1"), §17 item 30 ("App Check enforcement remains disabled; direct-APK and non-GMS support claims match actual device test results") and §18 item 14 ("App Check remains non-blocking"). §11 adds "App Check failures must not block v1 core functionality", and the §13 risk table scores "App Check configuration locks out sideloaded users" as Low *because* enforcement is off.

The implementation went the other way on the owner's explicit 2026-09-19 ruling: Firestore is enforced project-wide, and every deployed callable carries `enforceAppCheck: true` (`registerPairing`, `submitHeartbeat`, the three DMS callables, the four backup callables, the deletion callables, `relayMailboxMessage`, `appendUserEvent`) except the deliberately open read-only `getClientCompatibility`, so an outdated client can still learn why it is refused (§8.10). Identity Toolkit is deliberately **not** enforced, because anonymous sign-in necessarily precedes any App Check token. ADR #226 recorded the conflict rather than disabling a live control and deferred the reconciliation; this ADR closes it.

**Decision.**

1. **Enforcement stays on.** The owner's later ruling wins over the plan text (instruction hierarchy: the owner's explicit decision supersedes an earlier plan clause). Firestore remains enforced project-wide; every callable remains `enforceAppCheck: true` except the deliberately open read-only `getClientCompatibility` (§8.10).
2. **App Check is not the authorization boundary and never becomes one.** Every endpoint still authenticates, checks the profile/pair state, validates the exact input shape and applies the server-owned token buckets. The live abuse probe (failure-injection matrix, 2026-10-31) proves the layers independently: App Check alone → `401 sign-in required`; a valid ID token with no App Check token → `401 Unauthenticated`; both present with junk input → the validation error, never a write.
3. **Non-GMS devices lose cloud features by design; local core does not.** A device without Play services (or without the Play Integrity verdict) cannot mint an App Check token, so callables and Firestore fail closed. Blocking, the accessibility overlay, the local database, the usage ledger, the journal, insights computed locally and the recovery resources are all unaffected — none of them touches either service. `PushInstallationRegistrar` wraps token registration in a catch and skips it (requirement 27) instead of failing the app. Backup/restore, pairing, partner sync, SOS relay and account deletion are unavailable on such a device; existing copy surfaces the callable failure (retry), and no separate "this phone cannot use cloud features" screen exists in v1 — stated here as a known limit, not hidden.
4. **The test and debug rails stay exactly as shipped.** Debug builds may install the debug App Check provider through `AppCheckInstaller.factoryOverride` (gated to emulator/debug shapes); instrumented tests seed a per-run debug token through `AppCheckTestSupport`; the release build wires only `PlayIntegrityAppCheckProviderFactory`. Release builds for sideloaded distribution use the documented Play Integrity settings only — no Basic Integrity requirement, no Preview reCAPTCHA provider, no custom attestation provider.
5. **The plan's claims are amended, not ignored.** Dated notes are added at §2.1 item 28, §6.7, §10 item 17, §11, the §13 risk table, §17 item 30 and §18 item 14 pointing here.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Disable enforcement to match the plan* — turns off a live production control the owner ordered on, and the only effect is to widen the attack surface; rejected. (b) *Add a reCAPTCHA or custom attestation provider for non-GMS devices* — the plan forbids depending on the Preview reCAPTCHA provider, custom attestation is out of v1 scope, and a second trust root needs its own key management and incident path; rejected. (c) *Split into a second, unenforced Firebase project for non-GMS users* — doubles rules, functions, monitoring, budgets and deletion machinery for a device class with no tested user; rejected. (d) *Enforce only on the backup/deletion callables and leave Firestore open* — the partner mailbox and profile data are the largest surface; partial enforcement is harder to reason about than either extreme; rejected. (e) *Keep enforcement and document the non-GMS consequence* — chosen.

**Verified.** Enforcement state is read back live (Firestore ENFORCED project-wide since 2026-09-19; `enforceAppCheck: true` on the deployed callables, confirmed by the 2026-10-31 probe's 401/401/validation sequence on `beginBackup`, `initializeBackupKeyBundle`, `commitBackupManifest`, `requestAccountDeletion` and `requestGuestDataDeletion`). The emulator suites (12/12 green, 2026-10-31: rules, append, lifecycle, heartbeat, dms, dms-soak, transition, backup-key, backup-upload, storage-rules, deletion, sos) run through the debug-token rail because the emulator cannot pass Play Integrity. The X6532 is a GMS device and is unaffected. No non-GMS physical device exists in this project's test set, so the non-GMS limitation is stated from the provider's documented behavior, not from a device run — that absence is the honest gap in this ADR.

**Consequences / honest limits.** (1) Plan clauses are superseded by dated notes; the ADR is the authority. (2) Any future non-GMS support claim must come with a device-verified surface and a provider decision — it does not exist today. (3) The debug-token rail means emulator test results prove callable logic, not attestation; the attestation boundary is production-only and has never been exercised end-to-end by a non-release build. (4) Deletion and backup callables still enforce auth/profile/input/rate limits independently, so an App Check outage degrades availability, never authorization.

## #249 — Named Batches Are One Object to the Partner, and Rule Identity Rides the Wire (owner mandate, 2026-10-31)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented and JVM-verified 2026-10-31. Extends ADR #226 (per-rule assignment and routing) and supersedes its consequence "the recipient feed shows a verb without the rule's identity" and its alternative (e) "no notification for rule changes".

**Context.** The owner asked for one grouped object instead of dozens of individual rules: create a named batch ("Social media") containing apps and websites, preview the whole list, assign one partner, and have every partner-facing surface speak in the batch's terms — "you've been added to the Social media batch", "Social media (5 items)", and blocked-attempt alerts that name the batch. ADR #226 had shipped per-rule journaling with a UUID-only wire body and a deliberately nameless recipient feed, because at that time no name exchange existed and the closed allowlist of ADR #196 forbade free text. The owner has now explicitly made naming the target a product requirement, so the identity must be added without reopening the unbounded-body hole that ADR #196 closed.

**Decision.**

1. **Membership is denormalized on the rule rows** — schema v23 adds `batch_id` and `batch_name` to `restriction_rules` (additive `ALTER`s; `MIGRATION_22_23` upgrades, `MIGRATION_23_22` rebuilds the v22 table). There is no separate batch table: a batch is exactly the set of rules sharing a `batch_id`, which means the block engine, expiry sweep and policy bump keep operating on plain rules with no second write path to keep consistent.
2. **Creation is one transaction and one journal row per assigned pair.** `RulesRepository.insertBatch` validates every member, inserts them with `insertBatchAndBump`, and journals `CREATED` through `batchJournalRows`: for each non-null `assigned_pair_id`, exactly one row whose wire `rule_id` is the batch UUID, whose identity is `targetType = BATCH`, `label` = the batch name, `itemCount` = that pair's member count. An unassigned batch journals nothing.
3. **The whole batch verb set is batch-level.** Pause → one `DISABLED` row per assigned pair; resume → one `UPDATED` row and every member's `blockExpiresAt` is cleared, so a lapsed end date cannot make the sweep flip a resumed batch straight back off (owner rule #18: resume means "on again, no end date"); delete → one `DELETED` row that still states the batch size; `removeBatchPartner` → one `UNASSIGNED` row routed to the old pair, and a second call journals nothing because no member carries a partner any more.
4. **Expiry distinguishes whole from partial.** When every member of a batch has lapsed in one sweep, the partner gets one `EXPIRED` batch row with the member count; when only some members lapse, each lapsed member is told individually with `batchLabel` set to the batch name, and the surviving members keep blocking. This is the honest shape: the partner is told the batch ended only when the batch actually ended.
5. **Wire v2: a bounded, sanitized identity.** The sealed `RULE_CONTROL` body may now carry `RuleIdentity` — `label` (≤64 chars, control characters stripped, whitespace collapsed, required to equal its own sanitized form), `targetType` (`APP`, `WEBSITE`, `BATCH`), `itemCount` (present exactly for `BATCH`, `1..2000`) and `batchLabel` (a sanitized batch name on member rows). Schema v2 accepts v1 rows unchanged; a v1 row still delivers as a nameless verb. The constructor rejects any raw URL path, newline or oversized string, so the one free-text field ADR #196 warned about exists only in its bounded form.
6. **Every recipient surface names the target.** The receiver persists the identity beside the feed row; the activity feed renders the verb with the label (and the batch name for a member); `PartnerNotifications.notifyRuleChanged` posts a per-pair tray notification naming the app, site or batch and opening that exact partner's activity; the partner tab gains a dedicated Rules page listing the rule history. Blocked-attempt activity text appends `"|batchName"` so an attempt alert says which batch the blocked app belongs to.
7. **One partner per batch.** The batch editor offers the live roster (same source as the SOS recipient dialog) plus "No partner"; a batch assigned to a partner is told as one object to that partner only. A mixed batch (only reachable by mutating rows outside the editor) is told per pair with that pair's own member count.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *One journal row per member* — N notifications and N feed rows for one user action, the exact noise the owner asked to remove; rejected. (b) *A dedicated `rule_batches` table with a membership join* — duplicates the data the rules already carry and adds a second write path to keep transactionally consistent; denormalized membership is the simpler correct form; rejected. (c) *Send raw package names and URLs as the label* — unbounded, path-bearing strings leak more than the owner sees and reopen the ADR #196 hole; a sanitized display label is the bounded substitute; rejected. (d) *A batch-wide immutable UUID derived from members* — changes whenever membership changes, so feed dedupe would treat edits as new batches; the persisted `batch_id` is stable; rejected. (e) *Freeze the member list on the wire* — a batch already sends its size; sending identities of all members duplicates the per-member rows and grows without bound; rejected.

**Verified (JVM, 2026-10-31).** `BatchRuleLifecycleTest` **7/7**: a five-member batch assigns every member and journals one batch row (batch UUID, `BATCH`, name, `itemCount = 5`, no parent label); an unassigned batch journals nothing and a mixed batch tells A and B their own counts (3 and 2) while the unassigned member is never routed; pause/resume/delete produce exactly `CREATED, DISABLED, UPDATED, DELETED` as single batch rows in order and the deleted row still states the size; a resumed batch drops a lapsed `blockExpiresAt` so the sweep cannot re-disable it; `removeBatchPartner` writes one `UNASSIGNED` batch row and a repeat call writes nothing; a whole-batch lapse journals one batch `EXPIRED` with size 3 while a partial lapse journals the lapsed member with `batchLabel = "Study"` and the live member keeps blocking; the pending-delivery count reads one row for the batch and refuses to count a pair this device is not live with. Wire contract tests pin identity round-trip, v1 compatibility, the sanitizer and the unknown-key rejection. Full JVM suite **263 classes / 2,404 tests / 0 failures / 0 errors / 0 skipped** (2026-10-31). **Device-leg status (2026-10-31, honest):** the on-phone run started at 15:15 and hit a real user-facing crash in the app-label pipeline (`SnapshotApplyConflictException`, three fatal exceptions 15:18–15:24) whenever the batch picker was opened; the crash is fixed under ADR #251 and JVM-proven, but the fixed build has not yet been on hardware. The batch two-device legs did not run — the second device was returned to its owner, and the first device left with the owner later the same day. They are recorded as blocked, not passed; the emulator cannot stand in for pairing (attestation wall). **AVD follow-up (2026-10-31):** the local half of this ADR ran end-to-end on MyExodus_API37 with the fixed build — batch "QA temp batch" created from the picker (2 apps), the Rules page listed it by name with both member rows and "Blocked now", the delete dialog named the batch and its item count, and the delete restored the empty baseline with no residue.

**Consequences / honest limits.** (1) `itemCount` is the member count at the moment of the verb, not a live roster: the partner's feed is a log of what happened, not a synced copy of the rules. (2) The batch name is user-authored text; it is sanitized and length-bounded, but the partner will see whatever name the owner chooses, including personal details — that is the owner's intentional choice and is stated in the editor copy. (3) Member rows keep carrying a `batchLabel`, so an app that is removed from a batch later was still named as belonging to it in the events that already happened — a historical fact, not a mutable one. (4) Batches are created through the editor and are not renamed or re-membered in bulk; editing a member individually re-journals that member, not the batch, which is deliberate (the batch object itself did not change). (5) The partner's Rules page filters to the existing relationship window; rows older than that window are not shown even though the journal itself retains for 30 days. (6) A v1 APK can still receive v2 rows only as its shipped parser allows — the schema is additive and v1 readers ignore the added keys, so no downgrade path breaks.

## #250 — Delivery Guarantee: The Queue Itself Is the "Waiting to Be Sent" Surface, a Force-Prompt Retry, and a DEBUG Receive Breadcrumb (owner report, 2026-10-31)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented and JVM-verified 2026-10-31. Extends ADR #227 (delivered rows are deleted) and ADR #216 (signing heal).

**Revision 2026-11-05:** Decisions 1–3 (the journal-count banner, its "Send now" action and the forced authenticated prompt) are removed by owner ruling — the subject must not be able to suppress a partner notification, and every unlock already warms the signing window. The DEBUG receive breadcrumb (Decision 4) remains. See ADR #259.

**Context.** The owner reported the real failure mode behind "my partner never heard about the rule change": a rule mutation journals its row in the same transaction as the write, but delivery needs the sealed chain, and sealing stops at a cold signing window (screen locked / key not warmed). Nothing on the Rules page said a change was still queued, and the only retry was a global partner "Check now" elsewhere in the app. A cancelled signing prompt looked identical to a delivered change. There was also no way to prove on a device where a rule event stopped — received, stored, or notified — without reading code or attaching a debugger.

**Decision.**

1. **Pending work is read from the journal, never guessed.** `PartnerEventJournalDao.observePendingRuleChanges(pairIds)` counts journal rows whose `route_pair_id` is one of this device's live pairs; `route_pair_id` is non-null exactly for rule rows (ADR #226/#227), so no category predicate is needed. The Rules page collects it as a Flow and shows a banner when the count is non-zero.
2. **The banner clears only on real delivery.** A delivered row is deleted by the pass (ADR #227), Room re-emits, and the count drops — there is no "sent" flag the UI could set optimistically. Pairs this device is not live with are excluded so orphaned rows from a previous pairing never pin the banner on.
3. **"Send now" is the existing authenticated heal, forced.** The action calls `healBlockedPartnerSigning(forcePrompt = true)` (warm check → authenticated prompt → re-run the pass), bypassing the 10-minute prompt cooldown that background attempts obey. A cancelled prompt is "not now", not an error: the rows stay journaled and the banner stays up. Success re-runs the sync, which deletes the rows through the normal path.
4. **A DEBUG-only breadcrumb records the receive path.** `RuleDeliveryTrace` appends one line per stage — `received` (with change and resolved label), `stored` (with the receiver's boolean) and `notify` (`posted`, `failed <ExceptionClass>`, or `skipped no-enrollment`) — to `files/rule-delivery.log`, readable with `adb shell run-as com.example.myexodus cat files/rule-delivery.log`. It is a no-op unless `BuildConfig.DEBUG`, rotates at 256 KiB to `.1`, and an I/O failure logs and drops the line rather than interfering with receipt.
5. **No new delivery queue.** The sealed chain and the outbox already own retry and idempotency; the banner is a view over the journal work items, not a second tracker. A crash between sealing and row deletion leaves the row pending and the next pass resolves it as a duplicate and deletes it (ADR #227), which the count reflects correctly.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *A "last send failed" flag persisted in preferences* — a second state that can disagree with the actual queue; rejected. (b) *Prompt for signing on every blocked mutation* — prompt fatigue and a lock-screen loop at exactly the moment the device is cold; an explicit surface is the smaller interruption; rejected. (c) *Count every journal row* — includes rows routed to pairs this device no longer has; the banner would stick forever; rejected. (d) *An always-on trace file* — writes free-text labels into release builds and grows without a consumer; DEBUG-only keeps the evidence where it is needed; rejected. (e) *A notification when the queue is non-empty* — the Rules page surface is where the action was made; a tray notification for an unsent local change is noise; rejected.

**Verified (JVM, 2026-10-31).** `RuleDeliveryTraceTest` **3/3** (Robolectric): one single line per stage with the ISO instant, pair id and event id; a disabled trace writes nothing; rotation keeps the running file bounded to one line and moves the previous line to `.1`. `BatchRuleLifecycleTest.pendingRuleRows_feedTheDeliveryBanner_andClearWhenDelivered` proves the count contract: 0 on a quiet queue, 1 for a two-member batch's single row, 0 for a pair this device is not live with, and 0 immediately after the row is deleted by delivery. Full JVM suite **263 classes / 2,404 tests / 0 failures / 0 errors / 0 skipped** (2026-10-31); Android lint passes 0 errors / 0 warnings (run alone per ADR #208). **Device-leg status (2026-10-31, honest):** blocked by the same departure that blocked #249 — the 15:15–15:30 on-phone run hit the app-label crash (ADR #251) before a rule change could be driven from the owner's phone to the partner device, and the partner device was then returned to its owner. The receive breadcrumb is JVM-verified only; no device trace has been captured yet.

**Consequences / honest limits.** (1) The count is journal rows, not partner devices; one row is one event addressed to one pair, and a partner with two devices still gets one row. (2) The banner does not say which partner or which change — the journal row carries that, and the Rules page is an owner surface, not a per-row outbox viewer; a per-row UI is deferred until the owner asks for it. (3) "Send now" needs the device online for the pass to do anything; offline, the prompt succeeds and the rows remain queued, which the unchanged banner states honestly. (4) The trace exists only in debug builds and only proves the receive half on the partner device; the send half is proven by the row disappearing. (5) The banner appears on the Rules page, so a user who makes a change and never revisits the page still sees nothing — the partner-facing feed and the partner's Rules page remain the only proof the partner actually saw it.

## #251 — App-Label Publishing Retries a Losing Snapshot Apply Instead of Crashing the App (device crash found by the #249/#250 on-phone run, 2026-10-31)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented and JVM-verified 2026-10-31. Fixes a fatal crash first observed on the X6532 during the batch-creation on-phone run. Supersedes nothing; the crash did not exist before the background label pipeline (task #13/#75).

**Context.** The batch picker resolves a display name for every rule candidate off the main thread: `cachedAppLabel` and `preloadAppLabels` resolve through `PackageManager` on `Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(4)` and publish into the shared `mutableStateMapOf` label cache so rows recompose. Each publish was done with `Snapshot.withMutableSnapshot { labelCache[target] = label }`, whose `apply()` throws `SnapshotApplyConflictException` when a background apply loses the race with the main thread's composition apply. Compose's documented contract is not to throw but to retry; the call sites did not. Result on hardware: opening the batch editor's app picker pushed enough label loads that three consecutive runs died with `FATAL EXCEPTION: DefaultDispatcher-worker-N … SnapshotApplyConflictException` at `AppLabelsKt$cachedAppLabel$3.invokeSuspend(AppLabels.kt:171)` (15:18:40, 15:22:31, 15:24:08), after which ActivityManager logged "crashed too many times, killing! Reason: crashed quickly" and every subsequent dialog-confirm tap landed back on the launcher. The picker crash — not a UI-driving mistake — is what blocked the #249/#250 device legs.

**Decision.**

1. **One publish helper with the documented retry loop.** `publishLabel(target, label)` takes a mutable snapshot, enters it, and applies it; on `SnapshotApplyResult.Failure` it disposes the failed snapshot (`result.snapshot.dispose()`) and retries from a fresh snapshot until the apply succeeds. Every producer — the background loader (`cachedAppLabel`), the bulk warm-up (`preloadAppLabels`), and the synchronous seed used by block-fire paths (`seedAppLabel`) — goes through this one helper.
2. **Retry is safe here because each publish is a single-key write.** A lost race re-applies the same value for the same key; there is no read-modify-write on shared state to re-derive, so an unbounded retry cannot livelock on the map's contents — only on frame scheduling, which is bounded in practice by composition frequency.
3. **The composition-path read seam flushes apply notifications.** `peekAppLabel` (test-only) now calls `Snapshot.sendApplyNotifications()` before reading: a plain JVM thread has no `GlobalSnapshotManager` advancing the global snapshot after a background apply, so without the flush a test read could throw "Reading a state that was created after the snapshot was taken". Production reads stay on the composition path, where the global snapshot is advanced each frame.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Hop the write to the main thread* — turns every label resolution into a main-thread post and defeats the task #13 fix's purpose (the 4000-rule ANR); also breaks the Robolectric polling contract; rejected. (b) *Use a `ConcurrentHashMap` plus per-row `mutableStateOf`* — changes the reactivity model, needs one state object per row, and re-introduces per-row allocation where the shared map already recomposes readers; rejected. (c) *Catch the conflict and drop the label* — the row silently keeps showing the raw identifier forever; worse than the crash it hides; rejected. (d) *Retry loop at each call site* — three copies of the same loop; one helper is the correct DRY boundary; rejected.

**Verified (JVM, 2026-10-31).** `AppLabelsTest` **7/7** including the new `publishesNeverThrowWhileTheMainThreadKeepsApplyingSnapshots`, which runs a churning applier thread (take/enter/apply in a loop) against eight worker threads doing 200 publishes each — no publish throws and all keys land. The class was re-run **three consecutive times** with `--rerun-tasks` (green each time); the full JVM gate is **263 classes / 2,405 tests / 0 failures / 0 errors / 0 skipped**, and Android lint ran alone over the final tree: **"No issues found." (0 errors / 0 warnings)**. The API detail that first caused a compile error is pinned: in Compose runtime 1.12.0 `SnapshotApplyResult.Failure` exposes `snapshot` and `check()`, not `dispose()` — verified by `javap` on the runtime AAR and androidx-main `Snapshot.kt`.

**Verified on the API-37 AVD (2026-10-31).** With both handsets away, the fixed APK was installed on MyExodus_API37 (`install -r`): the batch app-picker opened **4× in cold processes + 1× warm** with the process alive every cycle, zero FATAL entries in the crash buffer, and real app labels resolved (Chrome/Calendar/…) — the phone crash does not reproduce post-fix. The full batch lifecycle then ran on the same build: name "QA temp batch", 2 apps, create → the Rules page lists the batch (2 items, both rows "Blocked now"), delete → the dialog names the batch and its 2 rules, confirm → the empty baseline is restored with no residue.

**Consequences / honest limits.** (1) **Hardware re-proof still pending.** The AVD smoke proves the picker no longer crashes on a real Android 37 runtime, but the physical picker flow must still be re-run (`install -r`, open batch editor → Add apps, open/close the picker a few times, then a real batch create/delete with no residue) before the release can be called physically proven. The emulator cannot complete pairing against the **live** backend (TEE attestation), so this AVD pass could smoke the picker only. *(Revision 2026-11-01: the two-AVD local rig does complete the production ceremony — `ATTESTATION_STUB=1` stubs only the verifier — and the two-device legs ran there; see deep-review-2026-10-22.md §LOCAL-RIG. The physical phone re-check above still stands.)* (2) The retry loop can spin under adversarial snapshot churn; it is bounded by composition frequency on a real device and the churn test exercises the worst case the JVM can produce. (3) `seedAppLabel` now retries instead of throwing, which changes a fatal path into a delay — a contended seed still lands, it just may take several applies.

## #252 — Plan Rows Feed the Orphan-Sweep Candidate Set, Making ADR #193 §9's Prune Real (rig finding, 2026-11-01)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented and JVM-verified 2026-11-01; device-verified end-to-end on the two-AVD local rig the same day. Implements the contract ADR #193 §9 already stated; does not change it.

**Context.** ADR #193 §9 promises that `sweepActivity` prunes plans whose pair no longer exists, alongside the activity rows for the same orphans — "unpairing therefore does not leave a plan pointing at a counterpart that can never receive it", with the stated limit that pruning happens on the next sweep, not at unpair. The implementation did not fully keep that promise: the orphan candidate set was built only from `projectedPairIds() + linkedPairIds() + consentPairIds()`, so a pair represented *solely* by a `partner_plan` row was invisible to the sweep. Rig evidence: after an unpair → re-pair cycle (same deterministic pair id `FTJv…_HPTf…`, epoch 6), device A still listed the test plan "Deep Link leg 71 B2" while device B's author copy had been wiped with its app data. Bilateral deletion (`BilateralDeletion.shredPair`) deliberately does not touch the encrypted rules DB, so if the sweep cannot name such a pair by its plan row, nothing else removes it. (In that particular residue the pair also held monitoring rows, so the device cycle demonstrates the symptom but does not isolate the cause; the JVM test below does.)

**Decision.**

1. **`PartnerPlanDao.pairedPairIds()`** — `SELECT DISTINCT pair_id FROM partner_plan WHERE pair_id IS NOT NULL`; private plans (null pair) are never candidates, matching their contract that they never leave the device.
2. **The sweep union includes it**: `orphans = (projectedPairIds + linkedPairIds + consentPairIds + pairedPairIds).distinct().filterNot { it in enrolledPairIds }`, feeding the existing `deleteForPairs(orphans)`. No new deletion path, no new timing: the same next-pass repair the ADR already described.
3. **`shredPair` still does not delete plans.** Pruning at unpair time would couple BilateralDeletion to the rules DB and duplicate the sweep; the ADR's stated limit (next sweep) is the designed behavior, not a gap.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Delete plan rows inside `shredPair`* — couples the accountability store's shred to the encrypted rules DB and changes the documented timing; rejected. (b) *A separate plan-specific sweep* — a second pruning loop with the same orphan semantics; duplication for no gain; rejected. (c) *Cascade at the DAO level via a foreign key* — the plan row and the enrollment live in different databases (rules DB vs accountability DB), so no FK is possible across them; rejected.

**Verified (JVM, 2026-11-01).** `PartnerSyncCoordinatorTest.sweep_prunesPlansOfAGonePair_keepingLiveAndPrivatePlans` — with one live enrollment, a gone pair's plan is deleted, the live pair's plan survives, and a private (null-pair) plan survives; class **55/55**. Room accepts the non-null `List<String>` return because the query's `IS NOT NULL` predicate removes the column's nullability (compile-verified by the same build).

**Verified on the two-AVD local rig (2026-11-01, honest split).** After installing the fix, a full unpair → re-pair cycle left both Plans pages at "No plans yet."; A's post-unpair pass logged `MyExodusPartnerSync: pruning activity state for 1 unpaired pair(s)` and the residue row was gone after re-pair. That pair also held monitoring rows, so the device run proves the end-to-end purge, not the plan-only candidate source in isolation — that isolation is the JVM test's job. Emulator `pairing_tokens` ended at 0 docs; pair doc `status=active`, epoch 6.

**Consequences / honest limits.** (1) Plans still prune on the next sync pass, never at the instant of unpairing (unchanged #193 §9 limit). (2) A plan is deleted whether the retired pair was cleanly unpaired or left otherwise-orphaned by a wiped peer — both cases mean no counterpart can receive progress. (3) Recipients have no in-app delete for a partner-authored plan (author-owned edit/delete only); that is a product surface question tracked separately, not a pruning gap.

## #253 — A Reach-Out Is a One-Way Named Signal: the "I'm here" Reply Is Removed (owner ruling 2026-11-01)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented 2026-11-01. Supersedes the 2026-10-03 card contract (plan §8.16 / partner-sos-dpia.md "three responses") for the reply half only; the ack path and FR-10 are unchanged.

**Context.** The recipient card shipped with an "I'm here" reply button (plan §6.9/§8.16: "I'm here" and X both acknowledge). On the physical two-phone rig (X6532 ↔ X6532C, 2026-11-01) the owner rejected the interaction outright: *"I could use a check-in doesn't need partner to respond 'I'm here' — why did you add that? It's for partner to know who it is exactly that needs me to reach out to them via call or WhatsApp or text… check-in is a signal informing partner who needs a check-in, just that, like a pop up. You did too much."* Two defects followed from the same misreading: (a) the card offered an in-app answer the feature never wanted, and (b) the card's title was generic — "Your partner reached out" — so the one thing the signal exists to say, *who* needs the check-in, was missing.

**Decision.**

1. **No reply action.** The "I'm here" button is deleted (layout and string). X remains the sole action: it acknowledges §6.9's fetched batch, retires the tray entry, and the card clears through the listener. The acknowledgement is local bookkeeping — FR-10 still guarantees the sender never learns of it — so removing the button removes a response affordance, not delivery state.
2. **The card names the sender.** The title is "`<partner label>` could use a check-in" (generic "Your partner could use a check-in" when the roster read yields no label — the same never-wrong-name fallback rule as the pinned card and D16's notification). The sender's message, when one was written, still renders in its bubble. The partner acts by calling or messaging that person, outside the app.
3. **Pop-up semantics stay.** The heads-up notification (D14 HIGH channel, D16 named body) is the pop-up; the Home card is the durable view. Nothing about delivery changed.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Keep "I'm here" as a soft ack* — the owner's point is that an answer implies an exchange the feature must not promise; the sender is never told, so the button could only ever be a local dismiss dressed as a reply; rejected. (b) *Replace it with contact deep links (call/WhatsApp/SMS)* — scope the owner did not ask for; the signal's job is to say who, not to place the call; not built (available as a later ask). (c) *Keep the generic title and add a name line* — doubles the type in the card's strongest position and leaves the title saying nothing; naming the title directly is the smallest change that answers "who needs me"; rejected.

**Verified.** JVM: `:app:compileDebugKotlin` green after the removal; full unit suite **2,417 tests / 0 failures / 0 skipped** (2026-11-01). Instrumented pins updated: `NudgeHomeSurfaceInstrumentedTest.card_rendersNamedFromItsFetchedData_andX_Acknowledges` asserts the named title ("Sam could use a check-in"), the absence of a reply action (the string no longer exists, so the old assertion is deleted, not muted) and the single X acknowledgement; `card_rendersTheSendersMessage` asserts the named title plus the message bubble. **Device-verified on the two-phone rig (X6532 ↔ X6532C, 2026-11-01):** X6532C showed "X6532 could use a check-in — Sent just now" with X as the only action; X cleared it; a fresh send from X6532 arrived again as the named card, confirming the sender→Firestore→recipient loop on the shipped build.

**Consequences / honest limits.** (1) The card is dismissible but not answerable — by design; if the partner wants to respond, they leave the app. (2) The 2026-10-03 §12.3 bullet 7 ("I'm here acks all fetched pending nudges") is retired in `partner-sos-mapping.md` §5 with this ADR; the X path still proves the batch ack. (3) `NudgeInboxViewModel.acknowledge()` keeps its name and single-call shape — the repository contract did not change.

## #254 — A Block Whose App Is Uninstalled Is Hidden, Not Deleted (owner request 2026-11-01)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented and device-verified on X6532 with a stub app 2026-11-01. Defines the Rules page's behavior for APP-target rules whose package is no longer installed.

**Context.** The owner asked that a block survive its app being uninstalled: hide the row instead of deleting it, adjust the counts, and bring it back active when the app is reinstalled. Before this change `RulesScreen` rendered every stored rule regardless of installation state, so a rule for an uninstalled app appeared as a normal row whose toggle enforced nothing — the row looked live while the app it named did not exist.

**Decision.**

1. **Visibility filter, not deletion.** `visibleRules(rules, installedPackages)` drops only APP-target rules whose package is not currently launchable (`launchablePackages(context)`); website rules are always shown because they have no installable artifact. Nothing is removed from storage, so the rule's schedule, limit, partner assignment and enabled state survive untouched.
2. **Reactive re-query.** `rememberInstalledAppPackages()` listens for `ACTION_PACKAGE_ADDED` / `ACTION_PACKAGE_REMOVED` and re-reads the launchable set, so the row disappears and returns live without leaving the page.
3. **Counts follow the filter.** The page's loaded total drives a hidden-only notice (`rules_hidden_uninstalled` plurals: "1 block is saved but hidden — its app isn't installed. It returns when you reinstall the app.") computed as `loaded.rules.size − shownRules.size`; Home's "Blocks" count reflects the shown rules for the same reason (device-measured 5 → 4 → 5 across the uninstall/reinstall cycle).
4. **Return is active, not reset.** A reinstalled app's rule comes back exactly as saved — enabled state, mode and partner line intact — because the row was never mutated.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Delete the rule on uninstall and rely on the journal* — simpler, but loses the user's intent exactly when a reinstall is likely; the owner explicitly rejected it. (b) *Show the row disabled with a "not installed" tag* — keeps a dead row in the main list and still needs the restored-on-reinstall path; the notice communicates the same fact with less noise; rejected. (c) *Filter in the DAO* — the database has no `PackageManager`; installation state is a UI-environment fact and belongs at the screen boundary; rejected.

**Verified (X6532, 2026-11-01, stub app `com.myexodus.uninstallproof`).** Created a rule for the stub → uninstalled the stub via `pm uninstall` → the row vanished live and the notice appeared ("2 blocks are saved but hidden…" — the second hidden block was pre-existing), Home Blocks 5 → 4 → reinstalled the stub → the row returned ACTIVE (Always on / Blocked now / toggle ON), the notice dropped to 1, Home Blocks back to 5 → uninstalled again → Blocks 4. The editor reopened with the unchanged rule (Block all day ON), proving state retention. Test rule and stub were removed after the proof. **JVM:** `InstalledAppsTest` pins the shared predicate — an APP rule is hidden only while its package is absent and returns unchanged when installed, a WEBSITE rule never depends on installation state, and a hidden rule leaves the visible set while surviving ones keep their order; the full unit suite passes 2,417 tests / 0 failures / 0 skipped (2026-11-01).

**Consequences / honest limits.** (1) The hidden notice is the only trace on the Rules page; a user who only looks at Home sees the adjusted count without the explanation — accepted because Home is a summary surface. (2) A package that is installed but has no launchable activity is treated as uninstalled; that matches the actionable definition (a block cannot be triggered by an app the user cannot open). (3) The partner is told nothing when a rule disappears from view — they still see it as a rule in their feed; the block is genuinely still enforced the moment the app returns, so no disclosure is warranted.

## #255 — Home Partner Cards Share One Visual Grammar: Glyph, Sender + Age, Message Bubble (owner request 2026-11-01)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented and device-verified on X6532C 2026-11-01. Visual contract for the two partner-authored cards on Home (reach-out and pinned message); it changes presentation only — transport, acknowledgements and FR-10 are untouched.

**Context.** After the reach-out card was rebuilt around a glyph + named title + message bubble (ADR #253), the pinned "From X" card was still the old flat layout — a bare header line, verbatim text as plain body copy, and no visual marker that the content is partner-authored. On the phone the two cards sat one above the other with unrelated shapes, and the owner rejected the inconsistency: the message card had never been part of the redesign pass.

**Decision.**

1. **One grammar for both cards.** Each card is: a 44 dp circular glyph tinted by the card's accent, a two-line header (titleMedium SemiBold title over a labelSmall relative age), and, when present, the author's words in a `surface` bubble with `bodyLarge` text. The message card uses the chat glyph on the `secondary` accent; the reach-out keeps the handshake on `primary`.
2. **Emphasis order on Home is fixed:** reach-out (`primaryContainer`, strongest) > pinned message (`secondaryContainer`) > operational cards (`surfaceContainerLow`). Both partner cards share `shapes.large` and 20 dp padding so they read as the same family.
3. **The pager moves to a footer.** When several partners have pinned messages, prev/position/next render as a centered footer row instead of inline with the title, which gave the sender's name room to breathe and stopped the title from clipping beside two 48 dp targets.
4. **The age line is the message's own send time**, moved under the sender name — the same honesty rule as before (a stale message must not read as new), now visually paired with the sender it belongs to.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Restyle the message card like a chat bubble with an avatar image* — no avatars exist in the roster and inventing one per partner adds an identity surface the app does not have; a chat glyph carries the authorship signal without it; rejected. (b) *Keep the message card quiet and unlike the reach-out* — the owner's point is precisely that partner-authored content should read as one family; rejected. (c) *Retain the inline pager* — measured tight next to a full sender name on the 720 px phone; the footer costs one row only when a second sender exists; rejected.

**Verified on X6532C (2026-11-01).** With the pairing live, X6532 sent "Thinking of you today." through the composer; X6532C's Home rendered the redesigned card under the reach-out card: chat glyph in the accent circle, "From X6532" + "Sent just now" stacked, and the message in its own white bubble. The reach-out card above it kept its own glyph/named-title grammar, so the two-family consistency is visible in one screenshot. Build installed on both phones via `install -r`; JVM suite 2,417 tests / 0 failures / 0 skipped.

**Consequences / honest limits.** (1) The card still pages across pairs only when more than one partner has a pinned message; the footer is absent otherwise, so the common single-partner case stays two rows shorter than the old inline pager. (2) A very long message expands the bubble; there is no truncation — partner text is content and is never abbreviated. (3) The glyph circle is decorative (`contentDescription = null`); TalkBack reads the card as the sender title, age and message, which carry the full meaning.

## #256 — Production-Test Fix Pass: Record Every Wall, Lock Both Strict Rows at Once, Bound the Send Legs, Present the Wall Instantly, and Make Rule Updates Send Themselves

**Status:** Accepted; implemented 2026-11-02. Six defects from `production-test-2026-11-01.md`, each with its own verification chain. JVM suite **262 classes / 2,406 tests / 0 failures / 0 errors / 0 skipped** (2026-11-02). Device legs that need a paired second phone or attached hardware are recorded as BLOCKED, never passed.

**Revision 2026-11-05:** Item 5's `forcePrompt = true` path is removed — automatic delivery never raises a device-key prompt or shows the pending-delivery banner (item 7's resources are deleted too). A cold signing window leaves the row journaled for the next warm pass. See ADR #259.

**Context.** The pre-production sweep found contract-level defects, not cosmetic ones: Path A blocks were never written to the attempt log (the ADR's "every enforced block is recorded durably" invariant was broken on the primary enforcement path), a strict-mode write was observable to one row up to 60 s late (a one-tap bypass of the 24 h lock that also disabled protection), the composer could hang on "Sending…" for ~40 minutes with every dismiss disabled, rule updates waited on a manual "Send now" the owner called a defect, and BlockerActivity inherited the platform open animation so the wall slid in over 273 ms while the blocked app stayed visible.

**Decision.**

1. **Every wall-showing site records.** FGS detection (`EnforcementForegroundService.kt:739`), FGS Path B daily wall (`:986`), a11y app decision (`BlockerAccessibilityService.kt:472`), a11y daily wall (`:764`), URL block (`:1087`). The old design recorded only where the FGS saw a *new launch*, which Path A eviction makes structurally impossible. Double-record protection lives in one place: `AttemptLogDao.countRecentBlocked(rule, target, sinceMs, nowMs)` — the two enforcement paths that observe one wall collapse into one attempt.
2. **The dedupe window is bounded on both sides.** `occurred_at_epoch_millis BETWEEN :sinceMs AND :nowMs`. A row stamped after the query's `now` is clock skew, not this launch; the original open-ended lower bound let one future-dated row (the AVD had once run a month ahead) suppress attempts forever. Regression `AttemptLogTest.recordBlocked_ignoresFutureDatedRows`.
3. **Both strict rows read one observable value.** `strictOn` is hoisted into `SettingsScreen` composition and passed to `StrictModeToggleRow` and `EnhancedModeToggleRow`, so the Strict write recomposes the Enhanced row in the same frame. The 24 h contract (`canDisable()` false while cooldown runs) is now enforced from the moment the switch moves.
4. **Every send leg is bounded.** `messageSendOutcome` wraps `authorize`, `runPass` and `stillPending` in `withTimeoutOrNull(45 s)`. Only an explicit `false` from `stillPending` reports SENT; a timed-out leg is honestly QUEUED because the journal-first emit guarantees a later pass. Tests: `anAuthorizationThatNeverReturnsIsSavedWithinTheTimeout`, `aQueueThatNeverAnswersNeverClaimsSent`.
5. **Rule updates send themselves.** `RulesRepository.journaled()` fires `PartnerSyncSignals.ruleChangesJournaled` + `enqueuePartnerSyncNow`; `MainActivity` collects under `repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED)` → `healBlockedPartnerSigning(forcePrompt = true)`, which bypasses the 10-minute prompt cooldown while a warm signer delivers silently. A stalled delivery remains surfaced and retryable. The manual banner is no longer the delivery gate.
6. **The wall has no window animation.** `Theme.MyExodus.Blocker` with `android:windowAnimationStyle = Animation.MyExodus.None` (all four activity animations `@null`) on `BlockerActivity`, matching the accessibility-overlay host's explicit `windowAnimations = 0`. Two enforcement hosts must transition identically.
7. **Pending-delivery body is a plurals resource**, so one queued update reads "to send it to your partner" rather than "them".
8. **The Recovery ticker reads the live session list every tick.** A captured `tracked` list rewrote removed sessions back into composition each second, so an individually cancelled timer's row survived on screen until the tab was re-entered; the tick now maps over the current `liveSessions` (found by the owner's multi-session acceptance test, 2026-11-02).

**Verified.** Attempt recording, device (AVD `emulator-5554`, 2026-11-02): `14:31:09.681 I/MyExodusAttempts: attempt logged: outcome=BLOCKED rule=9b871cf3-8fde-4dad-b43e-c3318367a008 target=com.android.chrome`, Home Chrome 10 → 11 attempts. Strict lock, device (AVD): cooldown expired via `strict_mode.xml`, process restarted, Strict ON → within ~1–2 s `Enhanced Mode enabled="false"`, `Strict Mode enabled="false"`, both with "inactive controls unlock in 23h 59m"; the 01:42 bypass tap is no longer accepted. Wall animation, structural (AVD): `dumpsys window` → `wanim=0x7f120005`, `aapt2` resolves it to `Animation.MyExodus.None` with `0x010100b8–bb = @null`. Composer, JVM only. Auto-send, JVM/build only. Full suite 2,406 tests green; Android lint run alone per ADR #208. Friction acceptance, device (AVD, 2026-11-02): Chrome 203:27 and Photos 240:50 coexisted as separately named cards with independent overrides; Photos' "End the block" logged `15:48:45.491 … outcome=OVERRIDE rule=e7b1a61c… target=…photos`, snapshot v64, the Photos row vanished within 2 s on the same screen, and Chrome kept counting (203:27 → 203:06). The pre-fix build left `Blocked: Photos` on screen for 4+ minutes (145:38 → 144:57) while Chrome ran — the regression this item closes.

**Consequences / honest limits.** (1) The 5 s dedupe window is a judgment call between poll skew and deliberate re-opens — unchanged from the original design, now two-sided. (2) Composer and auto-send device legs are BLOCKED (a paired second phone is required); the composer's Cancel button still disables while sending, so the worst case is a bounded 45 s wait rather than the observed trap — whether the button should also stay live is a UX question for hardware verification. (3) Hardware frame-level re-capture of the wall is BLOCKED (both phones detached); the AVD's animation scales are a harness artifact and cannot prove the absence of the slide. (4) The Strict fix shares composition state rather than making `StrictModeManager` itself observable; if a second surface ever renders the strict state, this must become an observable deadline. (5) The ticker fix changes composition wiring only — the per-rule store/DAO contract and its tests are unchanged.

## #257 — Attempt Events Carry the Sender's App Label, so a Partner Without the App Sees a Name, Not a Package Id (owner report 2026-11-02)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented 2026-11-02. Sender and payload halves JVM-verified; the receiver display leg on X6532C is BLOCKED (installing a new build there needs per-action owner permission, and the borrowed phone was left on the previous build).

**Context.** On the two-phone rig (X6532 sender ↔ X6532C receiver), the partner's "Recent activity" feed showed three blocked rows for `com.ichi2.anki` — the raw package id — even though the same partner's Rules & blocks page correctly named the rule "AnkiDroid". Cause: the attempt wire text (`blocked:<pkg>` / `override:<pkg>` + optional `|<batch>`) never carried a display name, and `rememberAppLabel` can only resolve labels for apps installed on the viewing phone; the rule-identity events do carry a sanitized label (`RuleIdentity`), which is why the rule rows were named. The owner asked whether the partner pages update accurately — they do (attempts in Partner → How they're doing → Recent activity; rule lifecycle in Rules & blocks), but this row degraded to an id.

**Decision.**

1. **The label rides the activity payload, not the text.** `EventPayload.appLabel` (optional CBOR key `al`, ≤80 chars) travels beside `text`. The wire text format is unchanged, so every parser and every stored history row keeps parsing exactly as before.
2. **The sender resolves it with the same seam rule identity uses** — `resolveRuleLabel("APP", attempt.blockedTarget)` wired to `appLabel(context, target)` — sanitized via `AccountabilityEventWire.sanitizeRuleLabel` and omitted when it would add nothing (blank or identical to the package id).
3. **The receiver prefers its own installed label, then the sender's.** `alertOf` copies the payload label onto `PartnerAlert.AppActivity`; `AlertRow` uses the locally resolved name when this phone has the app, and falls back to the sender's label only when the local resolve returns the package id unchanged.
4. **Backward compatibility is structural.** The chain-body decoder rejects unknown keys, but the mailbox payload decoder ignores them; the new key therefore never invalidates an event for an older receiver, which keeps today's package-id display. Unset fields are not encoded, so existing payload bytes are untouched.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Append the label to the attempt text (`<pkg>|<label>`)* — ambiguous with the existing `<pkg>|<batch>` suffix and old receivers would render the label as a batch; rejected. (b) *Add a key to the chained `AccountabilityEvent` body* — `AccountabilityEventWire.decodeOrNull` rejects any unknown key, so an older receiver would drop the entire attempt event, not just the label; rejected. (c) *Receiver-side package-id heuristics* (`com.ichi2.anki` → "Anki") — unreliable (`com.instagram.android` → "android") and dishonest; rejected.

**Verified (JVM, 2026-11-02).** `EventPayloadTest.appLabel_roundTrips_andStaysAbsentWhenUnset` (codec round-trip; unset stays absent), `PartnerPresentationTest.alertOf_carriesTheSenderAppLabel_andOldPayloadsStayNull` (receiver attaches the label; old payloads null), `PartnerSyncCoordinatorTest.blockedAttempt_carriesTheSenderResolvedAppLabel` (real crypto: the delivered, decrypted attempt payload carries `text = blocked:com.instagram.android` and `appLabel = Instagram`). Full-suite and lint results are recorded in the session's final report.

**Consequences / honest limits.** (1) The receiver-display leg is JVM-proven only; seeing "AnkiDroid" in place of `com.ichi2.anki` on a physical feed requires the new build on the viewing phone — X6532C stays on the previous build until the owner authorizes an install there. (2) Until both phones run the new build, the sender's label is simply ignored and the feed behaves exactly as before — additive, never a regression. (3) The label is the sender's locale, not the receiver's; that matches the rule-identity convention (the partner sees the name the owner sees).

## #258 — A Partner-Notification Tap Opens the Subpage It Concerns, for the Named Partner (owner ask 2026-11-02)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented 2026-11-02. JVM-verified. **Closed by owner 2026-11-05:** the rule-update tap was exercised on hardware by the owner (notification → Rules & blocks), and the Requests mapping is accepted on its JVM proof — no production entry point calls `ApprovalFlow.requestApproval` (only `ApprovalFlowTest` and `PartnerApprovalInstrumentedTest`), so no user-reachable request notification exists to tap. Re-open only if a requester UI ships.

**Context.** Partner notifications already named their partner and opened the Partner tab (`EXTRA_OPEN_PARTNER`, ADR #193/#250 line of work), but every event type landed on the Partner hub — one tap short of the surface that actually lists it. The owner asked for the tap to open "the relevant page … the new activity bit", while still switching to the partner the notification names when several partners exist.

**Decision.**

1. **The tap carries a subpage id.** A new `MainActivity.EXTRA_OPEN_PARTNER_VIEW` carries one of the Partner tab's existing `VIEW_*` ids; `PartnerScreen` sets its `view` state from it in the same effect that applies `EXTRA_OPEN_PARTNER`.
2. **Per-post mapping.** Activity-family events (attempts, streak updates, relapse, milestone, coaching step, motivational message) → Activity; rule/batch lifecycle → Rules & blocks; disable-approval request and decision → Requests. A published plan keeps its existing `EXTRA_OPEN_PLAN` landing, and `pairDeepLinkView` gives the plan precedence because both extras ride the same tap.
3. **The pairing selection and subpage move together.** Both extras are consumed in one effect, and consumption nulls the state so a later tap of the same notification produces a real state change and navigates again.
4. **No collision change.** Every post already owns a distinct data-URI identity per (category, pair); the new extra is written into that same PendingIntent and cannot rewrite another post's tap.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Land on the hub and let the owner tap the tile* — rejected by the owner's ask; it is the defect. (b) *Encode the subpage in the notification tag or id* — the tag is the tray identity (replace-in-place per pair); overloading it would break the multi-partner coexistence contract. (c) *Add a URI deep-link router* — the app's notification routing is extras-based and every surface already uses the same extras pattern; a router would be new machinery for one extra field.

**Verified (JVM, 2026-11-02).** `PartnerDeepLinkViewTest.pairDeepLink_opensTheSubpage_theNotificationNamed` and `pairDeepLink_planWinsOverTheSubpageExtra`; `PartnerNotificationsTest` — milestone/activity tap carries `VIEW_ACTIVITY`, every rule-change verb carries `VIEW_RULES`, approval requests carry `VIEW_REQUESTS`, all alongside the existing pair extra.

**Consequences / honest limits.** (1) The Activity and Rules mappings are device-proven; the Requests mapping is JVM-proven only and accepted as such (owner ruling 2026-11-05) until a requester UI ships. (2) The subpage ids are UI-layer constants referenced by the notification layer (the same cross-layer precedent as `EXTRA_OPEN_PLAN` and the tab constants); no new module boundary. (3) A stale PendingIntent from a pre-#258 build still opens the hub — additive, never a regression.

## #259 — Partner Delivery Is Promptless: the Pending-Update Banner and the Forced Signing Prompt Are Removed (owner ruling 2026-11-05)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented 2026-11-05. Supersedes ADR #250 (banner, "Send now", prompt cooldown) and the prompt half of ADR #256 item 5. Warm-window delivery and cold-window deferral both PASSED on hardware (2026-11-05).

**Context.** ADR #250/#256 made a rule change deliver on its own, but kept two subject-controlled cancellation points: the cold-window BiometricPrompt (dismiss it and the row stays queued) and the "1 update waiting to be sent / Send now" banner. Either one lets the subject suppress a notification the partner is owed. The owner ruled 2026-11-05 that no prompt, banner or confirm step may stand on the automatic path. What only the user can supply is device authentication — and every unlock already supplies it, re-opening the §8.1 900 s signing window.

**Decision.**

1. **One automatic delivery path.** `PartnerSyncSignals.ruleChangesJournaled` and `signingNeeded` both collect into `deliverQueuedPartnerEvents()` in `MainActivity`: one pass; if it reports `signingBlocked` and the window is warm, one retry pass; otherwise return. No prompt, no cooldown, no banner.
2. **A cold window is a delay, not a loss.** Rows are journaled in the rule write's transaction and deleted only by a delivered pass; the periodic 15-minute worker and the next foreground signal re-run the same pass after any device authentication.
3. **Explicit user-initiated integrity actions still prompt.** Check now, pairing/unpair, message send and backup keep `signWithAuthPrompt`. The automatic path never calls it.
4. **The pending-delivery surface is deleted, not hidden.** `PendingDeliveryBanner`, `onRetryRuleDelivery` (MainActivity → AppShell → RulesScreen), the `rules_pending_delivery_*` resources and `PARTNER_SIGNING_PROMPT_COOLDOWN_MILLIS` are removed. The journal remains the queue of record.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Keep the banner as status only* — rejected: it still advertises a tap the owner wants gone, and the queue is already durable without it. (b) *Warm the key silently in the background* — impossible: the platform requires user authentication; a cold pass can only defer. (c) *Let the partner pull the update on demand* — rejected: the row and the key are both on the subject device, so this adds a second trigger surface without changing the authentication requirement. (d) *Send rule events unsigned* — rejected by ADR #42/#196: the relay stays content-blind and signing is the E2EE boundary, not a UX toggle.

**Verified (2026-11-05).** Warm-window automatic delivery on the 16:22 build (banner and prompt removed): after X6532's 16:32 install, a partner-shared rule created on X6532 reached X6532C automatically — X6532C receipt `13:37:56.011Z … change=CREATED label=AI Gallery` → `stored=true` → `notify=posted` — with no Send-now tap and no device-key sheet; the partner Rules page named "AI Gallery · Rule created". Cold-window deferral PASSED the same day on the 17:24 build: a batch created at 17:49:27 hit an expired keystore auth token (`signingBlocked=true`; keystore2 `matching auth token is expired` → `KEY_USER_NOT_AUTHENTICATED`), showed **no sheet or banner**, and stayed journaled; after a normal owner fingerprint unlock (17:54) the next foreground pass delivered it with no interaction (`drainedCount=1`, partner posted "You were added as accountability partner on the QA check batch (2 items)"). `PartnerNotificationsTest` green, Android lint clean (run alone per ADR #208), `assembleDebug` green, APK installed on both phones.

**Consequences / honest limits.** (1) Delivery latency is bounded by the next device authentication or the 15-minute worker, not by a tap. (2) The owner loses the "what's queued" view; the partner's receipt remains the proof of delivery. (3) The subject can still suppress by uninstalling or force-stopping the app — a platform limit outside this ruling (the XOS OneKeyClean case is a real instance; see `xos-onekeyclean-force-stop-2026-11-05.md`). (4) A permanently cold device never delivers; the queue retains the rows rather than lying about delivery.

## #260 — Attempt, Override and Recovery Alerts Carry the Rule Alerts' Named Shape (owner ruling 2026-11-05)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented 2026-11-05. JVM-verified; partner display PASSED on X6532C (17:24 build installed 17:35:35).

**Context.** The owner reported two notification families that did not read alike: "Rule update from Musila — AI Gallery was deleted" for rule changes, but only "New activity from Musila" for a blocked attempt. The typed activity branch in `PartnerNotifications.notifyPartnerEvent` had no rich copy and fell through to the generic named text. The wire already carries everything needed: `blocked:<pkg>[|<batch>]`, `override:<pkg>[|<batch>]`, `recovery:<technique>:<outcome>`, plus the sender's `appLabel` (ADR #257).

**Decision.** `activityCopy` parses the wire text with the same `parseActivityText` the feed uses and renders: the title names the partner and the act ("tried to open a blocked app" / "used an override" / "logged a recovery step"); the body names the app (local label, else the sender's `appLabel`, else the package id) and the batch when present; the recovery body names the localized technique and outcome. Undecodable text keeps the generic named copy. Lockscreen public copy stays generic (FR-13). No wire change; batch attempts already append `|batchName` (ADR #249).

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Put the app in the title ("Musila tried to open AI Gallery")* — rejected: both families would then have different title grammars, and long app/batch names would be truncated in the tray; the rule family's person+act title is the consistent shape. (b) *Resolve the app label at send time and put it on the wire* — rejected: ADR #196's bounded allowlist and ADR #257 already send the label as a bounded field, and the receiver may know a better local label. (c) *Leave activity generic and rely on the tap* — rejected by the owner: the notification itself must say what happened.

**Verified (JVM, 2026-11-05).** `PartnerNotificationsTest` — `blockedAttempt_namesTheActTheAppAndTheBatch` (title, in-batch body and the lockscreen-public fallback), `blockedAttemptOutsideABatch_hasNoBatchTail`, `overrideAttempt_namesTheOverride`, `recoveryStep_names_theTechniqueAndOutcome` — green. Android lint clean (alone per ADR #208); `assembleDebug` green; APK (50,544,300 bytes, built 17:24) installed on X6532 at 17:25:20 and on X6532C at 17:35:35. **Partner display PASSED:** a blocked AI Gallery launch at 17:41:33 produced "Musila tried to open a blocked app" / "AI Gallery was blocked." in X6532C's notification record on the 17:24 build.

**Consequences / honest limits.** (1) Both notification families now name the person and the act, and the body names the target. (2) An app not installed on the partner phone falls back to the sender's label, then the package id (ADR #257). (3) A batch name is user-authored text and is rendered verbatim in the body (already sanitized on the wire, ADR #249). (4) The lockscreen deliberately stays generic, so the specific target is visible only after unlock (FR-13).

## #261 — The First Run Teaches the Capabilities Before It Asks for Permissions (owner request 2026-11-06)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented and device-verified 2026-11-06 (X6532). Replaces the missing-mechanism gate of plan §8 Step 7; the wizard itself is unchanged and still owns the permission steps.

**Context.** The V1 first run opened directly on the permission wizard, and only when Usage Access, Accessibility or overlay was actually missing; an install evaluated as complete never saw any onboarding. The owner's 2026-11-06 request: a first-run journey that teaches the three capabilities (app blocking, home-screen widget, partner accountability), then offers an account or a deliberate guest choice, and only then asks for permissions, at a visual bar that does not read as generated. The existing wizard, the Settings account form and the shared back affordance were all reusable; the missing piece was the journey around them.

**Decision.**

1. **One entry, one gate.** `ui/setup/OnboardingScreen.kt` replaces `SetupScreen` as the first-run entry in `MainActivity`; the gate is `!setupStateStore.setupSeen` alone. The "evaluate the required mechanisms and record seen if already complete" branch is gone: the journey teaches what the app does, so it runs once per install regardless of permission state. `SetupScreen` is reused unchanged as the journey's last page, so permission behavior, deep links, on-resume status reads and skip rules cannot drift.
2. **Journey order.** Slide 1 blocking, slide 2 daily rhythm (streak and widget), slide 3 accountability; then the account page (create, sign in, Google, or "Continue without an account"); then the five permission steps. Skip on the slides jumps to the account page. Back is the shared `BackRow` in the top bar for every page past the first (ADR #90); `SetupScreen`'s own `BackHandler` steps the wizard first, and at its first step the outer handler returns to the account page (ADR #91 behavior preserved). An `AnimatedContent` slide carries the journey between pages.
3. **The account form is the Settings one.** `AccountAuthForm` was extracted from `AccountPane.kt`'s `GuestAccount` into an `internal` composable and is called by both Settings → Account and onboarding, so validation and failure copy cannot diverge. Onboarding passes `prepared = false` (a fresh install links in place). A signed-in state renders a confirmation page the user leaves with Next; no auto-advance, so returning from the wizard via Back cannot bounce forward again.
4. **Visual system.** Photographic hero cards (282 dp, 28 dp radius, gold kicker rule and uppercase label over a bottom scrim), Fraunces `headlineLarge` (36/42 sp) for slide headlines, Work Sans body, segmented wizard progress (gold current, teal passed), gold Solar glyphs tinted at runtime. No tinted plates behind icons.
5. **Assets are sourced, licensed and recorded.** Photos from the Unsplash CDN; icons from Iconify's Solar set (480 Design, CC BY 4.0) converted to 384 px PNGs in `drawable-nodpi` and tinted by `Icon(painter, tint)`. CC BY requires credit, so Settings → About carries a quiet credits line naming Solar, its license and Unsplash. Exact files, source ids and licenses: `app/docs/MyExodus Build & Dependencies.md` → "Assets and licenses".

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Keep the missing-mechanism gate and show slides only when permissions were needed* — rejected: the journey is the product introduction, not a permission preamble; an install with permissions pre-granted still benefits from it. (b) *Auto-advance when sign-in succeeds* — rejected: Back from the wizard would land on the account page and immediately advance again, and it hides the confirmation that backup now exists. (c) *Require an account before the wizard* — rejected by the product rule that the app works without one; the guest continue is explicit and the hint names where to create an account later. (d) *A second account form for onboarding* — rejected: copy and validation drift. (e) *Tinted icon plates, a coloured box behind each icon* — rejected by the owner as the generated look being replaced.

**Verified (2026-11-06).** X6532, `install -r`, `setup_state.xml` deleted to force first run: slides 1–3 render; slide 1 has no back and a Skip; every later page carries `BackRow`; back from slide 2 returns to slide 1, back from the account page returns to slide 3; the wizard's five steps render with their own header, Back, Skip and Continue; finishing writes `setup_state.xml` (`seen=true`), leaves onboarding and lands on Home. Light and dark both rendered. JVM suite 2,416 tests / 0 failures, Android lint alone clean (ADR #208), `assembleDebug` green. Slide 2's photo was replaced after the owner rejected two earlier images as unrelated to the page; the marked-calendar image is the shipped one, device-verified.

**Consequences / honest limits.** (1) An install that finishes the journey and later revokes a permission is never shown it again; Settings rows and the degraded banner own those fixes (unchanged from the old gate). (2) The partner photo shows identifiable people without a model release (Unsplash does not provide one); it is used as non-endorsing editorial art in a free, direct-distribution app, so do not place advertising or implied-endorsement copy around it. (3) The three bundled photos add about 322 KB to the APK. (4) Slide copy is fixed English in `strings.xml` like the rest of the app; there is no dynamic personalization.

## #262 — Appearance Is a Stored Setting: System, Light or Dark (owner request 2026-11-06)

**Status:** Accepted; implemented and device-verified 2026-11-06 (X6532, both modes).

**Context.** The app followed the system dark-mode setting at its Compose roots. The owner asked for a Settings control. A per-activity `isSystemInDarkTheme()` call cannot honour a user override, and each activity had its own theme root, so the setting had to be readable everywhere and changeable live in the main activity.

**Decision.** `settings/ThemeSettings.kt` stores `ThemeMode.SYSTEM|LIGHT|DARK` in `SharedPreferences("theme_settings")`, default `SYSTEM`. `ui/theme/Theme.kt` gains `rememberDarkTheme(mode)`, the single ThemeMode→Boolean conversion, used by `MainActivity`, `BlockerActivity` and `WidgetActionActivity`. `MainActivity` hoists `themeMode` state at the theme root and passes it plus the setter (which writes the store and the state together) through `AppShell` to Settings, so a change repaints the whole app in the same frame. Settings' Appearance row shows the current mode as its subtitle and opens a radio dialog (`Modifier.selectable(role = Role.RadioButton)`).

**Alternatives considered.** (a) *Per-activity state only* — rejected: the store is the durable copy and three activities must agree. (b) *DataStore* — rejected: one enum over the project's established SharedPreferences stores; no async read is needed at startup. (c) *A three-way switch instead of a dialog* — rejected: the row pattern already carries a subtitle, and a dialog states the three named choices explicitly and accessibly.

**Verified (2026-11-06).** Settings row opens the dialog; choosing Light repaints immediately and survives relaunch; choosing Dark likewise; the block screen and widget action activities read the same stored mode on creation. JVM suite and lint green with the rest of the 2026-11-06 work.

**Consequences / honest limits.** (1) A mode change applies to another already-alive activity at its next creation, not while it is backgrounded. (2) The stored mode is read synchronously at startup, one small SharedPreferences read.

## #263 — App Icons Leave the Composition Path: the Rules Scroll Lag (owner report 2026-11-06)

**Status:** Accepted; root cause read from source; fixed, JVM-verified and device-measured on a populated list 2026-11-06 (X6532).

**Context.** The owner reported the Rules page scrolling badly and asked for the root cause. `AppMark` resolved every row's icon inside composition: `remember(packageName, sizePx) { packageManager.getApplicationIcon(pkg).toBitmap(sizePx, sizePx) }`. `remember` only avoids recomputation on recomposition of the same node; each row entering the viewport is a new node, so scrolling ran a binder call into the system package manager plus a bitmap decode on the main thread, for every icon, every time it came back into view. Labels had already been moved off this path (ADR #251); icons had not.
